#6736. If You Didn’t Already Think CrossFit Was a Cult, This Book Will Convince You

CrossFit could easily hold the distinction of being the most popular—and certainly the most universally recognized—fitness movement ever. At its peak, the company, founded in 2000, boasted over 15,000 affiliate gyms, or “boxes,” in more than 150 countries and was enlisting nearly 50,000 coaches each year. Somewhere along the line, to many people (including my mom), the word CrossFit became synonymous for working out.

But you may have noticed that people don’t talk as much about CrossFit nowadays as they used to. Following an assorted variety of allegations against its mercurial founder Greg Glassman in 2020, and the tragic and seemingly avoidable death of an athlete at the 2024 CrossFit Games, the company has been gradually losing its chalky grip on popular culture.

But the storytelling around CrossFit’s rise and fall is anything but done and dusted, as I learned while reading Calum Marsh’s new book, The Glass Box—a fascinating, staggeringly detailed account of not only CrossFit’s rocket-propelled rise and spectacular flame-out, as told by insider sources including Glassman himself, but a trove of previously unshared anecdotes that make it hard to put down.

A few days after the book’s late-October release, I spoke to Marsh about airing CrossFit’s dirtiest laundry, how the cultishness of CrossFit has spread to other fitness crazes, and why an old-fashioned barbell snatch is the ultimate kryptonite for the modern performative male.

Calum Marsh: The first 50 people I spoke to were basically warning me off the subject, telling me that it was going to be an uphill battle and that if the people that I was writing about were unhappy with how I wrote about them, they would criticize me or attempt to defame me. They have a long history, which I've chronicled in the book, of creating campaigns of bad will towards their critics. They are really experienced at mobilizing the internet and mobilizing social media in order to discredit people that they consider critics or, as I sometimes frame it in the book, heretics.

But, on the other hand, I knew that I was going to be approaching this from a journalistically rigorous perspective, and that it was going to be an account of what actually happened, from the people who were involved. It wasn't going to be a book about my opinion or my personal take on CrossFit. So I felt quite secure that the things I was writing in the book were the best possible representation of the truth.

There's been a lot of focus on some of the more, shall we say, sordid details. There was an article in the New York Post that basically pulled all that out and made the book seem like it was some scandalous hit piece. That's not the book I tried to write, and it's not the book I think I wrote. The book I wrote is a very fair, even-handed assessment of a man and the business that he created. It includes true stories about his behavior that may not be the most flattering, and it includes, I think, testament to the brilliance of what he created and all of the great things that he did.

It's been amusing to see the reception somewhat split among some hardcore CrossFitters. They're upset because they think it's a takedown of Greg Glassman that's biased against him. And then other critics think that I'm way too generous to him, or way too flattering. Someone said I was too affectionate towards him. It's funny to me that two different people can read it and have polar opposite views. But hopefully that means that it's just objective.

It’s something that is always mentioned in relation to CrossFit. There’s actually another book that came out while I was writing my book, called The Cult of CrossFit by Katie Rose Hejtmanek. It's an academic study of the history and sociology of cults, and how CrossFit is a cult by definition. I thought that was really illuminating. There are a lot of similarities that go beyond all the joking, and there are a lot of things about the cult-like nature of CrossFit that have made it intoxicating for some people, and maybe painful in other ways as well.

The thing that struck me was how a lot of people, especially earlier CrossFit enthusiasts or devotees, talked to me about the difficulty they had leaving CrossFit. Greg has said many times, and will still say, that they weren't a cult because you could leave at any time. And I always found that to be a fairly unconvincing argument, because many cults say the same thing. A lot of CrossFitters had this experience where they felt like they had really close friends—sometimes even family members or partners—who essentially excommunicated them—cut them off, iced them out, however you want to phrase it—after they either left CrossFit or spoke out against CrossFit. That, to me, is the strongest cult-like parallel.

It really wasn't. I had heard from people that Glassman was generous, and so I knew stories about him spending lavishly on dinners, for example. But it all seemed pretty much within the realm of normal spending for someone who's massively wealthy. It wasn't until I started speaking to people who were more familiar with CrossFit’s finances when I started to learn about the degree to which the spending was out of control. The amount of money they spent relative to what they earned is the most shocking thing to me, because it's not like they were spending that much money while wildly out-earning it. They were almost spending more than they were making. And they were not slowing their spending when the earning slowed. That, to me, as a business reporter, is very, very interesting, because you start to wonder how they let that happen. Was no one there to say, ‘Hey, we need to pump the brakes a little bit?’ As it turned out, there really wasn't.

A lot of people had this reckoning in 2020 after [Glassman’s George Floyd tweet] and some of the accusations that came out about Glassman then. A lot of gyms deaffiliated from CrossFit, and Greg, of course, stepped down and sold the company. I personally know many people who had a kind of personal reckoning with their level of comfort in supporting the company. But I think that was, at least in some cases, answered by Greg's departure.

Others went through this process of divorcing themselves from the CrossFit identity as a brand, but continuing to practice CrossFit as a methodology. There are thousands of gyms all over the world that are CrossFit gyms in all but name. They probably call themselves cross-training or functional fitness now, but if you go in, they still have a Rogue rig, they still have wall balls, they still do snatches—everything you'd expect to see if you walked into a CrossFit gym. The people there are still CrossFitters at heart. They've still given themselves over to the transformative power of the methodology that Greg Glassman invented. But they are no longer endorsing or supporting the brand or the company at large.

I would be willing to bet that if you walked into any CrossFit gym in North America and asked them what the difference is between when Glassman was in charge and when corporate private equity took charge, they wouldn’t know that even happened. The average person, who just goes to CrossFit to get fit and doesn't follow the CrossFit news and isn't obsessed with CrossFit Games, would not have any idea. And this is partly a consequence of the fact that the affiliate model is so loose.

I first started going to a box in 2018. I was doing personal training with someone at what I didn't realize was even a CrossFit box. I was doing that personal training for probably about a year before I realized I was doing CrossFit, and then I started doing classes in 2019.

I do! In fact, I coached a CrossFit class earlier this morning.

Yeah. Well, they don't allow you to call it a certification with the one I have. They're very clear about that language. But I do have my CrossFit Level 1 certificate. I did the course and passed the test.

I think that part of it is just the nature of fandom. If you become enthusiastic about something, you want to identify as an enthusiast, and that means wearing the T-shirt. I went to a Bob Dylan concert on the weekend. I bought a Bob Dylan hat. It's just part of the experience of being a fan of something. I think Hyrox is super interesting, because it does have a lot of cult-like similarities with CrossFit. But the really toxic side—the side that's a bit more nefarious, that involves really giving your life over to it—I haven't seen with Hyrox, at least yet. I feel like there's something missing at the center, possibly the guru figure that Greg Glassman was for CrossFit. Hyrox doesn't really have that. So maybe that missing ingredient has stopped it from being as intense. But, on the whole, I think it's just this level of fandom that is baked into everything in culture now.

There's a journalist named Hannah Singleton, who writes about fitness a lot. She recently wrote a piece about how athleticism is the new flex for people, and I think that’s sort of the direction we're moving in. For example, Hyrox. It's in the same vein as running a marathon or doing an ultra race, where it's an achievement that you can brandish. You can put it on your LinkedIn. You can say that you've done this and that. Maybe it's on your resume. You're almost putting up points on your scoreboard. And I think that we're probably going to find either more events along those lines, where it's something that you can be proud of because it's so difficult, or a system in which you can have an overall fitness score. I think people really want to show that they put in the work. They want to impress people with how fit they are. In the same way that people who are into running are obsessively posting about their marathon time or their 10K time, and those milestones are universally understood in running—everyone knows how impressive it is to run a sub-10-minute 5K or a sub-three-hour marathon—the fitness equivalent of that, I think, is still coming.

This is one of the things I find interesting in light of CrossFit—and I know that some people are going to think this is not true—but I really do think CrossFit, or let’s say functional fitness, is an antidote to this whole performative thing. It's so hard that it's humbling. You can’t really show up and pretend you did it. You cannot performatively do barbell snatches. If you see someone on social media snatching heavy, it's because they've worked at it for hundreds, if not thousands, of hours, and because they're really strong, really mobile, and really fit. And I say this as someone who both has a copy of Infinite Jest on my bookshelf and wears Satisfy.

You can ‘perform’ your sport of choice by posting about it, but things like snatches or ring muscle ups are so physically demanding that it kind of cuts through that bullshit. And I think that we're probably going to increasingly value things that we know on-site are authentic, because there's an authenticity built into it. There's no shortcut there. And that authenticity will become more and more valuable.

#6735. Meet the Cast and Characters of ‘The Good Daughter’

Excited to watch The Good Daughter on Peacock, but didn’t read the book by Karin Slaughter that it’s based on? Here’s everything you need to know about the cast and characters of The Good Daughter, without giving anything away. Well, maybe one thing. There’s a character who only shows up in one timeline for a reason. You might guess why, but I’m going to spoil it later just so we’re all on the same page.

First of all, no... this series is not connected to The Good Wife, The Good Fight, The Good Doctor, or The Good Place. As mentioned above, The Good Daughter is an adaptation of a bestselling novel that was published in 2017. The story is about two adult sisters who are reunited after a violent attack in their Georgia hometown brings up memories of the murder that tore them apart.

Slaughter herself adapted her book for the screen, penning the teleplays for all six episodes. Steph Green stepped in to direct and executive produce the series. As for the cast, here’s who you’ll see on The Good Daughter and who they play.

Sam, quintessential eldest daughter, left town and became a patent lawyer.

Rose Byrne’s breakout role in Hollywood was as a titular bridesmaid in Bridesmaids, though she had already appeared in films like Sunshine, Troy and Marie Antoinette at that time. That same year, 2011, she played Moira MacTaggert in X-Men: First Class and would reprise that role in a later film. She’s still best known for comedies, however, like Spy, Neighbors, and Neighbors 2 as well as horror movies like 28 Weeks Later and the Insidious films. Television-wise, Byrne played Gloria Steinem in Mrs. America and starred in both Physical and Platonic. She was nominated for an Academy Award for If I Had Legs I’d Kick You and a Tony Award for Fallen Angels.

Meanwhile, younger sister Charlie stayed in town and became a defense attorney.

Meghann Fahy was one of the breakout stars of The White Lotus’ second season, though she also hadn’t come out of nowhere. Prior to the HBO seires, Meghann made her Broadway debut in the Pulitzer Prize winning musical Next to Normal as an understudy and replacement for the character Natalie, then played Sutton on The Bold Type, and also acted in 83 episodes of One Life To Live. Since the HBO series, she has starred in the movie Drop and the Netflix series Sirens as well as The Perfect Couple and Your Monster. She is also a two time Emmy nominee, for both Sirens and The White Lotus.

Audrey Grace Marshall and Drew Cheek play Young Sam and Charlie

Flashbacks show who the sisters were before the trauma that shaped them.

Before The Good Daughter, Audrey Grace Marshall played Young Cassie on The Flight Attendent and was supposed to be in the Buffy the Vampire Slayer reboot. She did play Viv in the Fairly Oddparents live action reboot thing in 2022. Drew Cheek, on the other hand, has only one previous credit: a movie called F*ck Valentine’s Day.

Rusty is the sisters’ father and a former defense attorney with a reputation.

Brendan Gleeson is an Academy Award-nominated and Emmy Award-winning actor. He won the latter for playing Winston Churchill in the miniseries Into the Storm. You’ve seen him in the Harry Potter films, Braveheart, 28 Days Later, Gangs of New York, Troy, In Bruges, Edge of Tomorrow, Paddington 2, and The Banshees of Inisherin. Brendan has not done much television, but did lead Mr. Mercedes from 2017 to 2019, appear in the 2022 series State of the Union, and play Silvermane in Spider-Noir.

Lenore is Rusty’s secretary and the girls’ surrogate mother figure.

This is Harper Steele’s first ever professional acting credit. She is an Emmy winning comedy writer who worked at Saturday Night Live for 13 years and was a head writer for four of those years. Her other screenwriting credits include Eurovision Song Contest: The Story of Fire Saga and The Spoils of Babylon. Harper recently appeared with Will Ferrell in the road trip buddy documentary Will & Harper about their friendship before and after she came out as transgender.

Kelly is a suspect in a school shooting who Charlie chooses to represent.

Shayna Bernardo’s previous credits before The Good Daughter include the Lifetime movie Don’t Sweat The Small Stuff, an episode of Doom Patrol, and the horror movie Sorority Secrets.

Judith is an English teacher at a local middle school.

Paula Malcomson is probably best known for playing Katniss’ understandably checked-out mother Asterid Everdeen in The Hunger Games movies. She was also a series regular on the Battlestar Galactica prequel series Caprica, as well as Deadwood and Ray Donovan. She also recurred on Sons of Anarchy.

Huck is a teacher at the local middle school with a grudge against Rusty.

Jake McDorman is best known for leading roles in shows like Quintuplets, Greek, Manhattan Love Story, Limitless, Murphy Brown, The Right Stuff, Mrs. Davis and Dopesick. He also had a recurring role on Shameless. Movie-wise, you’ve seen him in Happiest Season, Lady Bird, American Sniper, Live Free Or Die Hard, Bring It On: All Or Nothing, and, of course, Aquamarine.

Olivia Williams plays Harriet ‘Gamma’ Quinn

First of all, no, this Harriet was the sisters’ mother and a genius physicist. Spoiler alert: she was violently murdered when Sam and Charlie were young girls.

You may know Olivia Williams from films like Rushmore, the 2003 Peter Pan, Anna Karenina, and An Education. Fun fact: Williams played Moira MacTaggert in X-Men: The Last Stand. She played Camilla Parker-Bowles on two seasons of The Crown and her other television credits include Dollhouse, Manhattan, and Dune: Prophecy. She’s also a prolific stage actress and starred as Nurse Ratched in One Flew Over The Cuckoo’s Nest at London’s Old Vic Theatre this year.

Ben is Charlie’s estranged husband, and also a lawyer. So many lawyers!

Michael Dorman is an Australian actor with many starring roles on television to his name, including shows like Wonderland, For All Mankind, Patriot, Territory, and Joe Pickett. His film credits include Leigh Whannell’s The Invisible Man and Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Men Tell No Tales.

#6733. Understated, Earthy, and Endlessly Wearable: The Best Olive Green Polishes

The earthy shade adds an edge to fall manicures while still wearing like a neutral.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Like all nail polish colors, green has a vast spectrum, one that runs from electric neon to bold kelly to soft sage and all the way down to deep, moody olive. Of all the greens out there, olive sits in a quieter place. The hue is earthy and a little mysterious, somewhere between a vintage army jacket and an actual juicy olive. It’s a shade we love for fall, since it pairs so seamlessly with black, rich browns, burgundy, red, and, of course, cream.

Once reserved for the brave few, olive has now gone mainstream. Part of the appeal is how wearable it is, offering an unexpected twist without ever feeling too loud. It’s also soft and soothing to the eye, making it an easy shade to wear day after day.

If you’re new to the shade, the easiest way in is to treat it like a neutral. Try it with a camel coat and chunky knits when the weather turns, or a crisp white shirt for something fresh and unexpected. A creamy, opaque finish feels polished and modern, while a glossy jelly or a hint of shimmer adds depth in low light. However you wear it, olive looks effortlessly considered and adds an edge to your style.

Below, we’ve rounded up the best olive green nail polishes to shop now.

A personal favorite, Elia is a muted olive green that looks rich from the very first stroke. The opaque formula glides on evenly in a single swipe and dries to a soft gloss that lasts through daily wear.

Manucurist’s take on olive green feels a touch brighter. It sits beautifully on light and dark skin tones alike and delivers an opaque wash of color. Part of the “Green Flash” collection, it cures under an LED gel lamp and lasts for nearly 21 days.

Essie’s Totally Plaid is an olive green polish with a cream finish that delivers a gel-like shine and depth while still removing as easily as a regular polish. The formula applies smoothly in two coats, giving you rich, opaque color without the need for a UV lamp.

This deep and moody olive green shade is the epitome of effortless chic, pairing easily with everything from neutral knits to bold jewel tones.

Inspired by the lush landscapes of the Mediterranean, this olive green evokes a lighter take on the olive color spectrum. It’s a tad brighter and slightly more yellow-toned, making it a great pick if you want a fresh, sunlit green this fall.

O.P.I’s Suzi is the chic olive green and wardrobe staple of the olive family. It’s a bit darker-toned, radiating earthy warmth and understated elegance. Plus, it’s fast-drying and offers up to seven days of wear.

For those seeking a little more sparkle, this olive green jelly is packed with large green holographic glitters that create a textured finish and catch the light with every movement, adding a spark of joy to your manicure.

Calming and serene, this moss green shade is part of the “Campground Collection”, a four-shade assortment of earthy, comforting colors. Its buttery-smooth application matches the shade’s peaceful look.

This may not look like your average olive green at first glance, but that’s because it has taupe undertones. Once it’s on your nails, you’ll notice the hint of green was there all along. The result is a soft, grounded neutral that pairs effortlessly with cozy fall knits and earthy accessories.

This nail color may be named Pickle, but we see the olive in there. This tangy green with muted yellow undertones feels lively while remaining neutral enough to pair with everything in your wardrobe.

A true olive green, Extra Dirty brings rich, earthy depth to your nails. All you need is one to two coats for a creamy manicure worthy of a fall-season spotlight.

#6732. No More Franchises

No more prequels. No more reboots. No more Harry Styles in Eternals. No more of these 71 other things.

No more movie franchises. No more shared universes. No more post-credits scenes. No more prequels. No more reboots. No more eight-hour streaming TV spin-offs. No more slates and phases. No more multiverses. No more crossovers.

No more movies that are only made to greenlight sequels. No more sequels made for getting you to sign up for a streamer that raises its monthly subscription price every year. No more Easter eggs. No more winks. No more fourth-wall breaks. No more action scenes that halt the story and are clearly directed by the second unit. No more teasers that lead to nothing. No more Harry Styles in Eternals. No more watch guides and chronological order explainers and breakdowns. No more asking, “Is it canon?”

No more four-quadrant tentpoles. No more movies based on kids’ stuff that my niece can’t actually watch. No more Superman movies that are so violent and destructive that they trigger my 9/11 survivor mother’s PTSD. No more R-rated films that sell Funkos. No more movies that have to appeal to foreign markets and all the meemaws and pawpaws in Idaho. No more quippy dialogue where characters remark, “Well, THAT just happened!” No more irony. No more grotesque violence set to upbeat pop songs. No more characters looking into their own phones. No more thudding exposition, and especially not in the first ten minutes. No more “no more romances.”

No more hiring interesting up-and-coming filmmakers with buzz coming out of Sundance and Telluride because they’re cheap and have credibility to exploit. No more boxing in those same artistes because they’ll say “yes” to all marching orders. No more rejecting established auteurs with an interesting pitch and a desire to play in the sandbox because it doesn’t fit into next summer’s tentpole. No more prioritizing release dates over craft and the well-being of everyone working on it.

No more geriatric thespians putting on spandex because today’s adult moviegoer refuses to grow up themselves. No more casting red-hot twenty-somethings and locking them into seven-movie contracts. No more firing those actors because they got into legal trouble so the audience gets gaslit into forgetting there was ever something called The Kang Dynasty. No more international talent getting nothing cool to do; no more Hiroyuki Sanada getting killed by Jeremy Renner in Avengers: Endgame. No more casting directors deciding based on their exact amount of Instagram followers. No more content creators getting cameos.

No more Comic-Con. Or rather, no more making Comic-Con into Coachella. No more sleeping on the sidewalks for a seat in Hall H. No more buzzy presentations that turn art and myth into product reveals. No more “we’re doing it for the fans” and “one more thing.” No more Oscar winners promoting movies that don’t even have a script. No more actors lying through their teeth about how they read the original comics growing up. No more trailers that shake the room for those who slept outside to get in, and then get uploaded to YouTube while they collect their sleeping bags.

No more press screenings with ridiculous embargoes. No more taking away my phone and stuffing it into a zip pouch because of a spoiler that heaven forbid leaks on TikTok when millions were spent making it in front of IMAX cameras and a unionized crew; no more thinking any of this is tantamount to government secrets. No more influencers on red carpets. No more junket “interviews” that are just quizzes and games. No more gushing. No more unprofessionalism.

No more studios that exist only to adapt in-house IP. No more C-suites rambling about the lucrative potential in old cartoons and ‘90s comic books like old-timey oil barons surveying land. No more touting the box office of one movie as evidence why they oughta make a dozen more. No more pretenses about the power of stories in earnings calls with Merrill Lynch. No more forgetting, and not giving healthy royalties to, the comic book creators whose imaginations filled the calendar slate and fueled the stock prices in the first place.

No more toxic fandoms. No more powerful studios kowtowing to the loudest, most obnoxious YouTubers who make a living screaming into microphones in their basements. No more chuds who bemoan wokeness in whatever the latest remake/sequel they’re supposed to be mad about, and use AI-generated thumbnails of themselves making the dumbest fucking faces with cherry-picked unflattering screenshots of actresses who wouldn’t give them the time of day anyway. No more abusers, sex pests, misogynists, and racists anywhere, let alone in charge.

No more ten-year plans. No more stoking tuckered-out fans to drum up excitement about the next Batman or James Bond. No more actors keeping up action figure physiques while they wait years to hear about the sequel. No more taking characters and stories people have spent their lives escaping into for comfort and deforming them into numbers on a spreadsheet. No more vague bullshit like “It didn’t capture the zeitgeist” to explain why you’re arm-swiping everything off the table again. No more using the word “zeitgeist” if you cannot define it without ChatGPT.

No more cowardice. No more promises no one can keep. No more of this circus. No more.

#6731. Bill Hader Has Highbrow Taste in Children’s Movies

You can trust Bill Hader on movies. From gushing about John Ford and Akira Kurosawa in the Criterion Closet, to spoofing Errol Morris and D.A. Pennebaker in Documentary Now!, to creating, directing and starring in four seasons of HBO’s Barry—the SNL alum’s cinematic expertise is well-documented. Hader knows a thing or two about kids’ movies in particular, having lent his iconic voice to animated tentpoles like Inside Out and Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs. This week, you can hear Hader in The Cat in The Hat, a new adaptation of the 1957 Dr. Seuss classic, in which he voices the titular troublemaking feline.

Written and directed by Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja, this new iteration of the beloved children’s story is an inviting romp that is mischievous enough for kids, grounded enough for grown-ups, and teeming with gags and good nature that all can enjoy. The film is an ideal showcase for Hader’s gymnastic vocal talents, and also boasts Quinta Brunson, Matt Berry, and Giancarlo Esposito among its cast. (It’s a more family-friendly—though no less amusing—take on the Cat than when Hader last played the character, in a 2014 SNL sketch.)

A father to three daughters, Hader has seen it all—from Frozen and Tangled to Off Campus—and does his part, when possible, to pass down the classic films that were formative during his own childhood. “You don’t want to push it too hard,” he tells GQ on a recent call. “For every one I show them, there’s 10 that I start and they go, ‘Ugh, Dad, this is boring.’” The rest of us, however, are eager to take note. Below, Hader shares some of his favorite quote-unquote “kids’ movies” whose cinematic merit makes them a must-see at any age.

“When I was young, my dad told me that was a movie that he watched as a kid. I didn't grow up in a time when there were a lot of Westerns, but [for] my dad and uncles, that was all that was on TV.

What I was moved by was the relationship [between] Alan Ladd as Shane and this little boy [Brandon deWilde] enamored with a gunfighter. It has this heroic sensibility to it, but underneath was this honesty of, ‘You don't want that life,’ which I thought was interesting. To me, Van Heflin, the dad, was the cooler guy. So it upended those expectations of what the movie was going to be.

It has this ending where it's poignant and kind of sad, but I remember thinking, ‘Oh, that's good that that's what happens at the end of the story.’ It's a good coming-of-age story… It's kind of sneaky. You could see it on the face of it just being this cut-and-dry, Western-hero type of movie. But when you really think about it, even as a kid, I got a sense that there's a lot of depth to it.”

“Buster Keaton is one of my favorites, and that was one I showed my kids. I have three daughters. Now they're 17, 14, and 12, but at the time, they were very little. I'm a movie nerd, so I was gonna show them some silent movies, and I was like, ‘I know. Everybody's gonna roll their eyes at me for showing the kids silent movies. How pretentious.’ But they really responded to Buster Keaton, specifically Sherlock Jr. and Three Ages, his take on the movie Intolerance by D.W. Griffith. They just loved it, and it was fun getting to watch it through their eyes.

I recently took my youngest [to see] it at the Aero Theater in LA, and it still was great. To see a movie that was made over a hundred years ago still work on all [levels], like… it works better than most movies now. It's just very simple. [Keaton] wasn't some kind of auteur guy. He was a vaudeville comedian that was curious about filmmaking; what you could do with editing, what you could do with shots. And I think he ended up making the blueprint of how you shoot physical comedy and action. It’s pretty amazing.

What's interesting about some of those silent movies is that they don't really know what they're doing. The best stuff comes out of, ‘I don't know, I had this idea, let's figure it out in a really open, curious way.’ And in doing that, you invent the language.

Charlie Chaplin, too. [I’ve shown] them City Lights and The Circus and The Gold Rush. But they were really drawn to Buster Keaton, I think, because he was kind of dry and you didn't really know what he was thinking, and so you could put all your feelings onto him.”

“That's one that my parents showed me when I was a kid. It's a long movie, but it has so many crazy [moments] and a lot of physical comedy. I just love all those comedians in the movie. Every time someone pulls up, you're like, ‘Oh my God, it's Jonathan Winters. I love Phil Silvers. Oh my God, Spencer Tracy's in this movie!’ Dick Shawn is my personal favorite in that movie, the guy who's the real mama's boy.

It's kind of the one Stanley Kramer movie I like. Stanley Kramer movies tended to be, I don't know, a little sentimental, or overtly didactic or something, [but] this movie is just having a ton of fun. I have very fond memories of watching it with my parents and my grandparents. My dad was in town recently, and when I came home, he was watching it with my kids, and they were all laughing really hard and telling me scenes from it.

They really loved it, but [just like] with the silent movies, you don't want to push it too hard. For every [classic movie] I show them, there's 10 that I start and they go, ‘Ugh, Dad, this is boring,’ and I go, ‘Alright, we can watch Nobody Wants This or Off Campus.’”

“The Secret of NIMH was one that I loved as a kid, because it was ostensibly a kid's movie, but it was incredibly dark and disturbing. It has stuff that I still find really frightening. And I loved the mythology of it. As a kid, I liked the idea that in your backyard [there] could be this whole kingdom that you don't even know about.

There's specifically a shot in it with the crow, played by Dom DeLuise, and in the distance they see this cat. There's this long shot [of] this field, and then suddenly, just really quickly, you see this cat pop up and go back down under [as] it's trying to catch a bird or something. That shot had a huge effect on me. I thought, ‘Oh man, that's so terrifying.’

And then the story of the rats and NIMH, and they're all being tested on, and they fall into this abyss, and the whole ending where they're having this sword fight… I just thought it was fantastic. Everything was high stakes. And it wasn't Disney. I liked Disney, but Disney never went that dark.

Maybe not a lot of people agree with me, [but] I’m definitely someone [that] likes when something's scary for a kid, within reason. A lot of people are like, ‘No, no, no, they can't see that.’ And it's like, ‘No, let them see it. Get scared. That's good.’ I was happy that I was scared.

I'm sure if The Secret of NIMH came out now, they would have a whole room of executives going, ‘You can't have the owl with its head upside-down, turning around and with cobwebs all over him. It's just too scary.’ But for me, it scared me to death, and then I would keep watching it, and then it became less scary, and then I started to appreciate it. I think it's good for kids to be scared.”

“That movie came out when I was a freshman in high school. I got a job on the school paper, and my first job was to write a review of all the new movies, and it was the week that that movie came out. And so I remember I went with a notebook, I was writing my thoughts down, and then I ended up writing a pretty bad [review]. I liked [the movie] a lot, but my actual writing was terrible. The editors took it and rewrote it all.

But I loved it. I love Tim Burton. I loved the music in it, specifically the song that Catherine O'Hara sings as Sally; I think it's such a moving song. And Henry Selick’s direction in it is amazing. People always think Tim Burton made that movie. He didn't. It's Henry Selick. He spent every day there with those animators making that thing work.

I love the scope of it and how grand it is, from the beginning—that ‘This Is Halloween’ song, there's something almost operatic about it. And it's its own thing. The best stuff, to me, is always when the filmmakers and the writers [are] doing a thing that they want to see, and they trust an audience will get it.

When it came out, I remember it wasn't what it is now. It was kind of this weird oddity. And then as time went on… I remember moving to LA, and it was the 10-year anniversary of it, and they had a screening someplace, and I drove past all these people dressed like the characters, they had Jack Skellington t-shirts on and all that stuff, and I went, ‘Wow, that's crazy.’ Cause I was a huge fan of it, and had the soundtrack, and I absolutely adored that movie.

[Once] I had kids, it was one of the first movies I showed them, and they watched it every Halloween and every Christmas. My youngest daughter [recently] played Sally in a school play, and she got to sing that song, and so it was full circle. I got very emotional. I was like, ‘Oh my gosh, there she is, singing that song.’ And I had become friendly with Catherine O'Hara, and she passed away, and it was really… Yeah, I was a blubbering idiot when she started singing that song.”

#6728. These Cashmere Perfumes Are the Equivalent of Quiet Luxury in a Bottle

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Like wrapping yourself in a $400 cashmere sweater.

Not much compares to the snuggly feeling of a cashmere sweater against your skin, especially in cold weather. But if you don’t want to drop the $$$ on a whole cashmere wardrobe (if you do, make sure it’s Quince’s affordable cashmere), the next-best thing is a cashmere perfume.

Obviously, cashmere itself doesn’t have a smell. It’s a fabric, after all! But perfumers have found a way to capture that fluffy, cozy feeling through an accord called “cashmeran”—a blend of fragrance notes designed to evoke the soft, warm sensation of cashmere. Usually, that means it’s aldehydic (like fresh linens and cotton), warm, and a little bit powdery. But perfumes can still fall into the “cashmere” bucket even without a specific accord, usually using notes like creamy sandalwood and vanilla, warm amber and tonka bean, and even cloud-like musk and jasmine.

Smelling like cashmere has been my preferred way to embrace the homey feeling heading into winter. Nestling beside a fire, drinking a hot beverage, and wearing—you guessed it—a cashmere sweater has never been easier, so long as I have one of the below scents sprayed on. Keep reading for Cosmo editors’ top seven picks from brands like Byredo, Orebella, Phlur, and NOYZ.

"I always thought powdery perfumes would make me smell like a grandma, but either I'm inching toward grandma status or Angel Dust by Fugazzi is built different. It's powdery but not from heavy florals. Instead, the scent combines a mix of skin-like cashmere, musk, and amber. It's soft and reminiscent of the inside of a knitwear shop.”—BETH GILLETTE, BEAUTY EDITOR

“It’s hard to find a fragrance that straddles freshness and coziness, but this one does exactly that. Its moniker comes from a Brazilian Portuguese expression that describes the sensation of good vibes, happiness, and optimism, and it’s fair to say this perfume captures that sentiment perfectly. It oozes Brazilian warmth and sunniness and makes me want to book a trip to Rio.”—CELIA SHATZMAN, CONTRIBUTING WRITER

“I rely on body mists immediately after I get out of the shower to lightly fragrance my skin without feeling like too much. This one is my go-to right now (and the inspiration behind my current cashmere fragrance obsession). Even with nothing on (spicy!), my skin smells so toasty. It makes me want to immediately nuzzle into a plush robe.”—BG

“Unmute has a little bit of everything—juiciness from the plum note, spice from the cinnamon, musk from the amber, warmth from the sage, and sweetness from the pistachio—all wrapped in a cozy, comforting vanilla base. There’s something sexy and self-assured about the scent, without feeling too put-on or artificial.”—DANIELLE HARDMAN, CONTRIBUTING WRITER

“Milky perfumes are my favorite category of fragrance lately, and this does the lactonic, creamy fragrance so well. It’s not too sweet or cloying; instead, it leans on resinous amber, oak, and tonka bean to balance the scent. It’s like sitting by a fire, wrapped in the softest knits.”—BG

"I usually associate floral perfumes with spring and summer, but this one is undeniably perfect for cooler weather. Odéon is a smooth, rich rose scent, with a hefty dose of amber and cashmeran that gives it depth. It's inspired by Parisian cafe culture—and since I studied abroad there (hold the eyerolls), I feel qualified to say that this scent embodies the city’s romantic allure. It smells like window shopping in boutiques I can't afford and moonlit strolls along the Seine."—LAUREN GRUBER, COMMERCE EDITOR

“It’s an icon for a reason! Cashmere Mist is the OG of cashmere scents—it’s musky, powdery, and creamy, with soft woods and airy florals. My aunt was obsessed with this perfume in my youth, and I remember sneaking sprays of it whenever I wanted to feel like a ~sophisticated lady~”—BG

The animal welfare nonprofit shared a photo of Swift and Kelce with Kelce’s longtime agent, Mike Simon, and his wife Lisa Marie, who attended their wedding. The post revealed a new detail about the newlyweds’ request to guests in lieu of giving them gifts.

“Four beautiful people, four generous hearts,” the West Virginia-based organization wrote. “The Hancock County Humane Foundation is honored to acknowledge a very generous donation from Attorney Mike Simon and his wife Lisa in honor of a very special wedding they recently attended. “Taylor Swift took on an industry that has long underestimated women and won on every front: artistically, commercially, and on the question of who owns her work,” the publication’s editor-in-chief, Maer Roshan, said. “She reclaimed her catalog, set new terms for the artists who follow her, and became the most popular musician in the world while doing it—and helping scores of other artists along the way. #6726. To Penny, or Not to Penny?

Few shoes are as essential in the modern menswear landscape as the classic leather loafer. Whether you’re dressing up or dressing down, it is the “the Swiss Army Knife of shoes,” an any-occasion solution to many footwear conundrums. But within the broader loafer genus, one particular species—the penny loafer—includes a divisive design feature: a small, coin-shaped slot in the leather strap “saddle” across the vamp of the shoe.

As the lore goes, Ivy Style pioneers and sock-hopping teens in the mid-20th century liked to store a penny in their shoes as “payphone change.” But now that payphones are a thing of the misty-eyed past and the American one-cent penny is no longer minted for circulation, is it still cool to put a penny (or any other coin, or coin-shaped object) in your penny loafers? What is the line between timeless and passé?

We invited two of GQ’s most well-heeled staffers, associate grooming and wellness editor Tyler Chin and senior style commerce writer Gerald Ortiz, to ponder the pros and cons of the penny loafer.

Mahershala Ali, an ostensible penny proponent, in London on October 19.

Tyler Chin, associate grooming and wellness editor: Sure! I’ve seen so many guys wearing loafers these days, and yet still haven’t seen any of them harking back to the shoe’s origins with a penny in them. Maybe I’m not looking hard enough or I’m not in circles where they are doing that, but it’s an inoffensive and easy way to accessorize the shoe. Plus, I had an English teacher in high school who did it, and while she wasn’t particularly cool, I did think the sartorial choice was neat.

Gerald Ortiz, senior style commerce writer: No. I feel like guys who put pennies in their loafers are either try-hards, or just learned about that particular piece of prep trivia. The only acceptable instance to wear a penny in your loafers is if you’re really about that prep/Ivy style, like Preppy Pete, or the guys who frequent Alfargo’s Market (shout out).

TC: I think the penny would be the most boring and obvious choice. If a quarter could fit in there, I think it’d be so funny if you were at a vending machine and short a few cents and settled up with the coin in your shoe. One time, the button on my pants fell off on the street and I lost it, but imagine I had a spare button in my shoe? I could reattach it right there and then! In the hypothetical I’d also need to be toting around a sewing kit, but hey, I’d love to think I could be MacGyver in that scenario.

GO: It doesn’t have to be anything at all. But if you’re going to do it, I don’t see why it couldn’t be another coin or object. It could be a Chuck E. Cheese token. Whatever you put in the slot, it would still be wack.

TC: I just got back from a trip to Tokyo, and I had a lot of leftover yen coins. Two of them—the five and 50 yen—have a hole on them, which differentiates them from your boring American coin. I’d throw one of them in my shoe and be one of those people who never stops talking about their travel abroad.

GO: I saw on Instagram someone stick a hundred dollar bill into their loafer and that was funny for a second. Then I scrolled on to the next meme.

TC: I’m pretty sure a coin that is that close to the ground will surely have a patina before the end of the day. Also, I can’t remember the last time I’ve seen a shiny new coin—who carries loose change these days anyway?!

GO: You know, it might be kind of cool to see a penny completely covered in verdigris slotted into your loafers. But maybe the coin should match the sheen of your loafers. I dunno, just don’t do it and you won’t have to think about it.

TC: Everyone I know is very familiar with my love of penny loafers. Lately I’ve been wearing them with bootcut jeans that are just a little longer than usual, so they have a nice drape over the shoe. Top-wise, I’d go with a tucked-in button up, T-shirt, or sweater. Pretty much anything that would go well with sneakers would be equally suited for wearing with loafers. Which is nearly all outfits.

GO: Penniless or not, a pair of wide khakis with a clean-to-slight break and a striped button-up is a failsafe outfit. It wouldn’t be very inventive, but it would pass muster for most conceivable situations. Vintage straight-leg jeans with good fades, a fucked-up band tee, and a sportcoat is also a great look. But the best looks are always the unexpected pairings.

TC: It’s sort of like how guys will go on and on about having functional sleeve buttons on a suit jacket. Is there any situation where you’ll actually need to unbutton those or do you just leave one or two undone to “stunt” on your unimpressed bros? If you really want to put a coin in your shoe for the sake of accessorizing your footwear, then by all means get a shoe with a functioning penny slot and use it! But if you’re doing it just so you can say “Yeah, these joints are the real deal!” and use it as an excuse to talk about the history of the shoe and why yours are superior, then I’d rather you wear lace-ups.

GO: I think it’s fine, even preferable to have a faux penny slot. It’s like how jeans still come with the watch pocket. It’s purely vestigial at this point, but would feel incomplete without it.

TC: One of these days, I’ll be telling my great-great grandchildren about the origins of the penny loafer and they’ll be confused because they would’ve never heard or seen the one-cent coin before. I’ll whip one out of my shoe and instead of being impressed they’ll chalk it up to another one of Old Man Ty’s tales from his youth, and tuck me back into the nursing home they checked me into.

GO: Lol. I guess it’ll make the penny more covetable. But it’ll be a long time before the penny becomes that desirable. That said, I love this British brand Six 95 that’s designing cool pieces using coins, so I can absolutely see more labels farming pennies for their clothes and accessories.

TC: Men will break up anything other than a toxic relationship. Loafers did nothing wrong and sometimes it’s just the person wearing them that needs to hit the curb.

GO: It makes sense. It’s like any trend, really. Even if they’re as versatile as we’ve been propping them up to be, loafers reached an inflection point where, for some guys, they’re just not the vibe anymore. But I don’t think they’ll dip so low to be thought of as cringe or as an emblem of the 2020s. They’re as classic as it gets and they’ll go through their own ebbs and flows.

TC: A quarter to increase my net worth 25-fold.

#6722. Meet the Husbands, Partners, and Exes of the ‘Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County’ Cast

From Jen and Zac Affleck’s divorce filing to Aspyn Ovard’s buzzy throuple, here’s the relationship drama to know.

Exactly one week before the premiere of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, OG MomTok member Jen Affleck shocked fans by filing for divorce from her husband of seven years, Zac Affleck. Of course, if you’ve been paying attention, then this update isn’t all that surprising…save for the fact that Jen is currently pregnant with her and Zac’s fourth child. And while fans have been predicting this split since season 1 of SLOMW, it seems things finally imploded amid filming for this new spinoff series.

Wondering what other kind of relationship drama SLOMW: OC brings? While most of the new cast members are in long-term, committed marriages, the season also explores the dynamic of Aspyn Ovard’s buzzy throuple with Billy and Bri Davis firsthand, as well as Bobbi Althoff’s budding romance with basketball player Tyler Hawkins. Here’s a rundown on everyone’s relationships.

Current relationship status: Married to Nathan Pease

Ashleigh tied the knot with Nate in September 2013, and four kids later, they still seem rock-solid.

Current relationship status: Dating Billy Davis and Bri Davis

Just about two years after filing for divorce from Parker Ferris in April 2024, Aspyn made headlines when she revealed she was in a relationship with married couple Billy and Bri Davis, who practice consensual non-monogamy. She later explained that the relationship started with just Bri before she became involved with Billy as well.

Current relationship status: Married to David Woods

Avery married former police officer David back in June 2016 and they still seem very much in love. David also has two kids from a previous relationship.

Current relationship status: Dating Tyler Hawkins

Once her divorce from Cory Althoff was finalized in August 2024, Bobbi struck up a romance with basketball player Tyler Hawkins in November 2024, per People, and two years later, they’re still going strong.

Current relationship status: Divorcing Zac Affleck

Number of kids: 3 (with a fourth on the way)

After seven years of marriage (and MONTHS of breakup rumors), TMZ broke the news that Jen had filed for divorce from Zac. The two tied the knot in June 2019 after meeting on the Mormon dating app Mutual the year before.

Current relationship status: Married to Corey McClanahan

Jordan and her firefighter husband Corey (who were high school sweethearts!) have been married since February 2017 and are seemingly still head over heels for each other.

Current relationship status: Married to Kyler Steven Fisher

Madison got married to Kyler back in April 2013 after meeting on Facebook, and now they share five kids and a wildly popular YouTube channel.

Current relationship status: Married to Kirk DaPron

McCall and Kirk have been married since September 2011 and (though they recently faced backlash for their controversial family Halloween costume) are still loved up 15 years later.

Current relationship status: Married to Aaron Brimhall

Number of kids: 2 (with a third on the way)

Despite a yearlong separation, Salomé and her photographer husband Aaron (who she married in December 2012) are now back together and gearing up to welcome their third child.

#6721. We’re in a James Bond Fever Dream Now

“Next James Bond ‘REVEALED,’” reads a headline published by The Sun last week. “After a loose-lipped co-star blabs secret after ‘a few lagers.’” The article suggests that Josh O’Connor, who has recently been named in the wider press as a last-minute hopeful in the race to find the next Bond actor, is the shoe-in to be 007—all based on what one of O’Connor’s cast mates in the theater production Golden Boy might have maybe told a stranger while drunk at The French House in London.

“They said that he had confided in them about getting the role when the cast of Golden Boy had celebratory drinks after the play finished its run on Halloween,” the article continues. So, there it is: we have our next Bond! Source: someone told someone else down the pub. No, really, honest!

This is nothing against O’Connor, mind. As Ben Allen argued in the latest edition of GQ’s Intermission newsletter, he would make for a killer, surprising pick, suggestive of an “actually new direction” delineating from the hyper-machismo that defined Bond through to the end of the Craig era. His characters tend to be quieter and more introspective; his performance style is similarly subtle. (The hipster choice? Maybe, but obviously a great one.) But the article is a symptom of how utterly insane the maelstrom of reports around the next Bond have become as we seemingly enter the casting endgame, with screen tests reportedly taking place in October. Further, producer Amy Pascal has said that we can probably expect an announcement to come before the end of the year.

Over the past weekend, Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult emerged out of nowhere as having taken part in those aforementioned screen tests. Both would’ve come as whiplash to anyone who has had a passing interest in the endless Bond casting conversation: sure, they’ve been in and around the pack over the years, but given neither are called “Callum Turner” or “Jack Lowden,” the only speculated names taken seriously for much of 2026, they’re big—but both welcome!— shocks. I’m as much of an RPatz supremacist as anyone else who likes to think they know ball about films, the actor routinely being the best thing about his projects, from Nolan’s Tenet and all of his zany arthouse movies to both The Odyssey and Primetime this year. Much love to our man Hoult too, an underrated cornerstone of franchise cinema writ large, from X-Men to the new Superman. But still: what the hell?

In their own article about Pattinson and Hoult joining the race, Variety might’ve actually buried the most baffling lede: according to them, Harry Styles has “had discussions about the part,” while they also note that The Gentlemen’s Theo James—long thought out of the running—is actually yet to be ruled out. No shade on Styles, but he hasn’t been in a film since he briefly dipped a toe in acting in 2022’s Don’t Worry Darling and My Policeman, neither of which exactly kickstarted his movie career. And, like, he’s Harry Styles. Bond song? Yeah, we can see the vision. But the idea of him actually being 007 feels more like the product of an ayahuasca fever dream.

Regardless, Styles’s suitability for the role isn’t really the point. What’s more insane is that the Bond casting conversation only seems to have hit a level of psychosis as it nears the finish line: every other hour, the reported frontrunner switches from Lowden to Turner to O’Connor or Pattinson, a fever pitch of speculation and rumor-mongering that was tired before it was tired. Gary Oldman reckons it should be Lowden! Pierce Brosnan backs Turner! As one person astutely put it on Threads: “OH MY GOD JUST PICK A JAMES BOND. DO ANY JAMES BOND, JUST JAMES BOND A JAMES BOND.”

But it’s not just Bond himself, it seems. As I sat down to write this piece, an email hit my inbox from the publicist for a betting company. Subject line: “Maya Jama odds slashed to star in the next Bond film.” Damn it. Just bring back Pierce.

This article originally appeared in British GQ.

#6718. Does Influencer Gifting Still Work in the Algorithm Age?

Influencer gifting, once a savvy play, is now standard practice: on affiliate platform ShopMy, the typical brand now sends 350% more gifts a year than it did in 2022, while rival platform LTK’s annual study with Northwestern University found the average number of creators brands work with rose 275% in the past year.

But more product hasn’t necessarily meant more visibility. Algorithms now reward reach beyond a creator’s followers, affiliate platforms have made posting feel transactional, and access to A-listers increasingly runs through paid placements and a gatekept network of stylists.

That gifting has become an overplayed strategy is precisely the problem. “There has just become too much of it all: too much gifting, too much content, too many paid posts,” says celebrity stylist Dani Michelle, who styles It-girls including Kendall Jenner, Hailey Bieber, and Daisy Edgar-Jones. Tyra Booker, assistant VP of integrated marketing at Rare Beauty, says at a past job, she witnessed the earned media value (EMV) of send-outs falling. “It’s not that these mailers are bad,” she says. “It’s just that fewer people are opening them.” (EMV is the monetary value of brand publicity or exposure that is gained organically.)

Creators are also less willing to post for free. “There’s now a healthier amount of awareness around being paid to play,” Booker says, meaning brands can no longer simply send product and expect content in return. “If a brand requires a guaranteed post, that’s a paid partnership, not organic seeding,” says Jenine Leigh, managing partner at LA-based influencer and marketing agency The A List. That means without an agreement, gifted goods are more likely to just vanish into the abyss.

Affiliate platforms offer a middle ground. On sites like ShopMy and LTK, brands upload a curated selection of products, often called a gifting lookbook, and creators choose what they’d like to be sent. If a creator then shares the piece, they do so with a trackable link, earning commission on any sales it drives, so the brand can see exactly which posts convert. Creators have an incentive to post, too: beyond the commission, a strong track record on the platform helps brands identify the creators who actually drive sales, which, ShopMy’s marketing head Ivy Zhang says, means gifting starts to work more like a sales channel than a marketing expense.

Sophia Geiss is one influencer who has embraced affiliate platforms like LTK.

The algorithms have shifted, too. Reach increasingly comes from those who don’t follow a creator at all: follower growth is down, while non-follower views are up, as social strategist Rachel Karten notes in her newsletter, “Link in Bio”. “I hear from brands all the time that follower count doesn’t correlate with engagement, clicks or purchases,” Karten says.

If gifting is no longer the promised publicity — and sales — boost it once was, how should brands evolve their seeding strategies?

Unlike gifting, a paid placement is a contract: a brand pays a stylist to put a specific piece on a client. These deals are nothing new, but over the past three to five years, they’ve spread well beyond a select few brands, says one PR agency founder who brokers them, speaking anonymously. What’s changed is the pay-off. Brands can now repurpose the image and link it directly to their shops, and the shots they prefer are the ones that look unplanned, like an airport outfit or a coffee run, the founder says.

“Brands 100% want a photo of a celebrity papped wearing their outfit more than an editorial shot, because it feels like the celebrity chose to wear it, even if they didn’t,” they add. In an era where consumers are hyper-aware of brand deals, this approach offers at least an air of authenticity — even if, behind the scenes, the brand PRs are the ones coordinating with the paps.

An average A-list placement costs $25,000 to $30,000, rising to north of $50,000 for a top name — and that’s often for a single piece, such as a necklace, or a pair of shoes or sunglasses, which the stylist works into an outfit. The fee usually goes to the stylist rather than the celebrity, though one stylist, speaking anonymously, says she splits the fee with her client. Payment only happens once a piece is worn and documented. “You still cannot ultimately control if they’re going to wear it,” says the agency founder. “At the last minute, the celebrity could be like, ‘Nah, I’m not wearing that.’” If a piece doesn’t work for the look or the event, no money changes hands.

Other arrangements are murkier. “Sometimes, the brand just has a really good relationship with the stylist. They gift them a lot, a bit of cash changes hands [for paid placements],” says the agency founder. “It’s a little less ‘get that dress on’, and more ‘keep us around’.”

The price to play may have skyrocketed, but the exact return on a paid placement is hard to quantify. Still, the agency founder says placements can earn back their fee and more in direct sales, though they concede it’s “case by case”. One brand recently paid an extra $20,000 after running a placement image as an ad without the rights, and shrugged it off: “We made so much money off that image. Who cares?”

Not every brand can make the math work, though. “You need a significant budget for paid partnerships with VIPs these days,” says Julia Chalmers, founder of LA-based brand marketing and communications agency Lucky Chalm, and “often a brand won’t see the return from such a high investment.”

For brands that seed organically, such as Colleen Allen’s self-funded label, the return depends on timing. Gregory Mitola, founder of brand development and communications firm Etagere, held off on influencer gifting until the brand was stocked at Net-a-Porter and Moda Operandi. “We weren’t at major retailers, so it felt a bit premature,” he says. Instead, the label built awareness through intimate salon-style presentations and by dressing industry women it believed in, offering them friends-and-family pricing, “so they’re out and about wearing the brand.” Its first round of gifting, focused on the new Bustle Bag, went out in late October, and even now, it’s measured. Mitola gifted 15 people: eight celebrities, five influencers, and two industry professionals. “We’re not gifting up the wazoo,” he says.

Carey Mulligan in a Colleen Allen FW26 look.

For brands unwilling or unable to pay the big bucks for paid placements, they need to get savvy about how they seed. Rather than sending product to as many people as possible, the brands cutting through are now focusing on a handful of the right names. “Volume on its own isn’t what drives value anymore, it’s the precision,” says Alison Bringé, CMO at Launchmetrics. “The real advantage in seeding today comes from knowing which talent is creating measurable impact for your brand, and building your strategy around them.”

For Rare Beauty’s Booker, that means specificity: a new, targeted list for each launch, built around niche creators, such as the early-2000s nostalgia accounts she targeted for Rare’s recent Selena Gomez x Demi Lovato campaign. It also means rethinking the send-out itself. Booker’s test is whether it’s worth filming. She also works as a model and content creator, so experiences it from the receiving end too. “I get a million boxes a day, and I barely post any of them. But I post the one I feel most compelled to take a photo or video of,” she says. This includes practical gifts: “Something I can use, like a fragrance tray,” or an experience. Luxury brands, she adds, often get it right by pairing a product with a way to use it, “like a skincare product with a gift of a facial.”

Given the diminishing impact of gifting, and the high cost of paid placements, some brands are leaning further into loaning for high-profile talent. “Each sample is worth thousands of dollars,” says Mitola, which is why premium labels like Colleen Allen lean on loans rather than gifts. “When we agree to dress somebody, in a way we’re paying for that moment, because we won’t be able to place it again in a big way once it’s worn.” The goal is consistency, to establish recognizability for the brand. “When you see a talent in Colleen’s work without a tag underneath it, you can just tell energetically that it is probably Colleen’s dress.”

When brands do carry out traditional gifting, they need to re-think the channels they go through. Chalmers has stopped gifting VIPs through their personal teams altogether. “We see a much faster return by working directly with stylists,” she says. Chalmers opens her Hollywood showroom on the weekends for last-minute fittings, since stylists rarely have time to wait for an international shipment. It pays off: when Sabrina Carpenter wore Australian label Kat The Label, the style immediately built a waitlist. Charli XCX’s wears landed just as press began covering the peek-through bra trend, placing Kat at the center of that conversation and boosting its global awareness almost overnight, says Chalmers.

Charli XCX performing at the 2026 Airbnb.org Gala in a peek-through bra look.

Michelle feels that stylist-placed pieces can translate better. “It has intention behind it. It’s chosen for them, fitted to them, and part of a bigger story. It means something.”

Sometimes, the best placement isn’t a placement at all. Jennifer Lawrence first came to Colleen Allen through being dressed in the brand by her stylist, Ryan Hastings, and soon became a fan. Recently, she was photographed in the label’s chartreuse velvet house coat, which she’d bought herself, and it sold out immediately. The moment that landed was the one no amount of brand investment could have teed up.

It’s why the stylist relationship is worth nurturing. “A PR I trust will lead you to a new like-minded brand that wasn’t on your radar,” says Michelle. “I go back to brands that I connect with, that fit the body well, that use great fabrics, that have great PR teams that make moments happen.”

#6717. 5 Expert Habits to Find Inner Peace From Best-Selling Author Yung Pueblo

This is Expert Habits, a regular column in which thinkers, leaders, and other high performers talk about the habits and routines that help them live a better life.

Yung Pueblo wants to be clear on something: “I’m not a monk.” Sure, in his lifetime he’s meditated for over 13,000 hours, but he still enjoys the drama and chaos of Love Island UK like the rest of us. The best-selling author’s philosophical thoughts on self-awareness, emotional healing, and mindfulness have reached over 3.5 million followers since he first started posting to Instagram in 2013. His digital presence has since grown into published works of poetry and prose, including the New York Times bestsellers Inward, Clarity & Connection, and The Way Forward. Now Pueblo, whose real name is Diego Perez, is releasing a new book: Journey: The Year That Changes Everything (Penguin Random House), a 365-day guide to finding inner peace.

What exactly is inner peace to Perez? “It means that you have a good relationship with your emotions,” he says. “It’s that you’re able to feel your emotions without necessarily fueling the heavy ones.”

Inner peace, per Perez, isn’t a final destination. It’s about recognizing negative feelings and using tools you’ve learned to acknowledge that they’re happening without allowing them to take over your life. That’s what Journey—which debuts on November 10—is about. The following habits are just a few of the techniques he’s developed to do exactly that. Below, Perez explains the creative benefits of walking, the value of daily gratitude, and why you should protect your own peace even when others around you are chaotic—the latter of which makes keeping up with reality TV that much more enjoyable.

Yung Pueblo: “Oftentimes we have a relationship where we’re afraid of change and we need to realize that the universe that we live in, it’s totally founded on change at every level of existence—the atomic level, the biological level, the cosmological level. It’s because of change that we even have the opportunity to experience things. If our universe was static, we wouldn’t be having this conversation right now. So changing our relationship with impermanence and making it one where we actually get inspired to be more present. When we’re with our friends, with our family, with your mom, with your dad, you know that they’re not always going to be around. So the times when you are with them, to be ever more present, because you know change will happen at one point or another. Being able to have that presence just makes you have this ability to really enjoy some of the most beautiful parts of life.

“When it’s a sad moment, you have to be like, ‘OK, this is not going to last forever.’ But also in the precious moments, this isn’t going to last forever, so let me be here in the moment.

“Another way to look at it is that it’s defined by your relationship with change. So the more that you’re able to embrace change and flow with change, then your mind’s going to have less stress. But it’s probably one of the biggest challenges any human being can accept— willingly trying to change their relationship with change.”

“So much of our impulsiveness just comes from these lightning-quick reactions that we think are our nature. We think that they’re unchangeable, but the reality is that we can train ourselves to slow down to be able to ask: OK, is this me having an impulsive reaction right now? and then asking ourselves: Is this actually useful? Should I act this out or instead should I actually choose something that’s different than what I would’ve done in the past? And in the act of slowing down and being intentional, you just end up finding way better results. This is a real habit. You can learn that from meditating, you can learn that from therapy, but you can also just teach yourself the raw skill of feeling impulsiveness coming up and then challenging yourself to slow down.

“I’m not going to jump to conclusions. I’m not going to say anything right now. Let me just check in with how I feel, what actually feels true to me, and then put forward something that I think is actually going to be helpful as opposed to just something that I later regret.

“So if a friend of yours is telling you about something that they’re really mad about, they’re offering an invitation for you to be angry with them on their behalf. But instead I found that I don’t necessarily want to be angry, but I want to be able to hear my friends and offer support or a listening ear or whatever the situation is needed. At the same time, I can remain in my own energy while offering support to this individual. We get sucked into the energy of other people really, really quickly, but instead of getting sucked into someone’s chaos, for the past two years, what I’ve been working on is: Can I live in my peace and offer my peace as an invitation? They can join me in my peace too, if they want to, instead of me just getting sucked into their drama.”

“We fall into self-analysis when we don’t feel good. It’s just the worst time for you to be analyzing yourself about what you’ve done right, what you’ve done wrong. Negative self-talk isn’t productive. It’s good for you to be honest with yourself, but honesty also can come with gentleness and with self-acceptance. But when your mood is low, it’s going to be really hard for you to be gentle with yourself. So one thing I realize is when I don’t feel good or I’m over-exhausted from too much work or too much travel or whatnot, that’s the time for me to just suspend self-analysis and just treat myself gently—be mindful of what I’m saying to other people too, and just let it pass.

“And in the act of letting it pass, then you can do some more proper self-assessment because your best assessment is going to be when your mind is calm, not when it’s heavy.”

“Life is a long series of ups and downs, and there’s nothing wrong with that. But in the down moments, we tend to look at everything with such darkness that we forget that we still have access to clean water, that we still have access to food, that we have a house over our head. A lot of people in the world don’t have that. Having gratitude for the basics and the fundamentals really helps reset the balance where if something went wrong at work, you’re going to be okay, you’re going to be fine.”

“This is my recent favorite and it’s the newest habit that I picked up. You got to walk. You got to go for walks. Walking supports clarity, and I think it really supports creativity. I find that whenever I feel a little stuck with writing, just going on a 20- or 40-minute walk really helps to regenerate and create this new sense of clarity.”

#6716. Culture Watch: What to See and Where to Go in November

Culture Watch is a series spotlighting the intersection of fashion and art, bringing you the latest must-see exhibitions, pop-ups, installations, and more.

November is a good month to make a little room in your calendar. As the holiday season starts to gather pace, galleries, brands, and creative spaces are offering plenty of reasons to get out and look around. In New York, Salon Art + Design returns for its 15th year, while Loro Piana presents its “Master of Cashmere” installation at The Brant Foundation; farther afield, international exhibitions offer even more to explore. Check out all of this month’s best cultural happenings below.

Louis Vuitton Presents ‘La Valise Bruno Aveillan’ at LV Dream

For 13 years, photographer and filmmaker Bruno Aveillan has taken his Louis Vuitton Alzer suitcase to more than 100 destinations, making it a recurring presence in his work. Now, the well-traveled case is at the center of “La Valise Bruno Aveillan,” an immersive exhibition at LV Dream, the house’s encompassing destination in Paris. Aveillan’s photographs appear alongside historic Louis Vuitton trunks and a closer look at the craftsmanship behind the Alzer, the brand’s hard-sided suitcase built around a sturdy wooden frame. The exhibition marks the final chapter in the house’s yearlong celebration of the monogram’s 130th anniversary.

Loro Piana Names Its Cashmere of the Year and Unveils a ‘Master of Cashmere’ Installation

Loro Piana put cashmere in the spotlight at The Brant Foundation in New York, where it marked the 11th edition of its Cashmere of the Year Award. Established in 2015 and held stateside for the first time, the prize recognizes the herders who produce the finest cashmere fiber. Coinciding with the honor, which went to three couples of cashmere herders from Inner Mongolia, is “Master of Cashmere: The Quest for Fiber Excellence,” an installation that traces the material from its origins to the Maison’s work with it. The multi-room experience features archival sketches, explanatory timelines, and, of course, soft-to-the-touch cashmere.

Salon Art + Design Returns to the Park Avenue Armory for Its 15th Year

The 15th edition of Salon Art + Design is now on view at the Park Avenue Armory—and it’s one of its most immersive, expansive editions yet. As is tradition, the event brings together collectible design, fine art, and jewelry. The event is open through November 8. Standouts include Jean Dunand’s 1929 La Forêt lacquered screen, Michel Dufet’s 1918 daybeds, and Jean Royère’s illuminated desk. Fernando Mastrangelo’s totem lamps add a sculptural note, while the jewelry lineup includes pieces from Fernando Jorge, Mellerio, Cora Sheibani, and Viltier.

Lara Saget Debuts Her First New York Solo Show, ‘And the World Came Apart’

Lara Saget brings more than a decade of material experimentation to her first solo exhibition in New York. At Trotter&Sholer’s new Elizabeth Street space, her sculptures and wearable works fuse glass, stone, and metal through heat, pressure, and time. Drawing on geological processes and NASA data, the show moves from ancient natural formations to humanity’s rapid impact on the planet.

The Phillips Collection Opens ‘Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea’

Milton Avery went to Gloucester, Massachusetts, to “live like an artist,” then brought Adolph Gottlieb and Mark Rothko along for summers of creative exchange. In Washington, D.C., The Phillips Collection’s “Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea” brings together watercolors and color-drenched canvases, tracing what those Cape Ann days set in motion.

Tate St Ives Spotlights Wilhelmina Barns-Graham

What does a landscape feel like in the body? Scottish artist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham spent eight decades exploring that question through art shaped by sensation and memory. The retrospective at Tate St Ives in Cornwall, England, is the most comprehensive survey of her work, moving from early landscapes and studio interiors to later works alive with bold color and sweeping gestures.

Taylor Swift, take note: famously hard-to-get-into New York City hotspot The Corner Store has officially landed at The Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas, marking its first-ever location outside Manhattan. Expect its adventurous martinis, signature wood-paneled interiors by Rockwell Group, and a handful of Vegas-exclusive menu additions, including a Butcher’s Counter serving up wagyu tomahawk and porterhouse steaks.
