The B Corp-certified brand, which is known for timeless designs inspired by men’s tailoring and British heritage, launched its first pair of trousers earlier this year and plans to expand further with blazers and knitwear at the start of 2025. With Nothing Underneath was named one of Walpole’s Brands of Tomorrow in 2022.

Lead investor(s): Pembroke VCT (portfolio includes: Tala, Me+Em, Bella Freud) and JamJar Investments (portfolio includes: Deliveroo, Oatly, Spoke).

Investor comments: “With Nothing Underneath (WNU) holds a unique position in the womenswear market. Pip and her team have built a fantastic brand around one staple item, the shirt — an essential in most women’s wardrobes. It has become a standout in the fashion industry and early growth metrics have given us conviction in the brand. This investment will enable this emerging British heritage brand to enhance its product range, assist with growth and support WNU’s international reach,” said Andrew Wolfson, CEO of Pembroke Investment Managers.

Company description: UK-based luxury retail platform that stocks a curation of independent brands. The retailer is known for its selection of vibrant eveningwear. Founded in 2019 by Nina Briance, Cult Mia initially received $3 million in seed funding in November 2023 led by Fuel Ventures, with participation from Morgan Stanley and David Wertheimer of the Chanel family.

Funding and round: $2 million, seed (bringing total seed funding to $5 million).

Investor(s): H&M Group Ventures (portfolio includes: Goop, Klarna) and existing investors.

Investor comments: “We are delighted to invest in Cult Mia on their mission to launch independent and diverse designers from around the world. We have been incredibly impressed by all that Cult Mia has achieved in such a short space of time,” said Nanna Andersen, chief of new growth and ventures at H&M Group.

Company description: Founded in 1997 by Dr Gregory Brown, Révive is known for its luxury serums and creams powered by bio-renewal technology. The brand was previously acquired by Shiseido in 2016, before it was sold to Tengram Capital Partners in 2017.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): S’Young Group (portfolio includes: Evidens de Beauté, Pier Augé).

#6702. Remember When James Bond Was an Adidas Guy?

The search for the next James Bond continues. Over the weekend, Deadline reported that Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult had also screen-tested for the role, in addition to Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O'Connor. But once we've worked out who's getting the tux, there's another question: What sneakers is he going to wear?

As it turns out, their predecessor Daniel Craig got that bit right, too. In 2012's Skyfall, 007 turns up for his MI6 fitness tests in a navy SIS tracksuit and Adidas Gazelle IIs. In the scene, Bond's trying to prove he's fit enough to get back to work, and it's not going particularly well. As a viewer, you'd be forgiven for missing the shoes.

Daniel Craig as James Bond in Skyfall (2012).

But take another look. These were off-the-shelf Gazelles from Adidas's spring 2011 line, the sort that anyone could have picked up the year before the film came out. Bond is a guy whose wardrobe gets examined down to the last cufflink, and there he was in a regular pair of Adidas. His pair came in “dark indigo” suede with “Argentina blue” stripes, white rubber soles, and gold Gazelle lettering along the sides.

(There's a slight difference between the shoes a civilian could buy and the ones in the movie, though. The retail pair had a light blue heel tab, while Bond's appears darker. The fan website Bond Lifestyle suggests the costume department may have changed it, although that hasn't been officially confirmed.)

The Gazelle launched in 1966 as a multipurpose training shoe, and was the German sportswear giant's first-ever sneaker made from suede. The choice to put Bond in the shoe felt notable in more ways than one: In the training scene, the slim sole kept things nice and light underfoot, and the color combo went perfectly with his trackies. But there's also the Gazelle's place in British culture, from the football terraces in the ’80s to the Britpop crowd in the ’90s. So, it makes sense for a Gen-X British spy.

By 2021, Adidas had an official collab to go with No Time to Die. The collection featured all Ultraboost running shoes, with slight nods to Bond's tuxedos and Safin's porcelain mask. The “Q Branch” edition even had a hidden compartment in the lacing cage, handy if your gym shorts don't have pockets.

For a pair that came from a regular ol' Adidas collection, Bond's OG Gazelles are surprisingly difficult to find now. But if you fancy something similar without spending the next six months refreshing eBay, you can start with these.

A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

#6701. The Secret to Kendall Jenner’s ‘Me Mode’

The model and founder shares her favorite ways to unwind and how the Therabody TheraFace Mask Glo fits into her nightly routine.

For Kendall Jenner, “Me Mode” is a time to unplug from the daily demands of work and social obligations and simply be still. “I have a really busy mind, so switching off has never come naturally to me,” says the model and entrepreneur. “I’ve had to build little rituals that help me slow down.”

One of those rituals involves Therabody’s TheraFace Mask Glo, an LED face mask that bridges skincare with wellness. Delivering full LED coverage across the entire face, including the lips and under eyes, the cordless device features 504 red, infrared, and blue LEDs, plus a relaxing scalp massage to help relieve tension. Best of all, treatment time is only 12 minutes, giving Jenner a quick, easy, and much-needed pause from her busy schedule.

“After a long day, it’s sweatpants, my dogs, and zero plans,” Jenner says. “Putting on the Mask Glo has kind of become my signal that the day is over. For those 12 minutes, my brain finally goes quiet.”

One thing Jenner loves about the TheraFace Mask Glo is how effortlessly it fits into her routine. “It’s hands-free, so I just put it on and do whatever I feel like that night,” Jenner says. “Sometimes that’s music or journaling, and a lot of the time it’s doing absolutely nothing. The scalp massage is my favorite part. It feels less like a skincare step and more like actually relaxing.”

It offers legitimate skincare benefits, too. Backed by the largest clinical study of any LED mask on the market, the TheraFace Mask Glo was shown to reduce under-eye wrinkles and fine lines, enhance radiance, and lift sagging skin in as little as eight weeks.

The TheraFace Mask Glo offers three LED settings to target different skin concerns. Red light helps improve the appearance of fine lines, wrinkles, and dark spots, while red and infrared light work together to boost collagen production. Blue light targets acne-causing bacteria, helping prevent future breakouts.

The key is consistent use, which Jenner has found easy to maintain. “If a routine is too complicated, I’m not going to stick with it, and I’ve learned that consistency matters more than anything,” she says. “With the Mask Glo, I pick red, red and infrared, or blue light depending on how my skin is acting, and that’s it. It’s easy enough that I actually use it, which is half the battle for me. It comes with me when I travel now, too.”

The LED lights are placed across the entire face, even covering overlooked areas like the mouth and eyes. The preset treatment runs for 12 minutes, cycling through four minutes of each light setting. Four-minute individual treatments are also available.

Combining advanced skincare and relaxation into one simple step, the TheraFace Mask Glo is ideal for anyone who wants to level up their nighttime routine with minimal effort. As Jenner has learned over the years, less is more when it comes to beauty and wellness.

“I’ve been sitting in makeup chairs since I was 14, so I went through a phase of trying everything,” she says. “Now I do a lot less, and I’m more intentional about what I put on my skin. I try to give it a break when I can, and I’ll use the Mask Glo before glam on shoot days.”

Jenner’s nighttime routine is just one aspect in living a more holistic lifestyle. “Wellness for me is mostly about balance now: being at the barn with my horses, getting outside, and protecting my nights,” she says. “My friends make fun of me for going to bed so early, but I’m not changing.”

#6697. 70 Best Gifts for Women in 2026, According to GQ

When it comes to buying gifts for the women in your life, we have one rule: Shop from her wishlist, not her to-do list. Maybe she's got a Sephora's worth of serums in her bathroom, a small fortune invested in vintage Italian glassware, or a closet full of capital-F fashion with “nothing to wear.” Whatever her particular brand of enthusiasm, we've got it well covered, from the latest and greatest beauty to old-fashioned fineries in cashmere and silk. Below, an assortment of some of the best gifts for women at every price point.

Good gifts don't stop here. Explore all our gift guides, then sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more excellent ideas.

British knitwear label &Daughter can count us among its devoted followers, not least for its Sligo V-neck, a Scottish lambswool sweater with a slightly shrunken fit that makes the traditional style feel decidedly of the moment.

Collina Strada made its name from its playful, offbeat designs, and this ring is the easiest way for her to add a little “festive” flair this season without resorting to sequins, though sequins are also welcome.

There's been a lot of commotion around the larger version of Coach's Kisslock bag, but this smaller iteration is every bit as chic. With its structured shape and classic clasp, it's prim and proper in a good way.

This Fair Isle scrunchie from Banana is a cheery finishing touch that makes even the simplest ponytail feel festive. If the wintry knit pattern ain't her thing, there are a few other fun designs to choose from.

We love a precious itsy-bitsy watch, and so does Brynn Wallner, the watch writer behind Dimepiece, who teamed up with Timex to offer up this dainty little number. It's simple, does the job, and makes a lovely gift for someone who feels the same way.

Alexa Chung has a few different irons in the fire these days, but perhaps none hotter than these snakeskin mules with a cute block heel.

A little playful, and straight to the point. Emily Dawn Long's IYKYK wares are modern classics at this point, and an easy gift for those you know who do indeed know.

A rugby for the girls. Boxy and cropped, this one from Buck Mason might finally get her to stop borrowing yours.

Sophie Buhai's signature egg pendant has been around since she first started, and a decade later, I gotta say, it's still a very good egg.

Done up in crocodile-embossed leather, Saint Laurent's giant bowling bag is a canny investment for someone who wants one very good bag to do it all: an everyday carryall during the week, and a posh getaway bag for the next weekender.

A mainstay from New York-based label Silphium, this leather sling bag flaunts a sculptural teardrop shape and an adjustable knotted strap. Each one is made to order, so you better get to it.

No one, at least that I know of, has ever been disappointed by a pair of Comme Si boxers, which can and absolutely should be worn out of the house.

A double-breasted peacoat is good. A double-breasted peacoat cut with these proportions is even better. Ideal for tossing over just about anything.

If she's a self-proclaimed cold girl, Quince's fuzzy merino wool balaclava will keep her noggin (and ears and neck) nice and toasty.

Earlier this year, Acne Studios followed up its much-loved collaboration with perfumer Frédéric Malle with a body wash scented with peach, sandalwood, and musk.

Pepper and rose make a glorious pairing, especially in the hands of Dries Van Noten, who makes some of the best formulations in the business.

Summer Fridays has bundled up a few sunny-day essentials—its lip butter balm, mineral milk sunscreen, and vanilla eau de parfum—in a charming little mini tote perfect for bringing poolside.

We recommended Therabody's Depuffing Wand last year, and we're running it back because it's just so dang good at what it does. Hot and cold treatments in one wonderfully unfussy little device make it a welcome addition to her skincare routine.

Combining gua sha with red-light therapy was only a matter of time. Ora Method's LED gua sha tool also throws gentle vibration into the mix, so she gets a little massaging, depuffing, and skin rejuvenation all in one go.

Between the biting cold outside and the bone-dry heat indoors, winter surely ravages the skin. But a good body oil, like this one from Nécessaire, can help keep her nourished and glowing through it all.

Chanel No. 5 needs no introduction, but I'll give it one anyway. Rose, jasmine, and a little citrus make up this grand dame of fragrances, which smells just as good today as it did a century ago.

If you haven’t heard of La Bonne Brosse, chances are she has. And if one of the French brand’s quaintly demure hairbrushes hasn’t yet found its way onto her vanity, you’d be wise to remedy that.

Over lunch at GQ HQ recently, a few of my colleagues were coming to terms with an inconvenient truth: Rhode's Glazing Milk is actually really good. But good it is: a milky, ceramide-packed essence that leaves skin hydrated, dewy, and looking like the hype machine is onto something.

Eadem's Le Chouchou lip balms have had BeautyTok in a tizzy, and at least a few GQ staffers swear by 'em. This set comes with three versions: Butter Mochi (the no-frills, clear one), Sakura (a milky pink with a sweet tooth), and Fig Sauce (a moody little mauve).

Burberry Goddess is a vanilla perfume for people who think they don't like vanilla perfumes. Warm, creamy, and lifted by a little lavender, it's sweet without smelling like a dessert.

It looks like something out of Ex Machina, and that's just one reason to like Dr. Dennis Gross's LED face mask. The others? Red light to help soften fine lines, blue light to target breakouts, and a purple setting that combines the two.

I won't pretend to know the first thing about hair tools, but the women I consulted for this guide assure me that Shark's FlexStyle is a worthy alternative to the considerably pricier Dyson Airwrap. Defer to their expertise and pocket the difference.

A good hair day is a gift. Kérastase's holiday duo helps make them happen. Inside: the brand's cult-favorite Elixir Ultime hair oil for shine, plus its night serum to work some overnight magic.

The original Glossier You fragrance is a modern classic, and this gift set doubles down on it, with a full-size bottle for her dresser and a travel-size one to take wherever she goes.

Sometimes, opposite dressers really do attract.

#6692. 'Wild Horse Nine' Should Win an Oscar for Its Signet Rings

Wild Horse Nine is a Western. Sort of. Yes, Martin McDonagh’s new film is set on Easter Island (known locally as Rapa Nui) in the Pacific Ocean. And yes, this is the 1970s, with John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell playing CIA operatives who take a break from plotting a coup in Chile to tour the stone moai heads.

But there are also—as the title suggests—a lot of wild horses about, plus a cameo from Tom Waits in a shack in Colorado’s Monument Valley and a hell of a lot of Western accessories. Rockwell’s turquoise belt buckle and cowboy hat almost had me wanting to jump back in time and become a paid-up member of the American deep state. And the big signet rings with chunky stones everyone’s wearing? Look, if you really need me to fictionally assassinate JFK and frame Lee Harvey Oswald for it, I’ll step up.

Costume designer Eimer Ní Mhaoldomhnaigh, who worked with McDonagh on The Banshees of Inisherin, had fun outfitting everyone in colorful shirts and flared trousers. “I really liked the way men dressed in the ’70s,” she says. “There was almost a dandyish quality to them.” But it’s the accessories that really makes the characters. “Anytime you’re doing a fitting [for] a male actor,” she explains, “you’re putting on the shirt and the trousers and they’re like, ‘Mmm, okay.’ Then you put on that belt, you give him a Cuban heel and a cowboy hat and a ring, suddenly they start to stand differently. They get the whole swagger. A costume is never finished until you have all those details.”

This is a film with a lot of those details. Rockwell’s cowboy hat, for example, was custom-made by the London milliner Sophie Lamb, who's worked on films like Phantom Thread. His belt buckle is in the traditional Navajo style of the American West: sterling silver with turquoise inlay, which Mhaoldomhnaigh says she “probably got it on Etsy.” That said, she does a lot of IRL trawling on London’s Portobello Road, too. “I really wanted Sam to wear a chain, but when we put it on with the whole outfit, it felt like overkill—like we were decorating a Christmas tree. You have all those things and then you have to pull back a little bit.”

There’s other great gear in the vein of brash, peacocking men of action. “It’s a very American look,” says Mhaoldomhnaigh. Steve Buscemi, who plays the CIA’s South American boss, is in Coblens glasses with gradated lenses, and a ’70s watch from Rotary. Rockwell has a chunky gold watch from Pierre Jacquard. Malkovich, whose character is still stuck in his ’60s glory days, has this whole pork-pie hat thing happening.

But what really gets me going is the rings. Pretty much everyone—including Waits, who plays Malkovich’s hippie brother—has got these chunky rings on, and of a kind we don’t necessarily associate with gray-suitness of the American establishment today. It’s more dandyish, as Mhaoldomhnaigh puts it: “I was a child in the ’70s,” she says. “I always remember older men wearing those type of rings. My dad had one.”

She was on the lookout for designs which matched her memories, both vintage and new—Malkovich’s ring, which is gold with a black onyx stone, was “actually bought in Liberty,” she says, referring to the famous British department store.

“Martin’s films are always a little bit heightened,” the costume designer says. “That’s part of the fun of it, being able to create these slightly heightened characters.” And dressing up those characters means you can have fun, as McDonagh does, in mocking their big egos. Even so, I’m being deadly serious when I say I’d ransack Mhaoldomhnaigh’s props box any time.

A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

#6691. Burberry Retail Sales Grow 4% in Q2, Carried by China and the US

Burberry’s comparable retail sales grew 4% on a constant currency basis in both the second quarter and first half of the fiscal year 2026/2027. For H1, Burberry’s group revenues grew 6% to €1.1 billion.

“Two years ago, we launched Burberry Forward [a plan to bring the brand back to where it was four years ago with a focus on outerwear and a diversified pricing structure]. Today, our brand is stronger, and our business is healthier,” said CEO Joshua Schulman on Thursday’s call. “We have delivered five consecutive quarters of growth and improved our quality of sales, which demonstrates that our strategy is working. This momentum stretches across product categories, channels, and geographies, and has translated into higher gross margin and increased profitability.”

Adjusted operating profit reached £62 million in H1, while gross margin rose to 68.3% — up 40 basis points from 67.9%.

Regionally, the Americas took the lion’s share of retail growth in Q2, up 11%, driven by local spending and activations, and healthy in-store conversion. Greater China followed, up 5% in Q2, a deceleration from Q1’s 9% climb. Burberry attributed this industry outperformance, in part, to the strong appeal of Burberry as a British heritage brand.

“We know that there’s been a lot of news about the challenging luxury market in China, but we’re being very deliberate, continuing to invest in our relationships with our customers in that part of the world,” said Schulman. “We understand that luxury customers around the world — particularly in China — are experiencing fatigue with exorbitant pricing, and in this context, our strategy of having enduring value and providing great value for money is resonating strongly with the Chinese customers.”

The Asia-Pacific region, excluding China, also grew in the quarter, up 3%, with South Korea growing 12%, driven by local demand. Japan was a weak point, down 1% in the quarter, attributed to softer tourism from mainland China. EMEIA also dropped 2%, due to softer tourism and traffic.

“It’s no secret that global tourism is down. So the local customer has been spending in their respective regions. We’re seeing globally that Middle Eastern, Chinese, European, and British customers are shopping at home,” said Schulman. “This is a trend we’ve been seeing all year long. There’s just less cross-border travel than there has been in the past.”

By category, womenswear led growth across retail and wholesale, growing 9%, followed by accessories (6%). Childrenswear and other also grew (5%), as well as menswear (3%).

The company didn’t share figures for outerwear, but reported double-digit retail growth in H1, led by the “rainwear” category. Lightweight gabardine designs and shorter styles performed through summer, while new cashmere and leather launches showed traction towards the end of Q2. Accessories also grew in Q2, and leather goods accelerated, boosted by strong performance in women’s handbags — particularly the vintage check and Cotswolds ranges.

Wholesale revenue grew 17% in H1. The company attributed this performance to the confidence of its partners, who are achieving high sell-throughs of Burberry products and continuing to invest in the brand’s designs. Licensing revenues dropped 5%. The brand opened seven stores and closed five, bringing the total to 412 directly operated stores as of September 2026.

The company also addressed its developing relationship with Frasers Group, which now has a 6% stake in the British brand. In October, Frasers Group had adjusted its stake in Burberry from 7.4%. This came after the growing retail group raised its position in the company from 6.3% earlier in the month, after upping it from 4.2% at the end of September. “We have a long-standing valued relationship with Frasers,” said Schulman. “They are an important wholesale customer for us in the United Kingdom, and now they are an investor. And just like we do with all of our investors, we will meet with Frasers Group in due course. In terms of their agenda, that would be a question for them.”

#6689. Get Huge’s Director on How Looksmaxxing Is a ‘Trap’ for Men

Chasing physical perfection is a hobby now. This year, the community of men obsessed with climbing the ranks of society via square jawlines and hunter eyes, became a subject of widespread fascination. Once a term known in niche internet forums in the early 2010s, the concept of “looksmaxxing” has gone mainstream. These days, even the casual scrollers among us have probably heard of techniques like bonesmashing and mewing.

But beyond a few self-appointed figureheads of the movement, the question of who is buying into these extreme self-improvement measures has loomed large. In Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death documentarian Stacey Lee gives viewers a deeper look into the lives of some of the looksmaxxing community’s more controversial figures. The three-part Hulu docuseries, out now, follows bodybuilding and biohacking influencer Dr. Tony Huge (whose real name is Anthony Hughes), controversial fitness personality, Connor Murphy, and a handful of other men.

Set largely in Thailand, the series tells the story of how these influencers decamped abroad and continued to post near daily videos of their body modification techniques. Lee also confronts the disturbing pattern of deaths among Huge’s inner circle, some of which have gone unsolved. Ultimately the series raises larger questions about the cultural, gender-driven motivations to push the limits of their bodies. GQ spoke with Lee about her nearly two-year immersion into a small corner of this community, the blurred lines between online persona and reality, and what it all reveals about a generation of young men who are seemingly searching for identity, connection, and purpose through increasingly unhealthy outlets.

These internet influencers create so much content, and there's a performance of masculinity that takes place within it. The topic is incredibly polarizing, but also very nuanced. We wanted to capture this world in a way that was more dimensional than what YouTube feeds allow, puncturing the veneer of performance to show who these people are beyond their online personas. I want audiences to see a more multifaceted view of this world and decide for themselves how they feel about these characters based on what they're seeing.

Looksmaxxing wasn't even a term when we started this project [in 2024]. We initially entered the bodybuilding, biohacking, and masculinity influencer community, which was still very fringe at the time. Tony had started making content nearly a decade ago, using shock value and radical transparency to build his brand. He was willing to do things on camera that others wouldn't, challenging social taboos. Ten years later, we're seeing a new generation of influencers who grew up watching Tony, [biohacking YouTuber Leo and Longevity], and Connor and are now using similar methods. But the algorithm has shifted the goalposts significantly since 2016, pushing the content into a much more extreme and nihilistic space.

I wouldn't necessarily say he was the godfather of looksmaxxing, but he was certainly influential in the biohacking and bodybuilding space. Connor Murphy was probably more directly connected to the origins of looksmaxxing, and Clavicular has referenced him as an inspiration. Tony was part of that same world, but represented a different generation.

Tony was a larger-than-life figure, but it was also a broader cultural moment. Around 2016, we were seeing the first Trump presidency, the post-Me Too movement, and the rise of Red Pill philosophy. There were several figures galvanizing these ideas, and Tony was among them.

I think what you're also referring to is this idea of legacy, right? He created something he believed was his unique gift to the world, but there's a sense that the next generation doesn't recognize him or understand his influence. That disconnect seems to drive some of his pursuit of the next big thing, which, in this instance, is looksmaxxing.

Look, Tony is incredibly charismatic and easygoing. Honestly, filming with him was a really respectful process. I think at times it was really discombobulating because he's always smiling in these videos, and he's presenting as this happy-go-lucky kind of guy, but then you're stopped in your tracks because he's doing and saying things that run against that.

The only other reference I'm thinking of is Andrew Tate, who presents in this very sinister way and has a darkness to him that's front and center. Tony doesn't present that way. For us, it was important to show that and to dimensionalize him. In his eyes, he didn't care if he was a hero or a villain. He just wanted to get his story out there. My approach was that I wanted to humanize him, but it wasn't about excusing what was happening.

It's important in this day and age to approach controversial subjects with an element of humanity while still maintaining journalistic independence. In this world, the boundaries are really slippery because people are performing so much. You really have to have your guard up about what's real and what's not. I don't think it's my job to tell audiences what to think of Tony. It's my job to provide a fuller understanding of who he is and allow them to make up their own minds. Discernment was something that was really important for us to communicate: What you see is not always what you get.

You see it in episodes one and two. [Editor's note: Tony lives with his wife and a group of other women he refers to as his girlfriends.] There's a very specific mentality rooted in Red Pill philosophy, where the role of a man is to control these women and provide for them, but also to assert himself. He's the leader, and they must follow. I think one of the things Tony is always battling is that he presents in such a nice way and isn't aggressive like [his friend and fellow biohacking influencer] Leo was, but there's still this desire to control the women. The women are very strong, opinionated women.

From conversations with Tony during the making of this documentary, I know a lot of the women didn't realize they were coming into a harem. They thought they were his one and only true love, and then they've entered this environment and suddenly they're in competition with one another.

That competition is part of the dynamic of how the harem works. The way Tony puts it is that if they're in competition with one another, they try harder to vie for his attention, love, and affection. That's an incredibly complicated way of pitting women against each other, and somewhat dehumanizing.

What I want to be really careful of is that these aren't a bunch of outrageous, crazy people doing crazy things from the start. It actually begins in a real human place, a place all of us can relate to. I want to be the best version of myself. Yeah, of course I do. That's very relatable.

What happens within this is that some of the needs, in Elon [Muscular, one of Tony Huge’s mentees and a content creator]'s case, a sense of belonging, a father figure, all of those kinds of things that he's craving, aren't solved by taking one pill. These are really deep societal issues that are complex and need to be approached with a multidimensional complexity.

Therein lies a lot of the challenges with this world, because the extreme and the attention keep pushing those goalposts further. You get a bigger jawline, a bigger penis, bigger muscles, and you're still not feeling happy. I think it creates this kind of trap that some men can get stuck within, because the original solution was never going to solve that problem to begin with.

Honestly, it was really important for me to make this. A lot of my prior work has centered on women and diverse perspectives, and it's such an honor and privilege to do that kind of work. But I also recognize I was existing in a bit of an echo chamber, so doing this project took me well outside my comfort zone.

I use this example with kids: When they're scared at night, you shine a light in the room. You look under the bed, you shine a light into it, and it makes the thing that's inside your head less scary. There was a little bit of that in making this documentary, of really looking at it and understanding it, witnessing how people come in, why they stay, and why they also can't leave, and using those things as what I need to teach my son. I need to teach him discernment. I need to teach him the difference between a YouTube influencer who's performing and one who's actually giving genuine, real tips.

In this day and age, where clipping culture and soundbites matter, there's no room for context. We're in a post-truth era, and no one's taking the time to provide context, human dimension, or other perspectives. I want my son to understand how the internet and influencer culture work so he can make his own decisions with more critical thought than what's often taught in the public space.

Yeah, of course. I never wanted to make something that was just another echo chamber. I want this documentary to reach people deep in the heart of the masculinity influencer space. I want them to see it. Everyone's going to have a different reaction, but most importantly, people are talking, and that's what I care about. I need the conversation, the depth of the conversation. That's what this is designed to have.

It's interesting because that question has come up a few times. There does appear to be a turning of the tides. Even within Tony's own universe, his sense of relevancy has shifted. He went from being the most masculine man he could be to wearing eyeliner. It's all become a lot more fluid and therefore a lot more interesting.

I think there's a time we're living through where the power structures that have existed for the last decade are starting to break down. People aren't feeling connected to them anymore, or they certainly aren't serving their needs.

I hope we're at a time of reckoning and change, where people are recognizing that this isn't working. There's so much more awareness about the issues men are facing, and there are specific influencers who are the opposite kind, who are speaking about this stuff more. There are some incredible voices in this space starting to counter the other perspectives out there.

#6688. The Great Bear Rainforest: How Fashion Rallied to Stop the Deforestation of an Ancient Rainforest

This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa. Read more here.

The Great Bear Rainforest, spanning 6.4 million hectares from the Alaskan border to just above Vancouver Island, is the largest coastal temperate rainforest in the world, a critical carbon sink, and the only known home of the extremely rare white-furred spirit bear. Whales migrate through the rainforest year-round, and it is a major breeding ground for all five species of Pacific salmon. Thanks to the region’s heavy rainfall and nutrient-rich ecosystem, it also houses an array of ancient trees over a thousand years old, including sitka spruce (among the tallest trees in the world) and red western cedar (which hold deep cultural significance for the 26 local First Nations).

Until 2016, 90% of the Great Bear Rainforest was open for logging, and fashion was one of the industries profiting from it. The industry uses large quantities of man-made cellulosic fibers (MMCF) like viscose, modal and lyocell, which typically come from wood pulp. It also has a direct link to deforestation through wood-based packaging, and an indirect link through leather and cotton, which are often grown on deforested land.

Now, thanks to fashion brands joining anti-logging campaigners at a crucial moment, 85% of it is legally protected from deforestation and logging, the First Nations whose territories overlap with it are co-decision makers in its conservation, and there is a $120 million fund helping them transition to conservation-based economies. This is a rare example of fashion rallying around nature restoration and using its purchasing power for good, in partnership with other industries. Experts say it’s a blueprint the industry could apply elsewhere.

This “seismic” win took decades to achieve, says Nicole Rycroft, founder and executive director of non-profit Canopy, which works to conserve ancient and endangered forests around the world. While anti-logging efforts in the Great Bear Rainforest pre-date Canopy, the non-profit joined the campaign at a critical junction, leveraging fashion industry partners including H&M and Zara, to secure the groundbreaking land use agreement when momentum was slowing. “Canopy was one of several organizations that started working with international corporate customers of forest products coming out of that region to send a very clear signal that we don’t want to be sourcing from clear cuts of massive, ecologically critical, temperate rainforests, and we don’t want to be sourcing from spirit bear habitat,” she explains.

A decade on, Vogue Business invited Rycroft to reflect on what the Great Bear Rainforest can teach fashion about nature conservation, and using its purchasing power for good.

Logging happens at the beginning of the supply chain, several steps upstream from where brand traceability programs tend to stop. With such a complex, sprawling supply chain, and such a small number of brands on the hook to comply with traceability regulations, few brands have visibility beyond Tier 1 (garment manufacturing) or Tier 2 (fabric production). Logging would come under Tier 4. That’s why meaningful action starts with traceability, says Rycroft, so brands can understand where their deforestation risks are.

But brands don’t need a direct link to deforestation to make a difference in conservation campaigns. “Even if it’s not a direct or immediate sourcing link, the adjacency is really relevant,” says Rycroft. “Brands are still seen as important even if they’re not existing customers, because there is the potential for them to be future customers.”

Anti-logging efforts in the Great Bear Rainforest started in earnest in the mid-1990s, with conservation organizations standing shoulder to shoulder with local First Nations. But the forestry industry was powerful, so media coverage was largely limited to British Columbia, framing the conflict as a domestic “war in the woods” and failing to break through on the international stage. The turning point came when international brands began sending clear signals to the forestry industry that they did not want to source from ancient and endangered ecosystems. This included home improvement companies such as Home Depot and Lowe’s, as well as major retailers like Sainsbury’s.

But even after the various parties agreed to work toward a land use agreement, progress ebbed and flowed. It took more than a decade to reach a legal agreement, during which time brands and conservations continually applied pressure to keep negotiations on track. “It took consumer companies making phone calls and writing letters to individual forestry companies,” says Rycroft. Fashion joined in later. “The process was long and arduous, and for a long time, there was a blindspot around fashion’s footprint in the Great Bear Rainforest.”

It was Canopy that rallied the fashion industry to get involved. In 2013, it created Canopy Style, an initiative where leading fashion brands commit to end sourcing from ancient and endangered forests. One of the early adopters was Stella McCartney. Within a few months of signing onto the pledge, McCartney canceled her contract with a dissolving pulp mill on Vancouver Island, which was sourcing directly from the Great Bear Rainforest, Canopy discovered. “It sent a very clear signal that fashion is a force to be reckoned with,” says Rycroft.

Later down the line, around 2016, progress stalled again. The land use agreement was 18 months overdue, and even the most ardent supporters were starting to feel stuck. Canopy teamed up with national newspaper The Globe and Mail to host a customer-investor roundtable. The date was set for a month ahead. They invited leading politicians, the forest industry and the First Nations leaders that had been involved in the negotiating process, as well as conservation partners and 70 people representing 70 international brands, including Stella McCartney, Eileen Fisher, H&M, and Zara. “Within days of issuing the invitation, the spirit and intent at the negotiating table changed,” says Rycroft. Twenty-four hours before the roundtable was due to take place, the British Columbia government announced the draft land use agreement.

“Brands have incredible social capital and influence, in addition to being an important economic sector,” says Rycroft. “They can’t be afraid to lean in and flex that muscle.”

Brands that sign up to Canopy Style — or Canopy’s equivalent packaging initiative, Pack4Good — commit to stop sourcing from ancient and endangered forests. That’s the baseline, says Rycroft, the Great Bear Rainforest case study shows that fashion’s nature strategies need to go one step further. They also need to include scaling next-gen and circular alternatives that can ease the industry’s burden on nature, and the risk that burden poses to supply chain resilience.

“Next-gen and circular alternatives are the off-ramp from deforestation and forest degradation,” explains Rycroft. “Brands will not be able to eliminate — or even substantially mitigate — their risk of sourcing from high-carbon, high-biodiversity forests unless we have scaled alternatives.”

At last month’s Textile Exchange conference, Canopy walked the industry through Next Gen Warp Speed, its new initiative that makes the business case for brands to convert 5% of their MMCF basket to next-gen alternatives by 2028. Fashion’s struggle to scale next-gen materials has been well-documented, but Canopy is hoping that a 5% commitment is enough to tip the balance without putting a substantial burden on brands to fund the transition. “A big focus for us now is: how do we create the right conditions and pre-competitive vehicles to scale next-gen production?” says Rycroft.

Moving forward, Canopy is applying its learnings from the Great Bear Rainforest win to other critical ecosystems around the world. Top of its list are the Amazon rainforest and the Leuser Ecosystem in Indonesia, where it already has brand buy-in from the likes of Eileen Fisher and Stella McCartney. Rycroft says she is hopeful that fashion can make a significant difference in these landscapes, just as it did in British Columbia.

A few weeks ago, Rycroft traveled up to the Great Bear Rainforest to see the ecosystem Canopy had worked for so many years to protect. She sat on a riverbank and watched a spirit bear pick salmon out of the stream. “So many people dedicated their lives to this cause, or made a call at a critical juncture, to enable that to happen. It has made such a dramatic difference to the landscape. And now the Great Bear Rainforest truly is a landscape of hope.”

#6685. Only Law Roach Could Source a Look From Marc Jacobs’s Louis Vuitton x Richard Prince Collab

Law Roach’s latest archival pull for Kim Kardashian was for the fashion (and art) history buffs.

In October of 2007, Marc Jacobs sent models down the Louis Vuitton runway dressed as an army of over-the-top 1950s-inspired nurses. As seen on the likes of Naomi Campbell, Stephanie Seymour, Eva Herzigova, and Nadja Auermann, baggy plastic coats were layered over colorful dresses and cinched with leather belts, and black lace masks were embroidered with the house’s logo. Each uniform was styled with white tights and white heels, and topped with traditional nurse’s caps—stitched with red sequin letters that together spelled out “Louis Vuitton.”

The campy Spring/Summer 2008 collection, presented during Paris Fashion Week under the helm of then-artistic director Jacobs, was inspired by Richard Prince’s 2003 “Nurse Paintings” series. The pop artist, who rose to prominence in the 1980s, shared Jacobs’s love for a reference—and for this particular body of work, he transformed the covers of mid-20th century medical pulp novels into eery, gory paintings, with messy paint runs and blurry red splotches that read as blood.

The result was a vibrant commentary on society’s portrayal of women as both pure caregivers and sexualized fetishes—an idea which further came to life on the LV models.

(One such painting was even featured on the cover of a Sonic Youth album, 2004’s Sonic Nurse.)

Nearly two decades later, the seminal collection returned to the fashion discourse thanks to Roach (and Kardashian). The stylist, a dedicated archivist who has pulled rare vintage gems for everyone from Zendaya to Ariana Grande, dressed the All’s Fair actor as a Louis Vuitton nurse.

The Spring/Summer 2008 ensemble was complete with the season’s Papillon Frame bag, made in collaboration with Prince, and the duo even worked with milliner Stephen Jones on a custom “K” headpiece.

#6683. What James Gunn’s Firing Means for the Future of DC Studios

For some reason, I foolishly believed they’d get it right this time. James Gunn’s Superman, which formally launched the DC cinematic universe he’s been masterminding alongside Peter Safran, was a refreshing take on a somewhat impenetrable character. I had some reservations about the rest of Gunn’s proposed slate—like following that movie with a Supergirl adventure, which proved to be every bit the misfire I imagined it would be—but bringing a contemporary Clark Kent to the screen was no small accomplishment. Gunn’s tone and his sensibility, I thought, might finally make way for the silver-screen Justice League adventure we deserved.

A silly hope, as proven by Monday’s big news: Gunn and Safran are out, in the wake of the WB-Paramount-Skydance unholy merger. Yet another auteur’s DC regime has been clipped before it could even find its footing. After the shock of the announcement wore off, my mind immediately went to that James Franco meme, the one where he’s about to be hanged. First time?

20 years ago, the idea that superhero C-listers like Iron Man and Thor would be at the top of the film adaptation pyramid while the stars of the Justice League toiled in a constant cycle of developmental destroy-and-rebuild would have been laughable. That’s part of what makes Kevin Feige’s MCU so impressive, of course: not just the scale and scope of his interconnected series of films, but doing it with a bunch of guys who were never all that popular in the larger superhero firmament. But as that regime rose, DC’s fortunes seesawed—with the Christopher Nolan Bat-trilogy as a beautiful outlier—and its fans have had to endure one indignity after another.

Us DC loyalists are basically like fans of the pre-2026 Knicks, or the pre-2004 Red Sox, or the pre-2016 Cavs—take your pick. I wouldn’t even call myself so hardcore, but those were the guys I grew up on, especially as more of a Saturday morning cartoon-watcher than a comics reader. Bruce Timm’s Batman and Superman animated series, the way those two shows dovetailed to make Justice League while also charting bold new territory with Batman Beyond—that was my jam. It was also the era of incredible Fox shows like Spider-Man and X-Men, but never did I think those two would continue to thrive while auteur after auteur tried and failed to do what Timm accomplished before a legion of appreciative 11-year-olds.

It goes back to Wolfgang Peterson’s aborted Batman versus Superman film, a Hollywood sliding doors moment that created the conditions under which a young, hungry Christopher Nolan could prove his blockbuster mettle with Batman Begins and give the greatest hero to ever do it a well-deserved cinematic reset. As Nolan’s stock rose, Bryan Singer’s attempt to restore ‘70s vibes with Superman Returns flopped almost immediately, leaving DC in a Highlander situation yet again. The goodwill Nolan generated with his trilogy gave way to what we came to know as the Snyderverse, starting with Zack Snyder’s Superman reset Man of Steel, a solid film that I could never bring myself to love wholeheartedly.

Historians will tell you it was shareholder thirst to compete with Marvel that spelled doom for Snyder—and the pressure to shoehorn Batman, Wonder Woman and the rest of their squad in to fast-track a Justice League movie. His era certainly cultivated a base of devoted, even rabid stans who will attack anyone who besmirches their leader’s genius. But personally, I spent all of those years in a state of disbelief about the way some of the genre’s sturdiest, best and most crowd-pleasing characters were being subjected to all of this Frank Miller-reject vibes: ultra slo-mo, fight scenes of wanton and artless destruction, not to mention the Gal Gadot line-readings and Bruce Wayne mowing bad guys down in between crossfit sessions. The illest superhero team to do it, in the hands of a guy who saw Jared Leto and thought, “There’s a guy who can succeed Heath Ledger as an Oscar-worthy villain.” Snyder’s step-down from Justice League after a family tragedy and seeing his vision superimposed with Joss Whedon’s was very undignified. But The SnyderCut? Still not for me.

James Gunn’s residency was the most promising thing to happen to the Justice gang in a while, at least for those of us who don’t chug Mountain Dew and listen to Eminem all day. He was the first director in a long time to really, truly understand Superman’s throwback optimistic essence and successfully repackage that for a contemporary audience. Forget about the larger DC universe—what Gunn built in Metropolis alone felt like the beginning of a beautiful universe. Corenswet’s affable take on the character paired with his chemistry with Rachel Brosnahan had me even hoping Gunn would ease up on the big picture and just luxuriate in more Superman adventures. Still, even his slate could only be so fresh: he started in the shadow of Matt Reeves and Robert Pattinson’s The Batman, a critically acclaimed reboot that didn’t square with his vision. At best, we were going to be subjected to the indelicate circumstance of having two different Batmen in production at once. (And that Gunn thought highly enough of Andy Muschietti’s The Flash to tap him for DCU’s Batman film was concerning, for sure.)

But he was building something, and he wasn’t wasting time. Even before he understandably stepped away for a family emergency, Reeves was taking his sweet time to get The Batman II off the ground; Gunn launched his Superman last July and intended to drop a sequel, Man of Tomorrow, next July, one that likely would’ve built up to a Justice League film a little more gracefully than Snyder was allowed to. He may have been indulging side quests a little too freely, green-lighting things like a spin-off series for Skyler Gisondo’s Jimmy Olsen, but his focus on the main play at hand never wavered. The narrative that he was meandering was always in bad faith; look no further than Superman's first act, which breathlessly goes about establishing the status quo of Gunn’s DCU at times to the script’s detriment.

We were already seeing those seeds planted: this past summer’s Lanterns series on HBO, for instance, through which Aaron Pierre managed to turn John Stewart into something closer to a household name hero. (Pierre and Adria Arjona, who is most likely playing Wonder Woman, were set to appear in Man of Tomorrow.) Gunn’s quippy, vibrant vision may not have been for everyone, but he at least deserved the chance to cook a little bit longer. In a weird way, Gunn’s firing feels like one of the first pushbacks to the midterms blue wave. Looking for politics in comic book fare is ultimately asinine, but there’s a reason Superman 2025 was one of the most meme'd movies during the post November 3rd wave of optimism, to say nothing of the movie's plot being a paper-thin allegory for Israel and Palestine.

So what happens now? Who knows. Man of Tomorrow might be released as a sort of post-mortem, or it could be shelved altogether. Does David Corenswet go the way of Brandon Routh? Have we seen the last of this iteration of John Stewart? Will Adria Arjona’s Wonder Woman even get off the ground?

We’re back to square one. Skydance head David Ellision has already replaced Gunn and Safran with ex-MCU producer Jeremy Latcham, a guy who’s more concerned about making movies that’ll play for meemaw, peepaw and the reverend. It appears he'll be a down-the-middle role player who can serve up the most basic, populist take on all of these adaptations. I’m giving up on ever seeing a coherent, let alone genuinely great take on this squad of heroes. Many have tried, all have failed, and the people in charge have only gotten dumber. Go with God, DC faithful. We’ll always have the Bruce Timm cartoons.

#6682. On the Podcast: Léa Seydoux Has a Shopping Problem. Plus: WNBA Star Gabby Williams!

More than a decade after winning the Palme d’Or for her role in 2013’s Blue Is the Warmest Color, Léa Seydoux—the self-proclaimed “queen of Cannes”—has confidently made the seaside city and festival her domain. Just earlier this year, she was there to celebrate two of her latest projects: Marie Kreutzer’s Gentle Monster, which comes to Netflix on November 18, and Arthur Harari’s The Unknown.

For this Thursday’s episode of The Run-Through, Seydoux gathered with Chloe Malle and Taylor Antrim to discuss both ambitious films, which she shot shortly after giving birth to her second child.

“I used this body as a tool,” she explained. “Most of the time you see actresses with bodies that are very controlled, especially here in America. And if I can speak for myself, I’m a bit tired of seeing all these bodies that are just very skinny and not very real. I’m proud to show this body that we’re not used to seeing onscreen.”

The group also got into Seydoux’s long-time friendship with fellow French actress Adèle Exarchopoulos, who sported a “Léa Forever” T-shirt at Cannes this year. “We have a great relationship,” Seydoux said of her Blue Is the Warmest Color co-star. “I mean, we grew up together. She’s a great inspiration as well. I love her freedom—the way she’s not polished, you know? She is herself and very genuine.”

In addition to being a massively talented actress, Seydoux is also a “shopaholic,” as she puts it. She is a huge fan of buying vintage and scouring online auctions, though on this latest trip to New York, she made a stop at Los Angeles Apparel; they don’t have outposts in France. Art is another passion: “I collect paintings that represent motherhood.”

Also on today’s episode, Senior Wellness and Beauty Editor Margaux Anbouba and Global Talent Casting Director Ignacio Murrillo sit down for a chat with Golden State Valkyries forward Gabby Williams about winning the WNBA championship last week.

#6680. Denis Villeneuve Talks ‘Dune: Part Three’ and Rebooting James Bond: ‘We Cannot F*ck It Up.’

“I’m out of a job,” Denis Villeneuve said, jokingly. Hours earlier, Villeneuve had signed off on the IMAX 70-milimeter print of Dune: Part Three, officially wrapping post-production on that film—and in turn, a decade-long chapter of the Quebecois writer-director’s working life.

Fresh off this milestone, Villeneuve and GQ had come to the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles for a conversation and a private screening of Dune: Part Two, presented by OMEGA, in honor of his anointment as GQ’s Director of the Year. Global Editorial Director Adam Baidawi introduced Villeneuve before the director and GQ’s Zach Baron dove into a conversation that covered his original Dune plans, where Dune: Part Three breaks from its predecessors, and Villeneuve’s feelings about taking over the James Bond franchise.

GQ’s Adam Baidawi and Zach Baron with Denis Villeneuve

“I feel light,” the director of the year told Baron, then added, “Numb.” He was still processing Dune’s end, he said—while also coming to grips with closing the book on “the most rewarding, inspiring, and best ten years of my life as a filmmaker.”

Villeneuve’s first two Dune films have raked in more than a billion dollars at the box office. Part Three appears likely to nearly double that when it hits theaters (and locks up most of the world’s IMAX screens) a week before Christmas. But at one point during his conversation with Baron, the director pushed back gently on the notion of these movies as a “franchise.”

“There was nothing industrial in the way they were made,” Villeneuve said. They were the work of “a bunch of friends”—a familial crew, out in the desert putting things together.

“In French,” the Quebecois director continued, “there is a word—artisanal. They are very personal. Made with a lot of care. They’re little big things—but in a way, they are delicate.”

After all, as sprawling and cosmically grand as they are, these movies are also a deeply personal project for the director, born of images that took root in his head when he first read Frank Herbert’s thick-as-a-brick, notoriously adaptation-resistant 1965 novel Dune at age 13. Later, as Villeneuve racked up credits and clout, people would ask him what his dream project was; the answer was always Dune.

“I kept saying to myself, Someone else will do it one day,” he told Baron. “Another filmmaker will adapt this book again. And I kept waiting, and I kept waiting, until I felt ready to do it myself.”

Herbert wrote five escalatingly bonkers Dune sequels before his death in 1986, but Villeneuve intended to walk away from the table after adapting the first book across two films.

“Trilogies are very dangerous,” he told Baron. “The first movie is a promise, and if you fulfill the promise with the second one, then there’s a feeling of security that comes with that, and you feel that you have a recipe…That’s the trap. Because then you repeat yourself.”

But after wrapping Part Two, Villeneuve found himself unable to stop thinking about Dune Messiah—the second Dune novel, which Herbert supposedly wrote in frustration, believing the audience had missed the point by embracing Paul Atreides as a hero.

Villeneuve said his take on Messiah is “a different beast” than the first two films, built it around the tension between Timothée Chalamet’s Paul and his Fremen consort Chani (Zendaya), who Villeneuve has re-imagined—in a pivotal departure from Herbert’s version—as a nonbeliever who takes a critical view of Paul’s rise to power.

Neel Shah, Timothy Simons, and Michael Lasker

Of course, the specter (S.P.E.C.T.R.E.?) of another franchise hung over the proceedings at the Lucas Museum. Villeneuve, after all, is only technically between jobs; he’s a self-described “monomaniac” who insists that he can only hyper-focus on one project at a time and has been locked in on Dune for a decade, but the as-yet-untitled 26th Bond film is in motion, with Villeneuve signed on to direct.

GQ’s Adam Baidawi, Denis Villeneuve, and OMEGA’s Lucien Jornod

He could say almost nothing in public about the project, or even when he’d begin shooting it—he joked about having “the target of the sniper” on his chest—but spoke of feeling the responsibility not to fail: “We cannot fuck it up. We do not have the choice.”

Over the past week, the casting rumors around Villeneuve’s Bond reboot have reached what our UK colleagues accurately termed the “fever-dream” stage. It might be Callum Turner or Slow Horses’ Jack Lowden, but it might be Robert Pattinson, who’s emerged as a surprise front-runner after months of supposition about the part being earmarked for a relative unknown. At some point, toward the end of Tuesday’s conversation, the subject of Bond 26’s lead could no longer be avoided.

“Has the role of James Bond been cast?” Baron asked the director.

“It’s—it’s in the process. In the process,” Villeneuve said with a smile. “I am pushing the gas.”

“Blink once for Robert Pattinson,” Baron suggested, “and twice for Callum Turner.”

Villeneuve, for the record, did not blink. ✦

GQ would like to thank Legendary Entertainment, Warner Bros., and Brianna Smith.

#6679. Ariana Grande Brings Her Two Great Loves—Ricky Álvarez and Rare Vintage—to the Red Carpet

Ariana Grande brought two of her greatest loves to the red carpet last night: boyfriend Ricky Álvarez and a very, very good piece of vintage.

At the New York premiere of Focker-in-Law, the singer and actor made her first red carpet appearance with Álvarez since rekindling their romance earlier this year. And if their constant embraces, adoring glances, and kisses were anything to go by, the pair are very much still in the honeymoon phase.

Stylist Law Roach selected a vintage 1990s Badgley Mischka gown for the occasion. The delicate, spaghetti-strapped design featured a pale silver-gray windowpane check, a fitted bodice scattered with tiny beaded flowers, and a voluminous floor-skimming skirt. She accessorized with Swarovski Matrix hoop earrings—a recent favorite—and traded the flipped bob she’s been sporting of late for a sleek micro ponytail, tied with a little ivory ribbon. Makeup was also her go-to style of glowy and highlight-dominant.

Roach is on a particularly impressive archival streak of late. He’s been mining the fashion vaults for Kim Kardashian’s All's Fair press tour, pulling everything from 1990s Dolce & Gabbana to Paco Rabanne couture. Just last weekend, he dressed Anya Taylor-Joy in a spectacularly ruffled spring 1997 Pierre Cardin ensemble for the LACMA Art+Film Gala.

Grande has long been a devotee of fashion’s more whimsical, romantic history. Her love of vintage reached particularly fanciful heights during the Wicked press tours, but the singer has since held firmly to her soft, ultra-feminine aesthetic with 1950s silhouettes and diaphanous fabrics. At one point, her dedication to the look was so pronounced that some wondered whether she was quietly auditioning for a rumored Audrey Hepburn biopic. Roach revealed that he’d bought the Badgley Mischka gown months earlier, drawn to its connection with the era of the original Meet the Parents film.

Álvarez, for his part, kept things considerably more low-key. The dancer and photographer wore a relaxed black blazer over an open-neck white shirt, tucked into dark indigo jeans with rolled cuffs, a leather belt, and brown shoes. Some classic easy-going boyfriend dressing. He spent much of the evening with an arm around Grande’s waist, while she leaned into him, held his hands, and beamed up at him for the cameras.

Of course, the couple’s love story has its own history. Grande and Álvarez first met when he worked as a backup dancer on her Honeymoon Tour in 2015. They dated for around a year before splitting in 2016, and he later received a memorable name-check in her 2018 breakup anthem, “thank u, next.” Almost a decade later, however, things have come full circle. Rumors of a reunion began circulating this summer when the pair were spotted together in Austin, Texas, during Grande’s Eternal Sunshine tour, before more sightings followed in Florida and New York. By August, they were Instagram official, and Grande had debuted a new tattoo reading “I do love you”, seemingly matching a similar inscription on Álvarez’s collarbone. The two were also spotted arm-in-arm around London, where Grande completed her 10-night residency at the O2. She even began rewriting the Ricky lyrics in “thank u, next” onstage. At one Brooklyn show, she sang, “Wrote some songs about Ricky / We always find our way back.” By the tour’s September finale in London, the sentiment had become considerably more definitive: “I’m tryna make him my last.”

More recently, they’ve been enjoying some more ordinary couple activities, including cheering on runners at the New York City Marathon earlier this month. Grande has also enlisted Álvarez for a particularly kiss-heavy R.E.M. Beauty lip-product guessing game on Instagram. The adoration and affection is showing no signs of slowing down.

Between a decade-old romance finding new life and a beautiful dress pulled from the archives, Ariana Grande is making a persuasive case for revisiting the past.

#6678. The Best Apple Deals to Shop Before Black Friday

AirTags and AirPods are already up to 20 percent off

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Black Friday is arguably the best time of the year to shop for Apple tech. While the tech giant doesn’t run sales of its own, other retailers often offer their own markdowns during this holiday sales event. Get a head start now, and you won’t need to wait until the holiday weekend to score markdowns on AirPods, MacBooks, Apple Watches, and other popular Apple products. Amazon is already offering over a dozen lead-up deals. Here, we’ll detail which Apple discounts are worth shopping early and which products you should wait to buy.

If you’re going to shop one product early, make it Apple AirTags, which dropped to their lowest price ever in time for holiday travel. Individual trackers are $23, but the discounted four-pack brings the cost down to $20 apiece.

The new AirPods 5 and trendy EarPods remain at full price (for now), but other headphones are already discounted. Currently, you can save $50 on the noise-canceling AirPods Pro 3 and $100 on the over-the-ear AirPods Max 2. These products could drop further during Amazon’s Turkey 12 sale—the e-tailer’s name for this year’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday event—but they could also sell out, as they have in years past.

If you’re in need of a new laptop, now’s a good time to make the purchase. Select MacBook models are already discounted. The 2026 Pro is still full price, but the 2026 Air is up to 15 percent off. The budget-friendly MacBook Neo hasn’t gone on sale yet, though we suspect it will be discounted for the first time during Amazon’s Turkey 12 sales event.

Apple Watch shoppers may want to wait, depending on the model they’re after. The Series 12 and SE 3 haven’t budged, but you can already save up to $100 on the giftable Ultra 4.

All three iPad models are currently marked down on Amazon. Based on past price history, there’s a small chance the Pro, Air, and classic 11-inch iPad will see a slightly deeper discount during the official sale, but we don’t expect prices to drop significantly. We’re also seeing strong early deals on Apple accessories like keyboards and chargers.

#6676. This Home Locker Made My Entryway So Much More Functional

Mustard Made home lockers blend utilitarian functionality and bold color for the perfect entryway and mudroom furniture.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

I’m always on the hunt for products that nail the sweet spot between form and function. And with a toddler at home, let’s just say we’ve accumulated stuff. Toys, shoes, kid gear, you name it. Our entryway, laundry room and pretty much every shared space could use a little organizational intervention.

So, when I first saw Mustard Made lockers online, I was intrigued. The bold colors and playful, schoolhouse-inspired design, coupled with the range of sizes, made them feel like a storage upgrade with personality. I was looking for a compact catch-all near the front door for the shoes, hats and everyday essentials we’re constantly grabbing on our way out.

The more I thought about it, the more I liked the idea of a home locker: sturdy metal, magnetic doors and an easy-to-clean finish. Sold. I ordered the two-door Midi locker from Mustard.

Of course, choosing a color was a whole ordeal. I played it safe with Chalk, expecting a crisp white, but it turned out to be more of a warm off-white. It’s not quite what I pictured, but it works in our space. That said, if I could do it all over again, I’d tell myself to be bold and go with Mustard or Olive.

Here’s how the locker came together, how it’s holding up and whether it’s helping tame the everyday chaos.

A utilitarian storage cabinet that pairs versatile functionality with a pop of color

The Midi arrived on my porch in a flat, narrow box that was easy to lift and carry where I needed to build it. Once I unpacked everything, I was happy to find that most of the locker simply slots and clicks into place. No tools, screws or complicated assembly required. The only tool I needed was a Phillips-head screwdriver to attach the door handles.

Mustard Made includes printed instructions, and you can also find them on the website, along with a step-by-step assembly video if you need a little extra guidance.

The trickiest part? Getting the doors on. They can take a bit of fiddling, but gently bending the small tab helps hold the L-shaped bracket in place and keeps the door steady while you assemble it.

Once assembled, the locker feels solid, sturdy and made to last. But it’s the brand’s attention to detail that really makes it functional. There are attachment points on the back for securing it to the wall (a welcome feature with a toddler around), interior hooks on each door for hanging smaller items, adjustable shelves and even a cable hole in the back for managing cords.

And the customization options are a bonus, even though they’re sold separately. Mustard Made sells extra shelves, super-strong button magnets and metal hangers for the Skinny and Twinny lockers, which can double as mini wardrobes. They also offer adorable alphabet and number magnets for displaying messages, labeling spaces or giving older kids something to play with.

Another thing I love? Mustard Made offers six different locker styles and sizes, so there’s an option for just about every room and organizational storage need.

My daughter loves using the locker as a little art gallery, proudly displaying her masterpieces. And it’s not just for artwork. The home locker is a fun spot for handwritten notes, photos, collectible magnets and other little things we want to put on display. The Mustard Made button magnets are surprisingly strong and sturdy, too, holding much more than your average fridge magnet.

If you have things you want to keep under lock and key, Mustard Made has you covered. Each locker door comes with its own lock and set of keys. It took me a little while to realize that the locks are different, so a heads-up: each door comes with two keys, and you’ll want to keep them organized. Mixing them up (or losing them altogether) could lead to frustration.

In our house, the locker is primarily a shoe drop zone by the front door, so we haven’t had much reason to use the locks. But I can see this feature coming in handy for storing valuables or keeping potentially hazardous household items out of little hands. Just be sure to use appropriate child-safety measures for anything that poses a risk.

With so many shapes, sizes and colors to choose from, Mustard Made lockers are a versatile storage solution for just about any room. Think mudrooms, laundry rooms, playrooms, entryways, porches and beyond.

They’re not limited to hiding clutter, either. Depending on the style and size, they can pull double duty as entertainment consoles, wardrobes, buffet tables or even drink cabinets. Basically, they’re as flexible as they are functional.

A colorful home locker for your entryway, mudroom, playroom, garage, porch and beyond

You can shop the Midi and the full range of lockers directly from Mustard Made. The Midi retails for $369 and comes in 12 colors. Want something a little more design-forward? The brand also offers lockers with fluted glass doors for a more elevated look.

#6675. Kim Kardashian Plays Nurse in One of Louis Vuitton’s Rarest Runway Looks

Kim Kardashian has been raiding the fashion archives with extraordinary enthusiasm of late, but her latest vintage pull comes with a health warning. Enter: a very rare, almost 20-year-old Louis Vuitton nurse uniform, complete with a monogrammed lace face mask, personalized cap, and coordinating accessories. The look, from Marc Jacobs’s spring 2008 collection for the house, is a heart-palpitating piece of runway history.

The ensemble was sourced by stylist Law Roach from the personal archive of Lauren Pyes, a Boston-based Harvard University employee and avid collector of Jacobs-era Louis Vuitton, whose extraordinary collection Vogue first explored last year. Pyes has spent years scouring resale platforms, boutiques, and obscure corners of the internet for some of the designer’s most coveted creations, amassing what she affectionately calls the “Marchive.”

“Law reached out to me a few months ago and was interested in pieces of the Marchive," Pyes tells Vogue. “Suffice to say, I was thrilled to loan them to him.” When Roach first contacted her, she could scarcely believe it was him. “I kept toggling back and forth to make sure it wasn’t a spam account!” she recalls. “Although he has a larger-than-life public persona, Law is deeply kind and gracious in addition to being the visionary he is rightly lauded as. I have so much respect for his dedication to telling stories through fashion and his commitment to finding the pieces that do exactly that.”

And few collections have quite as much storytelling potential as Louis Vuitton’s spring 2008 offering. Presented in Paris in October 2007, the show opened with a procession of supermodels—including Naomi Campbell, Stephanie Seymour, Eva Herzigova, and Nadja Auermann—dressed as nurses in sheer, pastel-colored uniforms, black lace masks, and white caps. The inspiration was the American artist Richard Prince, whose provocative Nurse Paintings informed the collection and accompanying collaboration with the house. Reviewing the collection at the time, Vogue’s Sarah Mower described it as a “typical Jacobs coup of multidimensional, referential, and self-referential significance,” and a “hilariously kinky parade” that “reflected Jacobs’s way of walking the line between creative freedom and commercial innovation.” It was one of Jacobs’s most deviant, deliciously strange runway spectacles.

The shoes from Louis Vuitton spring 2028.

The full look, as sourced by Lauren Pyes.

Kim Kardashian’s interpretation was remarkably faithful to the original. She wore the sheer, short-sleeved white nurse’s coat cinched at the waist over a delicate, peach-colored silk dress, with white stockings and peep-toe heels. A black lace Louis Vuitton face mask covered her mouth, while a white nurse’s cap (commissioned by Roach and reimagined by legendary milliner Stephen Jones) bearing a red “K” sat atop her sleek dark hair. In her arms was another treasure from the collection: an Aquarelle Papillon bag. The shoes also hailed from spring 2008.

Bringing together such a complete ensemble was no small undertaking. “I sourced these pieces from all over—including platforms like Poshmark and Vestiaire Collective—for over a year,” Pyes explains. The dresses have become a particular obsession: she has owned four, including a pink silk satin version that remains in her permanent collection. Vogue actually purchased another of the orange dresses—the same color Kardashian wore—from Pyes a little over a year ago. But the real rarity is the mask and overcoat, which Pyes considers among her most treasured finds. Earlier this year, the ensemble was exhibited at the Savannah College of Art and Design (SCAD), where it even caught the attention of one of its original creators.

“I had it exhibited at SCAD back in April, and Stephen Jones—who made it in collaboration with Louis Vuitton—was apparently surprised that it even existed!” Pyes says of the mask. “If the person who made it was in disbelief by seeing it, I guess that means it is pretty rare!”

Kardashian and Roach have been on a formidable archival streak throughout the All’s Fair press tour, resurrecting everything from ’90s Paco Rabanne couture to vintage Dolce & Gabbana and Jean Paul Gaultier-era Hermès. The Louis Vuitton nurse look is their most playful fashion deep dive yet.

And for Pyes, it’s precisely that irreverence that makes the Jacobs years so compelling. She points to the extraordinary creative team behind the collection, including Peter Copping, then head of womenswear and now creative director of Lanvin, and Camille Miceli, currently at the helm of Pucci. “This collection and these pieces are so special because they highlight what Marc and his team did so well—seamlessly integrating fashion and art into a cohesive and powerful narrative,” she says. She remembers the supermodel casting, the nurse uniforms, and even Jacobs taking his final bow beside a custom Vuitton trunk playing an episode of SpongeBob SquarePants. “There are so many elements that were unexpected and genuine in a pre-social media age.”

Pyes, of course, has continued to do some killer sourcing. She’s recently completed a “trifecta of accessories” from the Louis Vuitton fall 2011 collection, better known as the “Fetish Collection.” This includes a shearling porter hat, mask hair accessory, and a patent leather bib. On the non-vintage side of things? “I am champing at the bit to receive the custom order I put in from Marc’s Spring 2027 collection,” she shares. “After more than 40 years, he continues to create incredible fashion and I feel fortunate to be adding this ensemble to the Marchive!”

Whether Kim’s look was a Halloween latergram, another cheeky press tour outing, or just a moment of play inside an impressive archive, for now, is anyone’s guess. Whatever the occasion, Pyes is delighted to see the collection enjoying a new life in the public imagination. Nearly two decades after its debut, Jacobs’s peculiar, provocative vision remains as potent as ever. “These clothes are not just beautiful and special,” she says, “but also consequential. This collection walked almost 20 years ago and yet continues to figure so largely in pop culture and the imagination of fashion lovers.” Nurse Kardashia, the defibrillator please!
