#6636. The Best Oxford Shirt for Men in 2026, According to GQ

The story behind the Oxford shirt is a lot less thrilling than you’d expect. It didn’t earn that fancy-sounding sobriquet through some sacred connection to the tony British university; instead, the shirt's signature cotton fabric was just one of four named after a group of schools picked by a Scottish mill for their associations with society’s upper crust. (19th century marketing at its best!)

But of the quartet—the others were Harvard, Cambridge, and Yale, FYI—only the Oxford shirt achieved menswear icon status, becoming a quintessential emblem of American prep as a “sporting shirt” and then as a staple of casual attire. Nowadays, Oxford-cloth shirts come in every color imaginable, but none of ‘em look quite as classic as the OG—especially when they’re thoroughly worn-in and a little wrinkled. Below you’ll find 16 of our absolute favorites, each one more ready than the last to imbue your jeans, chinos, and trousers with the unmistakable swagger of adopted American royalty.

J.Crew’s Oxford shirts have been a staple of the catalog for decades and though its iconic Secret Wash shirts are the bestsellers of the bunch, we prefer its more recent release, the 1983 Oxford Shirt. It’s easy to miss the differences at a glance, yet the handful of subtle tweaks add up quick. First, the fit: a comfier, more relaxed silhouette that, despite its ‘80s reference, is spot on for 2027. Second, the fabric: a noticeably sturdier, heftier all-cotton Oxford that makes its best-selling Secret Wash shirts feel wimpy by comparison. Third, and most importantly, the collar: unlike its most popular shirts, the 1983 Oxford has a satisfyingly taller collar with a prep-approved collar roll. It gives the shirt more life and more nuance, but also looks great under a blazer.

If there’s any brand that could do the Oxford justice, it’s the British label, Drake’s, known for its none-too-posh take on all things tailoring. Its handsome entry into the Oxford shirt ring is a confluence of top-shelf materials and methodical construction, wrapped into a single shirt worth saving up for. Handmade in Somerset, England, Drake’s Oxford features single-needle construction with finished seams throughout, which takes the cut and sew process twice as long to complete—on top of the high-density stitching you’ll find throughout the shirt. Lustrous mother-of-pearl buttons make for a luxe upgrade while the collar—a button-down with a fabulous collar roll—is constructed with a floating interlining to give it a soft structure.

All in, Drake’s Oxford is what most other Oxfords aspire to be. And if you’re curious about what comes after J.Crew, this is your answer.

Wythe’s built its brand on western aesthetics with lasting quality—think properly-made cowboy boots, Yellowstone-worthy coats, and snap shirts. That the label would produce something as east-coast as an Oxford shirt is head-scratching. And yet, it’s one of the best versions we’ve tried. That’s because Wythe takes the same sort of rigor that it uses for its western and workwear garments and applies it to the preppy classic. This as close as anyone can get to a deadstock Oxford shirt plucked from a long-forgotten storage room. From the box pleat and locker loop to the unstructured long-point button-down collar, size-stamped collar stand and nostalgic paper packaging, it’s a good reminder of why prep in the ‘60s was so, so good.

Plain Oxford shirts too simple for your liking? Thom Browne's take isn’t overtly avant-garde, but it does boast a striped grosgrain placket that shows itself when you undo the top or bottom buttons, a stitched-on tag near the right hip, and a similarly striped locker loop beneath the collar. Each one is made in Italy from a soft, durable cotton fabric with noticeable cuffs and a sharply curved hem, making this iteration a better fit with sleek dress pants or even your most refined athleisure. (Talking to you, sneakers-with-suit crowd.)

This shirt won’t win you any browny points with the tailoring nerds, it will earn you cred with the fashion elite.

For the guy who’s quick to chat your ear off for 20 minutes when all you said was, “nice pants”, Jake’s is the go-to shirt whisperer. Jake’s began as founder Jake Wigham was amidst his studies at the London College of Fashion, honing his skills at a tailoring apprenticeship and fulfilling custom projects. It eventually blossomed into the talk of the menswear cognoscenti, who praised Wigham’s shirtmaking prowess. Each shirt is made-to-order, cut and sewn in the Jake’s studio by a small team of expert craftspeople, according to your specific measurements, with options for different collars, pockets, and fabrics. While we’ll always respect the old guard shirtmakers who’ve honed their style over generations, Jake’s bridges the gap between traditional craft and modern appeal—a Savile Row approach that speaks internet.

According to menswear lore, Brooks Brothers is responsible for bringing the Oxford shirt stateside. Quite a few decades later, everything’s still here, from the telltale collar to the button cuffs, patch pockets, and curved hems. One note: Brooks Brothers says it’s a ‘regular fit’, but there’s a bit more room in the chest than some of its counterparts.

Japan's obsession with Americana often comes full circle, as is the case with Kamakura. Its shirts are the envy of so many labels for its craftsmanship which parallels that of custom shirtmakers. We're talking mother-of-pearl buttons, high-density stitching, and major attention to minor details like the roll of the collar and single-needle seams.

Gitman Vintage's stateside-produced shirts have been a fixture of tasteful menswear shops for years not only for its high quality control, but for its tailored silhouettes and idiosyncratic details like chalk buttons, its signature contrasting horizontal bottom button hole, and soft collars.

J.Press's take on the Oxford shirt stands out as among the preppiest examples. Not only does it come from the storied uniform supplier of Yale's student body, but the perfectly rolled collar and flap chest pocket details give it a distinctly collegiate look that would pass muster on any Ivy League campus.

The Clark shirt is one of Proper Cloth's best selling shirts thanks to its beefy Oxford cloth material, bewilderingly good construction (felled seams, split yoke, unfused placket, shanked buttons), and near-perfect fit. For $125, you cannot get a better Oxford shirt. But you have to be willing to wait because every shirt is made to order and will take a couple weeks to get to you. If you can remember to think ahead and have some patience, it’s well worth the wait.

Swedish brand Rubato crafts its R Oxford less traditionally, but it’s no less an Oxford because of it. It might eschew the conventional button-down collar, but thanks its super-tight blue stripes, button cuffs, and a fitted body designed to look good tucked or untucked, it skews decidedly old-world. The real clincher though, is the fabric, a 100% Sea Island cotton so soft we keep trying to pet our computer screen.

With a nerd-satisfying 22 stitches per inch, troca shell buttons, and other refined details, you’d be forgiven for thinking this shirt was made on Jermyn Street, famed for its shirtmaking history. But Sid’s shirts are proudly made in Honduras which makes them a great value compared to the British alternative.

Todd Snyder's lightweight Oxford shirt takes the OG and makes it even more casual, a perfect piece for layering over a graphic tee thanks to its relaxed fit and feather-light cotton fabric.

The quality of an Oxford shirt comes down to the fabric, construction, fit, and collar. They’re a distinct kind of button-up that warrants its own buying guide separate from dress shirts. Why? There’s so much history behind the style and the fabric.

Oxford cloth is beefier than a typical dress shirt fabric with more texture and thus has a more casual quality befitting of rumpled chinos and sneakers, territory most dress shirt fabrics would feel absolutely out of place. Seph Skerritt, CEO of Proper Cloth, says “You can think of it as a tougher, more durable and more casual cousin to the pinpoint dress shirt.” The cotton yarns are thicker than broadcloth, twill, and poplin, so the hand is noticeably less fine. The heftier material means a high-quality Oxford cloth is more durable and can even last as long as a decade.

Construction-wise, you should typically look for the same sort of details as you would with other dress shirts. Clean stitches, felled seams, buttons properly sewn with shanks, and reinforced at the side seams. High-quality Oxford shirts will also feature a split yoke which is the panel that spans the shoulders and is cut on the bias to give the area natural stretch for ease of motion.

Fit is subjective, of course, but you want to make sure that the shoulder seams line up with your natural shoulders, if not a little below for a relaxed fit. The chest shouldn’t pull, but shouldn’t feel like a potato sack. As for the body, this is more or less subjective and delves into the kind of silhouette you’re after, but if the fabric is pulling around the buttons, your shirt is too tight. And, depending on whether you like to tuck, should be long enough.

Oxford cloth shirts can come in any variety of collars, but the most common are button-down, spread, and point collars. Big menswear nerds will obsess over finding the perfect collar roll, a detail found in the golden age of Ivy style by the likes of Brooks Brothers and J.Press.

Oxford shirts are near and dear to our hearts. They’re classic, versatile, and durable—true staples that every guy should have. So we had opinions on what we wanted out of them. It all starts with the star of the show—the titular fabric. The Oxford cloth has to be meatier than the average dress shirt and with some noticeable texture. They should ideally be able to rumple more than crease and wrinkle.

From there, we looked for Oxfords that are well-constructed with beautiful buttons and, crucially, handsome collars. And because you can be surprised no matter how much you’re paying, we looked at Oxfords in all price points to find the best ones regardless of the tag.

So we looked to the seasoned veterans that built the Oxford’s reputation as well as the newcomers that are pushing it into the 21st-century as well as the runway designers that have let their imaginations run wild.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6635. The Best Subscription Boxes for Men, Tested for Quality and Value

Tested by Emily Way, Paul Rankin and Caroline Lubinsky

From craft beer and gourmet jerky to bold coffee and unique snacks, these food and drink subscriptions are gifts any guy will love.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

When it comes to gift and subscription boxes for men, brands like Bespoke Post and Dollar Shave Club often get the spotlight. But at Taste of Home, food is our specialty, and we know a thing or two about food subscriptions. That’s why we’ve rounded up our favorite food and drink subscription boxes for men, with something for every palate, from savory jerky and craft beer to bold coffee.

We tracked down and tested some of the best food clubs to find boxes worth savoring. Whether you’re shopping for a hard-to-buy-for guy or treating yourself, these thoughtfully curated subscriptions make it easy to discover new flavors and enjoy something delicious month after month.

I’ve said it before, but if you ask my husband what his favorite part of my job is, he might say it’s when I get to test a meat delivery box. And Porter Road, essentially an online butcher shop, is one of my favorites.

The Best of Porter Road Box truly makes a fabulous gift for the meat lover in your life. With bone-in pork chops, ground beef, bacon, dry-aged steaks, breakfast sausage and chorizo links, this specific box offers a wide variety of all the brand has to offer. But Porter Road also has many other curated subscription boxes to choose from, too.

If you know (or you are) a meat lover who appreciates great-tasting cuts, it’s certainly a subscription  worth the investment. The meat I tried was flavorful, tender and high-quality, comparable to that of a local butcher shop with top quality meats.

Available every two, four, eight weeks or twelve weeks, you can choose how often your special, curated box of meat is delivered. And if you’d rather create your own custom subscription box to gift, you can do that too for a gift he’s sure to love.

Men like meat, right? If you’re looking for yet another meat subscription option, this one is bacon specific. Tester Marisa Hillman tried three months of Goldbelly’s bacon club, which offers approximately 2 to 5 pounds of bacon from a new butcher each month. Her first box, which was her favorite, came with four 14-ounce packages of bacon from The Loveless Cafe in Nashville: hickory, applewood, maplewood and peppered.

“I cooked a package of the Goldbelly bacon, immediately followed by a package of grocery store (Jimmy Dean brand) bacon,” says Marisa. “The difference was incredible. The Goldbelly bacon slices were thick and flavorful with minimal grease left behind. The grocery store bacon slices were thin and I had to empty the grease three times while cooking.”

Marisa’s second delivery was a bit more adventurous. It included two 12-ounce packages of bacon, one 8-ounce package of jowl bacon and one 8-ounce package of bacon bits from Smoking Goose in Indiana. While she didn’t love the jowl bacon, she did enjoy the bacon bits and Smoking Goose bacon.

Her third box included two 1-pound packages of regular bacon from Benton’s Smoky Mountain Country Hams. Marisa noted that the final shipment contained bacon which was mostly fat. While the fatty cuts didn’t particularly appeal to her, it may to folks who are open to non-traditional bacon—especially adventurous cuts.

With Murray’s Mac and Cheese Club, he can have fresh warm and gooey macaroni and cheese whenever. The mac and cheese arrives ready to be heated in the oven or stashed in the freezer, so a comforting meal is just moments away when the craving strikes.

You can opt for a three, six or twelve month subsctiption, and each month brings a shipment of two 32-ounce frozen mac and cheese portions. One is always Murray’s famous, classic cheddar flavor. The other is a different flavor each month that’s exclusive to the club.

“I received both a regular and spinach and artichoke mac. The mac and cheese looked good right out of the box, and both were still nicely chilled from the ice,” says tester Caroline Lubinsky. “I was a little surprised to see that they were a bit smaller than I expected for the price, but they looked appetizing in the pans.”

In comparison to other easy, cheesy brands (think Kraft or Annie’s), Murray’s definitely takes the cake. We also like that you receive a specialty flavor each month. While the packaging is more practical than it is pretty, this delicious subscription makes a great gift for someone who loves carbs.

Gourmet jerky delivered right to your door? Say less. If you have a jerky lover in your life, this is the gift for them.

Our own resident jerky lover Paul Rankin tried Jerky Dynasty Club and was impressed by everything from the presentation to the products. “I loved how much variety there was in the box, definitely plenty of jerky to get me through an entire month (or more),” he says in this Dynasty Club review.

Paul’s box contained three big bags of jerky and some smaller meat sticks. While the contents were mostly beef and pork jerky, there were also some unexpected meats like venison, elk and wild boar. In total, he received bags of Carnivore Candy Peppered Brisket jerky, Ayoba-yo Droëwors beef sticks, Smoking Gun Wicked Mary jerky and Hunters Reserve Roadkill summer sausage. He also enjoyed an Indian Valley Venison Pepper jerky stick and a Dill Pickle jerky stick. “The flavors were intense and interesting,” says Paul.

In addition to delicious jerky, Paul points out that this subscription is a great value. “Considering how much a regular bag of jerky is at the grocery store, this subscription box is a great deal,” notes Paul. “A regular bag of jerky is around $12 at my grocery store (for under 3 ounces), and this box gives you 16-24 ounces, so your dollar is really stretching far.”

The City Brew Tours club really is a club, complete with its own monthly podcast for die-hard brewski fans, making it the perfect subscription gift for hop heads.

The City Brew Tours staff curates each selection and includes a detailed printout containing information about the tasting notes and breweries chosen, plus a little about the featured city. Inclusions range from sours to IPAs and everything in between, so it’s an ideal subscription for those who appreciate beers of all kinds.

“My box arrived filled to the brim with brews from Pittsburgh. The insert with an overview of the city, facts about Pittsburgh brewing and info about each beer was incredibly enlightening and a great introduction to what the city offers,” says Shopping Editor Emily Way. “It was also cool to have access to the tasting notes and enjoy two brews from each brewery—not to mention all the one-on-one insight gleaned from the Zoom call.”

You don’t have to know the ins and outs of his home coffee setup to gift this coffee membership subscription. The Cometeer coffee subscription features the convenience of instant coffee without the taste of instant coffee. Score! These genius recyclable capsules rely on flash-frozen coffee concentrate and ship directly to your door.

“I tried several types of Cometeer coffee a while ago, and I’ve been thinking about it ever since. I can’t get over the convenience factor,” says Deputy Editor Katie Bandurski. “The pods are perfect on busy (or, let’s be honest, lazy) mornings when I don’t want to pull out my grinder and make a mess of grounds all over the countertop.”

Simply grab a pod from the freezer, mix it with hot water or milk and enjoy it as hot coffee, an iced latte or even an espresso martini. No brewing required! Moreover, Cometeer offers multiple roast options from over a dozen roasters.

And don’t forget to check out the Cometeer Advent Calendar this year as an early Christmas gift for java lovers!

If he likes to indulge in a little charcuterie every now and then, a cheese of the month club is a cool way to shake up the usual cheddar or brie boards. Of all the options we’ve tried, Murray’s reigns supreme for its cheese of the month club. Rather, its cheese of the month clubs. Our favorite is the Cheese Explorer’s Club, which contains three different cheeses from a variety of cheesemakers across the globe each month.

We love the brand’s bold, outside-the-box cheeses from domestic and global cheesemakers, and the fun facts and serving tips included in each box.

“I got three herby Vermont Creamery Goat Cheeses in the first box of the month. The second month’s box had more variety: Murray’s Gemma Di Langa, Meredith Dairy Sheep and Goat Cheese and Alisios,” says tester Caroline of her three-month subscription. Even more notably, each box arrived completely chilled.

And surely, you can’t go wrong gifting a snack club. Whether it’s savory or sweet, a box full of delicious treats is a surefire way to show your favorite foodie you care. Universal Yums is our favorite snack subscription that allows you to experience popular snacks from different countries.

In addition tasty treats, each snack delivery box also includes an illustrated map, a tasting worksheet, allergy labels and a pamphlet full of cultural facts, fun quizzes and background info on each treat. The snacks in this international snack box are genuinely sourced from their featured countries, which adds to the authenticity.

“I received the Yum Yum Belgium Box with 10 snacks,” notes product tester Annamarie Higley. “Unpacking this box made me want to pack my bags and head back to Belgium. The snacks were so authentic—every one of them was made within the country’s borders, excluding the chips, and this fact was very prominently noted.”

Universal Yums is a fun way to explore different cultures through snacks. With three box sizes to choose from, each package includes 5 to 18 snacks. You can choose a one-year subscription, pay for six months, or purchase one month at a time. To get started, pick from about 10 different destinations for your first box and enjoy a taste of somewhere new.

If you want to give the gift of snacks with a healthier twist, the monthly HealthyMe Living Snack Box is a great option. Each box includes 8 to 10 snacks carefully curated by a certified holistic health coach. Even better, the snacks feature minimal, high-quality ingredients without unnecessary fillers or artificial sweeteners.

The box arrived packed with 10 snacks wrapped in blue tissue paper, and all but one were new to registered dietitian and product tester Nancy Snyder. “From protein bars and popcorn to infused almonds and ginger chews, I was pleasantly surprised by the quality and taste of each snack. I loved the variety and getting to try treats I couldn’t find at my local grocery store,” she says.

Prefer a specific diet? Choose a vegetarian or gluten-free box. Nancy found that the regular box also offers a nice mix of snacks to suit different dietary preferences.

This one is definitely an acquired taste, but seafood lovers and fans of trendy tinned fish will appreciate the Tinned Fish Club. Each month, members receive two to four premium tins of seafood, plus seasonings and pairing suggestions.

Tester Emily was impressed with the packaging and the flavors. “If you love fish and flavor, you really can’t go wrong with this box, which pairs uncommon, flavorful tinned seafood with mouthwatering seasonings, all shipped directly to your door,” she says.

Each box also includes a brochure with tasting notes, product details and pairing ideas, making it fun to discover something new. “As a big-time tuna fan, I loved receiving a tin of Santa Caterina tuna in Molho Cru sauce, along with mayo, crushed red pepper and pink sea salt to enjoy alongside,” Emily says.

For anyone who loves sardines, mussels, tuna and other seafood specialties, this subscription is a real catch!

To find the best subscription boxes for men, we considered our own extensive testing with gift clubs. Over the course of testing for other lists, we compiled our “best overall” picks to inform this piece. Our expert team of editors and product testers thoroughly tested and evaluated each option in our own homes and kitchens, and we took notes on the following aspects:

When it comes to gift and subscription boxes for men, picks from brands like Bespoke Post and Dollar Shave Club are often recommended. But at Taste of Home, food is our specialty—and we know a thing or two about food subscriptions. That’s why we’ve rounded up our favorite food and drink subscription boxes for men, with something for every taste, from savory jerky and craft beer to bold coffee.

At Taste of Home, we’ve tested countless food and drink subscriptions, informing pieces like the best food subscription boxes, gifts of the month clubs, fruit subscriptions, chocolate subscription boxes, and so many more. For this roundup, we drew on that hands-on experience and our expertise in sampling and evaluating a wide variety of food and drink clubs to find the best options worth gifting to men.

#6634. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6633. Jennifer Lawrence Elevates the Humble Track Pant Twice in One Week

Leave it to Jennifer Lawrence to make even a gym outfit stylish.

This morning, the actor schlepped to a workout dressed in a pair of black Adidas track pants and some well-soled running shoes. But Lawrence, ever the eclectic dresser, is capable of turning any outing into a fashion statement. Today, that meant elevating her track pants with a cherry red cardigan (pop of red theory at its finest!) over a white T-shirt, rectangular sunglasses, and—the pièce de résistance—a leopard faux fur coat from Jacquemus.

This is the second time this week that the actor has demonstrated just how to dress up the workout staple; Earlier this week, Lawrence styled her sporty trousers with a blue Auralee chore coat, a bohemian patterned scarf from Yaser Shaw, and oversized wraparounds.

So, although she is, in fact, heading to a workout, let Jennifer Lawrence’s latest look remind you that track pants aren’t just for the gym. With a piece of statement outerwear, a vibrant jolt of color, and some high-octane accessories, these sporty pants are well suited for a day out.

#6632. Is It Safe to Eat Raw Cranberries?

This holiday star rarely turns up in the fruit bowl. Could you eat cranberries raw if you wanted to?

Most of us have likely eaten cranberries without ever trying one on its own. The fruit is familiar enough to be indispensable at Thanksgiving, but rarely considered when we’re in the mood for a bowl of berries to snack on.

I live near Bandon, the Cranberry Capital of Oregon, where enthusiasm for the fruit extends well beyond Thanksgiving. Cranberry bogs are part of the landscape, and local berries fill jars of jam and syrup at roadside stands. This fall, my family attended the annual cranberry festival, where a friend of ours was crowned Cranberry Queen. (It’s a small town.)

Even here, though, cranberries generally arrive at the table with enough sugar to soften their bite. That sharpness is welcome in a buttery loaf or in a cranberry sauce alongside a rich turkey dinner, but a plain berry is a very different experience. So is all that preparation a matter of preference, or do cranberries actually need to be cooked before you eat them?

Yes, cranberries are safe to eat raw. There’s no need to cook them first; simply rinse them under cool running water and discard any that are soft, shriveled or spoiled. What happens after that is largely between you and your tolerance for sour foods.

Raw cranberries are firm and sharply tart, with a bitterness that can get lost beneath the sugar in cranberry sauce and muffins. They’re also astringent, meaning they leave you with a dry, puckering feeling in your mouth. If you loved the sour fruit trend of adding citric acid to grapes, then you might happily eat a few plain cranberries, but their absence from the average person’s fruit salad is understandable.

They have plenty to offer nutritionally, too. One cup of raw cranberries provides about 4 grams of fiber and 13 milligrams of vitamin C, along with naturally occurring antioxidants. They’re also naturally low in sugar, though that tends to change once we start mixing them with the things that make us love them.

I like cranberries best when their tartness is balanced by something rich or sweet. In a cranberry orange bread, the berries become little pockets of sharp fruit that break up the sweetness, while orange zest and warm spices round out the flavor. They do the same for muffins, cakes and scones, where an acid bite is particularly welcome among all that butter and sugar.

Of course, making sauce remains a very good use for a bag of cranberries. Simmering softens the berries until they burst, and sweetening lets you appreciate their flavor without quite so much puckering. At Thanksgiving, that acidity is part of the appeal: A spoonful brings some relief to a plate largely devoted to gravy, cream and butter. I’m equally happy to see the fruit on the next day’s turkey sandwich along with plenty of mayonnaise.

If you’d rather leave the berries uncooked, chopping them finely makes their intensity easier to distribute throughout a dish. A fresh relish with orange and sugar preserves their crisp texture, while cranberry salsa takes them in a savory direction. You can also blend a small handful into a smoothie with sweeter fruit.

And if you bought more than you need, cranberries freeze beautifully. Set some aside for baking after the holidays. A cranberry-orange loaf will be just as appreciated when the oven has considerably fewer obligations.

#6631. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6630. Haven and Converse Made One of the Coolest Chucks of the Year

As perfect as the Converse Chuck Taylor is, that hasn’t stopped the OG sneaker brand from pushing the sneaker's limits through countless collaborations that remake the classic Chucks in a million different images. While most of those collabs tend to be flashier, there are a few that stand out for their restraint. Or at least, what appears to be restraint at first glance. After a sellout partnership, Canadian outfitters and tastemakers Haven have reunited with Converse for its second team-up, lifting the vaunted Chuck 70 to new heights.

Haven’s disciplined approach to design considers its roots in Vancouver, the topography and climes therein, and incorporates that into its garments. Think waterproof shells, lightweight insulation, gussets for range of motion. “We think about the real world. What do you actually need to wear and what do you need to make you comfortable, and how to make your day a little bit better,” Haven cofounder Arthur Chmielewski says. “It could be just 1 per cent better. But those little details over time, they make your life a little bit better, right?” But it’s not just optimizing in the most sterile sense. Chmielewski also goes to great lengths to consider both comfort and craft in every product, employing details like Japanese denim and Loro Piana cashmere into the brand’s range. So when it comes to tackling an established iconic product, how does Haven do it?

“If you were to think of a farm-to-table kind of approach, it's like using the best ingredients to make the best food. And we're always thinking about that approach as well from a product standpoint,” Chmielewski says. The sneakers are all about subtle details that sum up to a better experience of something that was already pretty great to begin with. A tonal color palette combines different textures of leather, cashmere suede and hairy suede, giving each pair tactile depth that only becomes more pronounced with wear. The Chuck Taylor’s signature rubber toe cap is also replaced with a natural white leather toe cap, a detail that would go undetected more than five feet away. Practically, Haven’s also added an easy-access side-zip made from high-quality custom YKK Excella zippers as well as an additional rubber sole for longevity.

The full magnitude of the sneaker’s design is left for the wearer to experience. Details like reinforced vamps and eyestays, soft leather lining, and an upgraded Ortholite cushioned insole make the shoes more than just pretty to look at.

”The crew at Haven are just so good at translating their signature aesthetic across all products they touch,” says Matt Sleep, Design Lead for Converse Energy. “You see the shoes and instantly you know it fits into their aesthetic ecosystem. You just know it’s Haven without needing to see a logo wildly emblazoned anywhere.”

For a modern label rooted in the classics, the Chuck Taylor is a fitting project. Because, for Chmielewski, it’s all about making things that will last a long time. From the components to the iconic silhouette, you can bet you’ll see a pair of these knocking around for years to come.

“Doing this video with Vogue made me realize I use quite a lot of products compared to others,” he jokes. Whatever it is, it’s working for him.

#6627. 20 Food Advent Calendars to Buy Before They Sell Out (2026)

Nothing sparks joy and jumpstarts the Christmas season like a food advent calendar. You get 25 tiny compartments, each housing a festive treat hidden behind a perforated door. They’re not just chocolate anymore. These days they’re filled with everything from gummies and chili crisp to whiskey and coffee. And if you’re thinking of ordering one to enjoy this year, the time is now. December 1st is only seven weeks away, and after reporting on these things for the past five years, we’ve seen these calendars sell out months in advance or get backordered every year.

The best advent calendars contain high-quality sweets, booze, condiments, snacks, teas, or coffees you’ll be genuinely excited to open every day. And who knows, they might even introduce you to a product you’ll want to buy on repeat once the holiday season has come and gone.

This list is filled with advent calendars for every type of food and beverage enthusiast, many of them from brands we’ve long known and loved: a chile crisp-filled calendar from Fly By Jing, a Bonne Maman calendar filled with mini jam jars, and a chocolate advent calendar for mythology heads from San Francisco-based Dandelion Chocolate. Pick one up for yourself, or snag a few to gift to friends in the lead-up to the holiday season. Order soon, though. These sell out well before December hits.

We try not to play favorites here at BA, but I’ll be honest: This is the advent calendar fellow commerce writer Wilder Davies and I most look forward to receiving every year. If you’ve never had Lakrids by Bülow, allow me to explain. Every perforated door reveals a pack (or four) of spherical licorice candies, each coated in a white or milk chocolate shell flavored with passion fruit, strawberries and cream, salted caramel—you get the idea. These candies are indescribably delicious and guaranteed to convert even the most staunch licorice haters.

If you, like me, are an absolute fiend for gummy candy, there’s no better advent calendar for you than Sockerbit’s. The New York-based Swedish candy company makes some of the tastiest gummies I’ve ever had, and their 25-day calendar features a selection of favorites from the brand’s vast catalogue. I won’t give the exact contents away, but know that the hefty box holds two pounds of gummies running the gamut from sour sugar-coated fruit slices to generously portioned colorful candy mixes.

This one’s for the chocolate lovers who appreciate a little mythology lesson, too. Hailing from San Francisco-based bean-to-bar chocolate maker Dandelion Chocolate, this advent calendar features handcrafted chocolates from 24 acclaimed chocolatiers, all of whom earned their spot through a series of blind tastings. Along with the chocolate (which is packaged in individual ornament boxes you can hang on your tree), you’ll receive an illustrated storybook full of tales adapted from Nordic mythology, a decorative keepsake star, and daily digital content to be enjoyed along with your treats.

Luxury Collection X Laila Gohar Chocolate Advent Calendar

The Luxury Collection of hotels, a portfolio of dozens of boutiques on every continent but Antarctica, is trying something new this year along with designer and artist Laila Gohar in the form of its first advent calendar. The whimsical art is by Joana Avillez, the chocolates by Casa Bosques, with flavor profiles to match Luxury Collection hotels in locales like Waikiki (banana), Chennai (coconut and ginger), and Kyoto (black sesame) where senior editor Noah Kaufman recently stayed.

If you’re looking for a fun, interactive take on the classic chocolate advent calendar, check out Delysia. The Austin-based chocolatier releases a new themed calendar every year that acts as a guessing game, with clues as to what each of the 25 truffle flavors is. This year’s edition is holiday movie-themed, and each chocolate corresponds to a classic festive film—think hot cocoa for The Polar Express, sesame praline and banana sour lime for The Grinch, and raspberry rose for It’s a Wonderful Life.

If you’ve got a hot chocolate lover in your life (or if that hot chocolate lover is you), this advent calendar from UK-based chocolatier Hotel Chocolat is the move. It contains 24 single-serve sachets of the brand’s signature velvety hot chocolate mix in a range of flavors, including some limited-edition seasonal varieties.

Venchi has been making chocolate in Italy for over 140 years, and its chocolates, bars, and gelatos can now be found in more than 70 countries across the globe. The brand’s Advent Calendar Deluxe Maxi would make a handsome gift for any chocolate lovers in your life who would appreciate a bit more variety than your standard selection of chocolate truffles. In addition to individually wrapped chocolates, this calendar also features bars, spreads, and small gift tins, so rest assured you’ll never be bored.

We’ve previously recommended the amaro from this Portland, Oregon-based craft cocktail brand, so it’s no surprise that they make a great advent calendar too. Straightaway’s 12 Nights of Cocktails calendar would be a welcome offering for any drinks lover in your life who’d appreciate the gift of 12 iconic cocktails, without the fuss of actually making them or acquiring all of the ingredients to do so. Each Straightaway cocktail is single-serve and ready to open, pour, and sip—no measuring required.

If you’ve ever dreamed of embarking on a month-long wine tasting, Vinebox’s wine advent calendars make that a reality. Choose between two 12-day options (“Vine” or “Velvet”), or opt for a 24-day set that includes both. The wines are sourced from all over the world, and each bottle contains 100 milliliters. If you’re curious to learn more about a particular variety, the advent calendar grants you access to sommelier-led virtual tasting videos to accompany each wine.

The Nespresso devotee in your life will delight at the chance to try a different classic or limited-edition coffee capsule every day in the lead-up to Christmas. This year’s calendars are part of the brand’s new collaboration with Swarovski and come in two versions, one for the original machine and one for the Vertuo. The last day contains a special gift, which I won’t spoil here.

Whiskey enthusiasts will love Flaviar’s luxe advent calendar, which includes 24 whiskies from all over the world, including pours from Japan, Ireland, and Finland. Along with the liquor, each kit comes with a set of two collectible Glencairn glasses, a free year of access to the brand’s Flaviar Black membership, and a tasting booklet with information on each variety and a QR code you can scan to learn more and purchase full bottles of anything you love.

Palais de Thés’s advent calendar makes our recommendation list year after year for a few reasons. For one, it’s beautiful and luxe-feeling while ringing in under $40. But the main reason is the quality and variety of what lies within each perforated door: an assortment of 24 tea bags that are, in commerce writer Wilder Davies’s words, “genuinely lovely.” Each calendar includes a mix of classics and more interesting festive blends far removed from the stereotypical holiday flavors that so easily stray into Bath and Body Works scented candle territory. Consider this the ultimate way to settle into cozy season.

Coffee purists will love every day of this advent calendar from Bean Box, made in collaboration with Onyx Coffee Lab. Each of the 24 days includes a signature blend or an exclusive Advent-only single-origin release, perfectly portioned for a 24-ounce pour-over.

There’s a chance you’ve seen this calendar from Bonne Maman on your Instagram feed, and we can confirm it’s worth the hype. The 24 mini jam jars are adorable, of course, but what we really love about this set is the unique flavors it includes—flavors like apricot lavender, cherry pink peppercorn, and raspberry lychee that you can't find in Bonne Maman’s regular lineup.

Tinned fish hive, rise up. This advent calendar from fan-favorite conservas brand Fishwife features 12 days’ worth of tasty tins and some exclusive fish-adjacent goodies. I won’t spoil exactly what’s in it, but know that some of our favorite offerings from the brand’s lineup include the Albacore Tuna with Spanish Lemon, Smoked Rainbow Trout with Red Chimichurri, and Smoked Salmon with Fly By Jing’s chili crisp.

12 days of cheese? Sign us up. This calendar from Murray’s Cheese sells out every year, so we’d recommend snagging one while you still can. It’s filled with a host of cheeses (like Parmigiano Reggiano, Gruyère, and truffle cheddar) and accoutrements (like apple butter and oat cakes) that you can fashion into a festive cheeseboard or enjoy one by one. And don’t worry, it arrives in an insulated shipper, but you do have to keep the whole calendar in the fridge throughout the holiday season.

2026 Limited Edition 12-Day Advent Calendar

2026 Limited Edition 24-Day Advent Calendar

Give the gift of 12 or 24 days of chile crisp and chile crisp-adjacent surprises with this advent calendar from one of our favorite spicy condiment brands. It contains an assortment of mini sauce jars, packs of the brand’s best-selling noodles, and some limited-edition surprises—so even if your pantry’s already stocked with Fly By Jing, you can find something new to love here. This calendar tends to sell out in October, so we’d recommend buying one soon.

This luxe advent calendar from Williams Sonoma has a little bit of everything. Balsamic vinegar from Modena? Check. A bundt pan-shaped ornament? Also check. This is the calendar to splurge on if you can’t decide whether you want chocolate or trinkets.

We all have that friend who seemingly can’t eat a meal without dousing it in hot sauce first. #6626. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6625. Stanley Tucci’s Airplane Snack Is the Messiest Meal Ever

Stanley Tucci isn't settling for pretzels and peanuts on his next flight!

Between busy airport security lines and delays, eating while traveling can be unpredictable. And sure, maybe you ate breakfast before leaving the house. But then suddenly it’s six hours later and you’re struggling to navigate your way to baggage claim with a headache and a growling stomach. Trust me, I’ve been there too many times!

Which is why I have one simple rule when traveling: Eat when you can. Packing plenty of plane snacks is important, but getting a full meal is really ideal. So when I saw the kind of food that Stanley Tucci brings on flights, I felt incredibly validated. However, I don’t know if I could manage something quite this messy in the air.

In a very charming TikTok video, Stanley Tucci’s wife Felicity Blunt records him as he unwraps his plane snack. I watched in shock and awe as he unwrapped aluminum foil to reveal a sandwich. But not just any sandwich—I mean, this is Stanley Tucci we’re talking about. He’s known for whipping up Italian meals for pop stars and cooking cozy comfort meals on a whim. It’s no real surprise then that he brought eggplant Parmesan on a plane!

His wife joked that they should “film a before and after” of his shirt. I mean, this sandwich looks incredible. It’s got tons of creamy marinara sauce and is piled high with thinly sliced eggplant and cheese. The bread is toasted and really looks like it’s doing the best job it can at containing the feast within.

Would I have the confidence to eat an eggplant Parmesan sandwich on a plane? Probably not. I am a notoriously messy eater to begin with, and if bibs were more socially acceptable for adults, I would wear one with every meal. So I can’t imagine diving into this on a plane!

But Stanley loves it. In fact, he’s the one who made the sandwich, or “Stan-wich” as Felicity calls them, for the plane ride. So maybe I need to amend my earlier assertion: I would eat eggplant Parmesan on a plane if Stanley Tucci made it for me.

What’s your go-to airplane snack? Is it as messy as this one? Sound off in the comments below!

#6624. Get to Know the Watchmaker Behind John Mayer’s Latest Pick-Up

When looking for the next big thing in the watch world, there are few better places to check than John Mayer’s wrist. The super collector can make his own Audemars Piguet Royal Oaks, skyrocket the value of a previously underappreciated Rolex Daytona, and help establish new indies. This week, Mayer is co-signing a hyper-limited-edition piece from FVF Genève, a watchmaker you should get to know.

FVF Genève is the brainchild of Spanish-born, Geneva-based watchmaker Franc Vila. Mayer is wearing his latest release: FVF2 Time & Day “Happy Monday,” made in partnership with American watch and jewelry retailer Material Good. On his Instagram, Mayer referred to the collaborators as a “Trifecta of Greatness.” There’s more to this piece than its mesmerizing mother-of-pearl, though. The watch’s design celebrates the idea that, if you love what you do, Monday mornings are actually something to look forward to.

The “Happy Monday” is a limited edition of seven pieces, each of which is engraved with a different day of the week on its rotor. The design is a reminder, as the brand says, that “each day is an opportunity to embrace our calling.” It helps, of course, that this message is delivered by a truly beautiful movement with black-polished surfaces, plenty of beveling and polishing, and great typography. Then there’s the rad day-of-the-week indicator on the dial. Situated between 6 and 9 o’clock, it takes the shape of a subtle gold track with a letter for each day of the week in French. To go with the “Happy Monday” theme, “Lundi” (Monday in French) is the only day represented by a standout green letter.

The dial is the showstopping element on this piece. It’s executed in a sparkly deep-blue mother-of-pearl and accented with thick gold-tone printing in the form of an outer minute track, a sub-seconds display between 4 and 5 o’clock, and bisecting lines that create a classically inspired “sector” design. The interplay of the sector when combined with mother-of-pearl is unusual enough, but add in the retrograde day-of-the-week indicator, and you’ve got a truly compelling combo.

The watch’s 39.5mm case is made out of Grade 5 titanium and features a Titalyt treatment—an electrochemical surface treatment that creates a ceramic-like layer and increases durability and hardness. F.P. Journe is a big fan of this treatment, and FVF uses it to great effect here. The finishing gives the Happy Monday a dark, industrial aesthetic that plays off the mother-of-pearl and gold tones on the dial for a distinctive feel. The watch comes on a matching beads-of-rice bracelet with straight endlinks, further adding to the interplay between vintage and modern inspiration. Finally, the crown and date corrector are located on the left side of the case rather than the right, where they typically sit.

Limited to just seven pieces—not including a unique piece that went to Material Good’s Yoni Ben-Yehuda—the $125,000 Happy Monday is the latest independent watch to receive a co-sign from super-collector John Mayer. Despite his role as Audemars Piguet's “Creative Conduit," Mayer has been known to support high-end independent makers such as F.P. Journe, and famously helped propel Vanguart onto the horological stage over the past year.

Vila, who established his eponymous luxury watch brand in the early 2000s, is a prime candidate to receive his flowers from the modern collecting community: marrying avant-garde case and dial designs with high complications. Vila sold his initial brand in the late 2000s, but he’s now having another go at creating modern classics with FVF. He’s come at the right time. It’s boom times for independent watchmakers as collectors try to identify the next big thing, and a co-sign from Mayer makes FVF a strong candidate to catch fire.

And on Tuesday night, that infectious energy permeated a private dining room at the Beverly Hills Hotel, where the Milan-based label threw a dinner party celebrating its new collaboration with supermodel Carolyn Murphy. “It’s relaxing to have fun with your guests—otherwise, it’s no bueno,” the label’s founder, J.J. Martin, told Vogue. “You have to raise the vibration yourself and exude that energy around the room.”

The storied venue was a sentimental location choice for Martin, who grew up in the Pacific Palisades. “My family is from Los Angeles, so this hotel is just like a classic center of gravity for the city, and also a great point between East meets West,” she explained, adding that her grandfather lived in Beverly Hills.

It felt as if the founder had invited a large group of friends—Liv Tyler, Abby Elliott, Jackie Tohn, Sepideh Moafi, and Natasha Rothwell among them—to her splashy, eclectic Milan home. The tables were a feast for the eyes, adorned with multicolored flowers and bright dinnerware, and dressed in a floral tablecloth.

Lela Becker, co-founder and president of Mother, introduced Martin and Murphy at one of Mother’s events around the time of the tragic Los Angeles wildfires, which had destroyed the model’s home. “Lela was like, ‘You’ve got to get out of your hotel,’” Murphy recalled. As it turned out, Martin’s warmth and uplifting spirit were exactly what she needed. “When J.J. and I met at the event, it was like fireworks went off right away.” After the two got to know each other better, Martin floated the idea of a collaboration.

“But I don’t wear prints,” Murphy recalled telling Martin with a laugh. Indeed, the model is a longtime minimalist, but even she couldn’t pass up the opportunity to enter the lively, colorful world of La DoubleJ. “I’m pushing myself out of my comfort zone, and I think that’s why the collaboration was a lovely marriage of our sensibilities,” Murphy explained. Fittingly, she was clad in a champagne-hued two-piece set with bezel-set stones from the collection, which is named Sisterhood of Light.

“My daughter, Dylan, is standing here in the Camelot dress,” Murphy said, pointing out the 25-year-old, who was socializing behind her. Meanwhile, Moafi, who stars in season 2 of The Pitt, was in awe of the collaboration. “It is so diverse and a cross blend of so many different cultures and time periods,” the actor, dressed in a 1970s-inspired patterned blouse and matching trousers, said.

On the outdoor patio, where guests chatted and sipped on cocktails before dinner, Rothwell, known for her role in The White Lotus, looked as though she had just stepped off the set in Thailand, wearing a flowing green-and-teal printed dress. “My stylist Katie Bottomler is the one who introduced me to the brand while I was doing press for The White Lotus,” she shared, with Bottomler standing by her side. Luckily, the label’s airy designs helped Rothwell beat the heat while in Thailand, too. “I’m a plus-size girly, and so I love a brand that considers that and looks good on all body types,” Rothwell added.

After admiring the aforementioned tablescapes and snapping photos, attendees began finding their seats, where copies of Martin’s book Table Energy: Entertaining with Italian Spirit awaited. “By the way, product plug, everything on your table has been made by La DoubleJ,” Martin told the crowd, prompting laughter and applause as they enjoyed artichoke salad, grilled branzino, and filet mignon.

#6622. This Simple Storage Trick Can Keep Lettuce Fresh for a Month

The trick to keeping lettuce fresh for a month is already in your kitchen.

There are few things more irritating than throwing away food you had every intention of eating. Fresh produce is especially frustrating because it seems to operate on its own schedule. You buy a beautiful head of lettuce, imagining all the fresh salads and sandwiches you’ll make that week, only to find a head of wilted leaves waiting for you when you finally get around to it.

Enter Chef Charles Kim, better known as Chef Fatty on social media. He has an impressive knack for making me rethink my cooking. He’s already changed how I caramelize onions and make the juiciest chicken breasts, and now he’s apparently coming for my crisper drawer. His trick promises to keep lettuce fresh for an entire month using nothing more than aluminum foil—a claim I couldn’t resist investigating.

The idea is simple: Instead of leaving your head of lettuce in the plastic produce bag, loosely wrap it in aluminum foil before putting it in the refrigerator. That’s it. No special containers, paper towels or elaborate produce-preserving rituals required.

Chef Fatty recommends removing any yellowing or deteriorating leaves before wrapping the lettuce. If it’s dirty, you can wash it first, but make sure it’s completely dry. Then loosely fold the foil around the head and place it in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer.

The reasoning has to do with moisture and airflow. Lettuce loses its crispness as water escapes from its leaves, but trapping too much moisture can also encourage decay. A loose foil wrapping strikes just the right balance, protecting the leaves from drying out without sealing them inside an airtight container.

I wanted to see the difference for myself, so I bought two heads of romaine lettuce at the same time. I left one in the plastic produce bag from the grocery store and loosely wrapped the other in aluminum foil. Both went into the same crisper drawer in my refrigerator, where I left them undisturbed for a month. When I finally pulled them out, the difference was unmistakable.

After 30 days in the refrigerator, the foil-wrapped romaine was in dramatically better shape than its plastic-bag counterpart. The lettuce stored in its original bag had deteriorated considerably, while the foil-wrapped head had retained much more of its original appearance and crispness.

I had to peel away several of the outer leaves of the plastic-bag lettuce before I found anything resembling a crisp texture. The foil-wrapped head wasn’t perfect, but it was still pretty crisp, with leaves so fresh that I happily turned them into a Caesar salad for lunch. This was an entire month after I’d bought it. I’d call that a successful experiment.

While I tested the method with romaine, it’s also worth trying on other lettuce varieties. How long each stays fresh will depend on its condition when purchased, the refrigerator it’s stored in, and the variety itself. And lettuce isn’t the only vegetable that might benefit. Taste of Home senior editor Lindsay Mattison told me she uses the same aluminum foil trick to store celery, which makes sense given its tendency to lose moisture and go limp in the refrigerator.

I wouldn’t necessarily recommend buying lettuce with the intention of ignoring it for a month, and it’s still important to check for slime, mold or other signs of spoilage before eating it. But knowing I can give my produce a much longer window before it ends up in the compost is reason enough to keep an extra roll of foil handy.

#6621. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6620. A Costa Rican Beach Resort with a World-Class Coffee Program

In Hotels With Great Taste, we’re pulling back the curtain for a peek at the “special sauce” that hotels use to create memorable, meaningful culinary experiences for their guests.

Check-in at Nekajui on Costa Rica’s verdant Papagayo Peninsula happens inside a sparsely furnished bungalow the staff call La Casita. But walk across the drive, past a massive ceiba tree hung heavy with lanterns, and all humility vanishes. The whole property sweeps out before you: an endless green lawn, pools cascading down two levels, and, finally, the serenely sparkling bay beyond.

Nekajui is Ritz Carlton’s first Reserve resort in Central or South America. The Reserve’s are Ritz Carlton’s nod to the idea of complete escape, often in the far flung retreats—the Chinese Himalayas, or the Saudi Arabian desert.

Now, the recently opened Nekajui allows you to unwind on the lush Costa Rican coast teeming with wildlife like capuchins, coatis, and iguanas. Hidden away at the remote property, you’ll also find a local coffee program that’s on par with the best big city cafes in the world.

Sprawling over 1,400 acres, Nekajui is a dreamy jungle beach resort that opened its doors on the secluded peninsula in February 2025.

Each of the 107 rooms and suites peeks out onto treetop and ocean sunset views. Inside, the decor features outdoor access and carved wood motifs typical of the Guanacaste region.

Many rooms also have access to patios large enough for morning yoga sessions and private plunge pools (take note: if a guest above you has one, you may see water splashing down your way). For larger parties, treetop tents and villas on the property afford even more space than standard rooms.

The main campus includes rooms, restaurants, and a spa, but the property’s grounds extend: a funicular (like a tiny cable car) runs dramatically down the cliffs, past howler monkeys, to the beach with water warm as a pleasant bath and a cave to explore.

Peruvian chef Diego Muñoz, whose career includes stints at world-renowned Spanish restaurants El Bulli and Mugaritz, leads the culinary program at the property’s main restaurants Puna and the tiny, six-seat chef’s counter within, Paruro.

At Puna and Parura, Muñoz’s menu is filled with dishes with the layered flavors and artistic compositions that helped push Peruvian cuisine into the spotlight on a global stage. Puna has a fusion feel , sliding flavors and spices from Munoz’s international travels into Peruvian classics like a robust sudado, and zippy ceviche. Paruro, the chefs counter located inside Puna, is an East Asian experience with bites like a nori-cured tenderloin and a seabass curry. You’ll find one of Munoz’s best creations, a deboned, prawn-stuffed chicken wing, on both menus.

It’s important to Muñoz that Puna uses local ingredients that are uncommon on Costa Rican menus. Fresh seafood, for example, can be a particular challenge to source, even as the overwhelming majority of Costa Rican territory is marine.

Aspirations are high for the beverage program as well. Cooper’s is a moody, mysterious cocktail space with a menu full of unexpected Guanacaste ingredients. It leans into the speakeasy style, and as such, is invite-only, but don’t be intimidated—schmooze your server a bit, or ask your personal concierge to score you an invite.

Inside, the menu is ambitious, dotted with some adventurous local distillates—goat cheese, cascara, mango leaf—which find their way into thrilling riffs on classics like the martini-esque Turrialba using fino sherry and the aforementioned goat cheese distillate.

Elsewhere on the property, you can dine at Niri Beach Club, with an Iberian-focused menu, and the all-day Cafe Rincon which has sandwiches, bowls, and pastries.

Nekajui’s commitment to on-the-ground ingredients shines brightest in its coffee program atCafé Rincon. Fabi Rojas operates the micro-roastery at Nekajui, which features always updating selections from each of Costa Rica’s seven coffee growing regions.

For a country about the size of West Virginia, Costa Rica produces an impressive diversity of coffee: easy-drinking crowd pleasers in the lower elevations of the coastal west, bright acidic pops from Valle Occidental in the north, fruity, prize-winning geishas—one of which fetched over $300 per pound at auction—in the mountainous Los Santos region of the south central. And Fabi has nurtured personal relationships with farmers all over the country to ensure she has access to all of it.

And while she’ll make your coffee however you want it, the move is to have it brewed in a vandola. The one piece clay carafe and pour-over cone looks like something that might date back hundreds of years, but the design actually came from Costa Rican coffee roaster and barista Minor Alfaro in 2015. Brewing in clay helps maintain aroma longer, and the valve into the base of the dripper allows more gentle oxygenation according to Alfaro. Oxygen is usually the enemy of coffee, but allowing a small amount in through the valve can sweeten the flavor.

Besides brewing coffee better than my Chemex, each vandola is a handmade work of ceramic art—an apt vessel to showcase coffees grown, roasted, and brewed with exquisite care.
