#6619. My Friend Joe Vanella Is a Traitor

I have known Joseph Vanella for multiple decades. The world has known him for about nine weeks, ever since he showed up on the latest season of The Traitors: New Blood as one of the civilians airdropped into a Scottish castle so they can be barked at by a feather-clad Alan Cummings while trying to determine who amongst the group are actively “murdering” the others. Vanella, as it turns out, is one of the murderers, and spends his time lying to almost everyone around him, feigning innocence in between doing ren faire cosplay in a turret with the two other traitors. He’s also on the ropes: this week’s episodes has the walls closing in, as one player (the dreaded Victor) convinces the group that Joe is…well, what he actually is, a Traitor.

Joe Vanella—his actual last name, not at all made up!—is a Sopranos character come to life: big laugh, big body, big heart, proudly hails from Long Island, calls it “prazhoot” instead of prosciutto. He’s a family man (a wife, three small cute kids) and a funeral director (a job that runs in the family), and if you have a couple drinks with him, he will share stories about some truly absurd funerals he’s directed. Unlike many of his Traitors costars, he was not some form of influencer prior to getting cast.

He’s also now the subject of, like, three or four Traitors memes. People dressed as him for Halloween! And so I’ve spent a significant amount of time lately watching Joe, my friend, a guy I love, who texts the groupchat about gastronintestinal distress (tbh, we all do), also become a kind of breakout reality star. And not to make his newfound fame about me, but I wanted to know what’s going on with a guy who’s achieved that specific level of renown best described as A Guy.

So we talked about that—on zoom, with two kind NBC chaperones to make sure, I assume, Joe didn’t share any spoilers. We talked about how his wife feels about him being very good at lying. Being recognized at funerals he’s overseeing. And his now-complicated relationship with apples (Traitors fans will know).

GQ: Joseph Vanella, it’s great to meet you.

Vanella: Jon, thanks for being on time, buddy. That helped me out a lot.

I’m sorry I’m five minutes late. I’ve got a lot of meetings going on. I’m a very busy person, but not as popular as you.

Are we going to talk about how I beat your ass in fantasy baseball every year? Do we get to touch on that?

We absolutely will. But first, Joseph Vanella—Joey, as I know you; Joe, to the rest of the world now that you’re on Traitors—why did you go out for Traitors? Because we’ve never actually gotten into this, and I find it fascinating. A lot of people that I know, who also know you, have asked me, “Wait, why is Joe on Traitors?”

Okay. So we’ll start at the beginning. My wife, Meg, and I were looking for a show to watch, and my sister-in-law is like, "You guys got to watch Traitors." And it was after the first season. And we put it off, and then we watched it, and I immediately fell in love. We went through, I think, the first season in two days. We got into the second season. It sort of became a routine in our house. Every Thursday, I’d go to Carvel, get two sundaes. After the kids went to bed, we’d sit in there, we’d watch the new episode of Traitors. So, completely enamored with the show. There’s a casting call after season four, the Rob Rausch season. And Alan’s on TV, and he’s like, "We’re going to let regular people into the castle."

My sister-in-law, Erin, is going, "You got to do it. You got to do it." I’m like, "Ah, I don’t know." I haven’t been to the gym since my oldest kid was born. I’m like, this is the fattest I’ve been. Do I really want to be on TV? But I had a day at work, and afterward I made a video—and next thing I knew I was on a plane to Scotland. It was crazy. And also, as you saw how fat I am at this point in my life, it’s a show where I feel like I could get away without the athletic prowess needed for most other shows. So that was a positive, too.

Yeah, we’ll discuss your cardio at a later point in this interview. I do have to ask, did you go into this trying to get famous? Are you hoping to be famous? Do you want fame?

No. I went into this just to... You want to know the truth?

I went into this because I wanted to see the castle, I wanted to meet Alan, and I wanted to be on my favorite show. It’s the equivalent, at this point in my life, if you pick me up when I was 13 and drop me in The Simpsons, this is what this is to 44-year-old Joe Vanella. It’s picking me up and dropping me into my favorite show. And how many people get that opportunity?

Only 20-something people per season it looks like, and some didn’t make it very far, though you’ve made it pretty far. You did skip over a moment that I got to be part of, as you were in the process of possibly joining Traitors, where you were trying to figure out what to wear for a particular casting interview. And I’d like to revisit that moment because this is GQ, and so it’s apropos: at one point you texted me, midday, freaking out about needing to wear something to show yourself off properly. And what you texted me were a series of pants folded up into thirds, so I had no clue what they looked like. And then you also sent me some Vans that had tombstones on them, that you said you’d never worn.

They were caskets. They weren’t tombstones.

A pair of pants I was asked to assess as interview-worthy.

Sorry. Caskets. And I guess I wondered, what did you end up wearing that sealed the deal on your opportunity at Traitors? And did the casket Vans ever actually see the light of day? Will we see them on the Traitors?

The casket Vans sadly are still in a box up in my closet. I have not gotten to take them out yet. That particular interview, I wore a black shirt with pink flamingos on it.

A black button down shirt, pink flamingos. And I feel like, what did I have on…chinos? I think, were they chocolate? They were chocolate colored khakis.

Yeah, it was cool. And then the chunky Vans, the ’90s sort of Vans, silver, you’ll see them on the show all the time with a silver stripe on them. So you did help me out. I did not know what I was doing, and you were my most fashionable friend, so I needed support in that area.

Absolutely do not put the flamingo shirt on me. That is a hundred percent you, and I will not be accepting that.

Jon Wilde said, "That flamingo shirt belongs everywhere."

So that was another question I was going to ask, which is: Do you dress yourself for the show? Did you have to just bring three suitcases of clothes with you, or do they help dial in the Joe Vanella aesthetic?

So mainly we provide our own stuff. There’s no makeup people. There’s nothing like that. We dress ourselves. We get a little guidance because in the past there’s Housewives and they got Dolce Gabbana, they’ve got Chanel—and then I roll up and I got a bunch of Hanes Beefy-Ts and American Eagle jeans. It’s a very big switch. But yeah, that stuff, that’s mine. I love Hawaiian shirts, so it worked out well for me.

I am. Nothing says Hawaiian shirt climate like the mountains of the Scottish Highlands, right?

The most tropical place you can think of.

Absolutely. You’ve had some amazing moments. I would say you have been by far the most memed-slash-memeable contestant on this season of the Traitors. You kicked that off with a wink directly at the camera in episode one, and from then on, you’ve really manufactured a few wonderful ones. We’ll get to the apple in a moment, but what I wanted to talk about really briefly was the moment with Michael, who’s no longer on the show. You guys had a really lovely, beautiful moment where you were at the round table at the end of the day. You gave him some support in saying you did not think he was a Traitor. And then there’s this really beautiful moment afterwards where he—and I’m paraphrasing here—but as a gay man, he says he grew up with a bunch of guys who looked and sounded like you—a.k.a., an extremely Italian dude from the deepest parts of Long Island. And he says he did not get a lot of respect, and did not feel very supported by those people as a gay kid. And he told you how much he appreciated that you stepped out and offered him support. I’m interested in what that moment was like for you: if you expected that, if you two had built something up until then? And also, how much weight you feel representing Long Island, which does come with some comical, but not always so comical, stereotypes.

The Michael thing, when he came up to me in the Armory, I didn’t expect it at all. I defended Michael because I got to know Michael. Michael was my day-one. We were in the Land Rover together going into the castle. I knew him from the very beginning. And he dropped that on me. I didn’t think that I was doing anything except defending a friend at that point. It had nothing to do with gameplay. It’s just somebody I care about who I saw was kind of getting railroaded, and I wanted to step in and stick up for him. But when he came up to me and he hit me with that, I was so honored. It’s not anything that I ever expected, and it hit me in that moment. I’m like, man, I didn’t want him to think it was gameplay.

That was the most important thing. I didn’t want to come off as not genuine. I didn’t want him to get out of the game and be like, "Oh, this guy lied to me. What an asshole." So to have him feel that comfortable with me, to come up and share that moment with me, it just meant the world. And Michael and I are still such great friends. He’s truly one of my best friends to come out of that castle. I talk to him every day. He’s funny as hell. He’s a great human being, and it feels so awful to hear that he had such a tough go in his childhood, especially being a father myself. I don’t want any of my kids to feel that way. They’re free to love whatever way they want to love, and everybody should feel that way. And to hear that he had a negative time growing up, it hit me right in my gut.

Yeah, it was a really beautiful moment. You’ve mentioned maybe once or twice or 13 times that you’re from Long Island.

Yeah. Why won’t you let me be proud of where I’m from?

I want you to be proud. You’re clearly proud. I love that about you. You’ve always been proud to be from Long Island. You love the Jets and the Islanders. And so in that way, I’m like, this is not a thing people choose. This is a thing they’re obviously born into. But have you felt the need to represent Long Island in a better light? Is that fair to say? In a better-than-its-stereotype light?

Long Island gets a bad rap. Long Islanders get a bad rap. I think, what was it? What was the show with the Seavers? Was that Family Ties? Michael J. Fox was on it? They lived on the North Shore of Long Island. They represented great. And sometime between Family Ties and now, Long Islanders get this rap like we’re all loud oafs.

[Laughing] When I think of loud oafs, Joe Vanella is at the very bottom. But I came into the game and the most important thing, I wanted to show myself as somebody from Long Island who’s representing in a positive light. And people from Long Island have been so great and warm about backing me. My DMs are constantly filled with people saying, thank you for representing Long Island this way. And it warms my heart, because I love where I come from. I’m so proud. I think this is one of the greatest places to live. I think it’s one of the greatest places to raise kids. Everything that you want is here. It’s incredible. The people are awesome. Yes, they’re loud. Yes, they’re opinionated, but that doesn’t make them bad. It just makes them sure of who they are. And I think that’s a typical Long Islander.

And for what it’s worth, my dad is a Yankees, Giants, and Rangers fan, and I went against all his fandom to try and stick it to him, and it backfired totally against me.

Yeah, that was brutal. That was a horrible choice on your part. You, by trade, are a funeral director. You’ve now achieved a fascinating level of public fame. Are people-

You’re re-’Gramming people who are going as you for Halloween and you’ve not been canceled. That’s a pretty positive version of fame in 2026. It’s not easy to thread that needle these days. Have you-

People going as me as a Halloween costume is one of the craziest things that’s ever happened. It’s insane.

Have people recognized you while you were…funerarily directing? Has that happened yet?

Yes. In a couple of the funeral homes, I have been stopped and they’re like, "Hey, do you ever get that you look like... Are you Joe from the Traitors?" And I’m like, "Yeah." And they’ve stopped me for pictures. I hate to say it’s a fun thing because they’re in this time of awful grief and then they’re like, "Oh, they’re the loud guy from Traitors. Let’s grab a pic before we get into the limo." So it’s sort of providing them with a story and some humor before they head off to the funeral. So I’m glad to bring that to them in those situations.

What’s it like walking around and having people know you? I mean, a month and a half ago, nobody save the most blessed among us knew Joe Vanella. And now you can walk around and people are like, "Oh wow, it’s the Joe Vanella."

The first time it happened, I was in Penn Station and I was Googling how to get to wherever I was going, and this girl came up to me and she’s like, "Are you going to be on The Traitors?” I guess the cast was just released. And I’m like, "Yeah." And then she’s like, "Oh, can we take a picture with you?" And I’m like, "For what?" And then they said, "Well, you’re on The Traitors." And it took a minute. I’m like, "Oh, people actually want my picture." It’s completely, completely bonkers. I had one person come up to me and they’re like, "I’m so nervous." I’m like, "Why? Who cares? It’s me. What am I? Just take my picture. You’re fine. We can hang out." I was trick-or-treating with my kids, and I knocked on somebody’s house, and the guy came to the door and he’s like, "I was just watching you on the TV." And he called to his husband, and his husband came out and they’re like, "You’re literally on my TV right now.”

It’s crazy. It’s something I can’t wrap my head around because, like you said, six weeks ago, nobody really knew who I was. And now all of a sudden it’s like, "Hey, can I get your picture?” all the time. And it’s so cool, because I’ve always been a picture taker when I’ve seen anybody out who I recognize. I famously bothered Gina Gershon one night at a bar in, I think it was the Lower East Side, and she was an absolute sweetheart. But now people are doing that to me, I want to make sure that they walk away with a good opinion of me. And that’s what I’m trying to do. I’m trying to show them I am who I am on the show, even outside.

You want to pay it forward from Gina Gershon, as you rightly should. How does Meg, your wife, feel about this? She didn’t get a choice in this matter.

Well, listen, this whole thing without her never would’ve happened. I’m the luckiest guy. Today’s actually my anniversary.

Thank you. Thank you. I’m the luckiest guy in the world to have her because if she said no, if I couldn’t go to Scotland, I would’ve never had this opportunity. And she stepped up so big, took care of the kids, took care of everything that had to be at home, didn’t even hesitate. She goes, "If you get the chance, I want you to go." So she’s handling this well. Again, this is her favorite show too. Her biggest thing, when I came home from Scotland, she said she didn’t want to know anything. She didn’t know if I was a traitor. She loves the show so much that she wanted to be surprised all way around.

Was she surprised that you’re such a good liar? Is she feeling good about that? It turns out you’re a pretty solid liar. People believe that you’re a good guy when you’re out here murdering them night after night.

No, I’m done. I’m cooked as far as that goes. The facade is down. She knows when I’m lying at this point. She doesn’t trust me and she’s right not to. I mean, you see what I’m doing every week. I wouldn’t trust me either.

It turns out you’re spectacularly good at lying and you’ve let the whole world know about it. It seems like maybe misplaying your hand, but it’s working out for you. Earlier, we briefly touched on your athletic ability, your prowess. It’s not been great. Certainly the show spent a few moments within the scope of the challenges showing you splayed out, just really sucking air. And I wondered how that felt, seeing yourself laid out on the ground just like a fish on a pier.

So if you watch that scene... Now, first of all, we’re not even going to get into the fact that as time’s expiring, I flew through the air like a Michael Jordan poster from 1993, dunking the bag of money into the barrel. I should be a poster in children’s bedrooms at this point, just gracefully flying. But at that particular moment, I was lying on the ground and I remember looking up at the sky, and if you watch it, at first I’m distressed, but then I’m kind of smiling. As I’m collecting myself to continue to live, I looked up at the sky like, "How the hell did I get here?" It was such a great experience, and I was just in it at that moment, and realizing the gravity of everything, as exhausted as I was. And yeah, my cardio, not great, not great. I got a five-year-old, a four-year-old, and a two-year-old. I don’t have time to go to the gym. My cardio is chasing them around the house. So at that particular moment, sweating next to a barrel in the Highlands of Scotland, I’m just like, man. It all hit me at once, and I’m just having the time of my life.

I feel like we’ve got to really quickly talk about the apple. Obviously, the other big, big meme, and why people are dressing like you: As a traitor, you had to murder someone by throwing fruit to them. Hard episode to watch, because I was like, "Wow, only Victor’s catching onto this?” The edit made it seem really obvious what you were up to. And what came out of that, across several episodes, besides what Victor termed “Fruitgate”, was you having to say the word “roughage” a lot as defense for why you were suddenly so obsessed with having an apple. But have you been eating more apples and roughage? Did that change your own approach to roughage and apples?

Jon, I never want to see another apple in my life.

I went to a wedding yesterday, somebody tossed an apple at me. It’s like an everyday occurrence now. But what I want to point out is how important the social aspect of gameplay is there, because what was going on with Victor at that particular moment…Victor and I have very different styles. Victor’s very analytical. He’s good at what he does in that way. I’m very social. I’d pick up gummy bears and throw them at Mark. Mark would catch them in his mouth. I’d pick up beef jerky, which is constant. I was tossing something to somebody all the time. So now-

You treat everybody like they’re a Labrador retriever?

Exactly. Listen, I’m telling you, Mark would win best in show if he ever tried in Madison Square Garden. But everybody’s coming down on Morgan. They’re like, "Morgan, you don’t remember catching an apple?" Well, one, my social game I feel was strong enough that nobody’s antenna was up on me at that point—except for Victor, because Victor and I had beefed, going back to the Michael thing, going back before that. And Morgan knows me as somebody who’s playful, knows me as somebody who throws things around the castle, so she probably didn’t think anything of it. Joe’s just goofing off. That’s what I was doing.

What was the original question? I definitely talked too much.

Mostly just, are you eating apples and roughage?

Yeah, I’m trying to. My daughter has been shaming me. She’s like, "Dad, you need to eat more fruits and vegetables," even though she doesn’t eat any fruits and vegetables herself. So I have been trying to eat more. I’ve found a particular type of apple that I love. I think it’s called Snapdragon or something like that, and it’s very spicy. There’s an apple orchard or an apple place out in Syosset over here that I go to and I get them, and they’re fantastic. So I have been eating more apples.

If nothing else, that’s a win. What do you-

Do you know how much haggis binds you up? The normal American hasn’t had haggis. I ate about three tons of haggis when I was in Scotland. It’s like cement, but it tastes great. People want to rag on haggis. I know in Armageddon, one of the greatest movies of all time, there’s a haggis joke in it. You do need apples to move that stuff around in your stomach, otherwise you’re going to have a real hard time.

Got it. So it really was the haggis we’re looking at as the problem. Were they serving haggis in the castle?

Yeah. It’s Scotland, baby. You get haggis all the time.

Were you the only person eating haggis? It’s not a thing most people coming from the U.S. are into.

A lot of people were shying away. But you know what? They’re just not adventurous.

I know we’ve got to wrap up in a minute, but I do have to ask you: we go back a ways, known you more than 20 years. Part of that has been we’ve had-

Did I drive you into Brooklyn when you moved there the first time? I feel like I did.

We listened to Wu-Tang clan and I moved you into Brooklyn.

How else could we do it? So, most of the time we have spent as friends, we’ve also been in a fantasy baseball league, of which you’ve been commissioner. We’ve had our differences in terms of your commissioning style. But as I think you remember, I won the championship this year.

That’s right. Anyways, thank you for the interview. It’s been a pleasure.

Because I was in Alan’s castle for a period of time during this season. We’re going to leave that out.

I’m sorry you lost this season. It’s been a pleasure speaking to you. I’ll see you, I don’t know…I’ll see you on my TV, I guess.

#6618. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6617. Sticky Miso Chicken

Miso, soy, and honey are a powerful trio, creating a savory marinade that could make just about anything sing (cod or salmon, broccoli or zucchini, tofu). Do have a keen eye on your chicken (especially if you have a drawer-style broiler at the bottom of your oven), checking it every so often to prevent a completely blackened cook.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: My Go-To Marinade for Chicken Is 3 Ingredients.

Heat broiler. Whisk ¼ cup honey, ¼ cup white miso, and 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a large bowl to combine. Add 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (the miso and soy sauce are plenty salty, so no need to season the chicken) and toss to coat. Arrange on wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet lined with foil and spoon any marinade remaining in bowl over. Broil chicken, turning halfway through, until cooked through and deeply charred in spots, 10–15 minutes (keep a close eye on it). Thinly slice chicken. Serve over steamed white rice, topped with thinly sliced scallions, if desired.

#6616. Sneak Inside GQ’s Breakouts Houseparty Deep in the Hollywood Hills

GQ’s Breakouts have officially broken containment. Last night, high up in the Hollywood hills, at one of LA’s most famous spots—the glass-and-concrete modernist sculpture known as the Sheats-Goldstein residence—GQ toasted to a new class of stars who spent 2026 commanding our attention.

First, they had to get in—down the palm-lined path, past the apple-red twin-engined car brought by presenting sponsor Hot Wheels, across the mildly perilous path over a koi pond—to a tucked-away den where GQ Editor-in-chief Adam Badawi quickly toasted the 13 Breakouts of 2026. “The double edged sword of success is that sometimes you’re so out-of-your mind busy and stressed and locked in, that you forget to enjoy it,” he told the room. “I hope you find a moment to enjoy it tonight.” And then he laid out the evening’s goals: have a hell of a house party. Everyone obliged.

GQ Breakouts Stavros Halkias and Pablo Torre huddled with Hasan Piker, who later chatted with Jake Shane, creating a powerful personality vortex. Amelia Dimoldenberg sipped an espresso martini at the bar in the house’s club. Breakout Belmont Cameli hung out poolside on the terrace, soaking up cinematic views of a glittering LA, while DJ Alice Longyu Gao played classic bangers like Drake and Future’s “Diamonds Dancing” filled the air. Later, towards the end of the night, two guests went rogue and got themselves escorted out for diving into the pool in their underwear. (In a shocking twist, it was not Stav, who had shouted “Cannonball!” earlier, by the house’s other pool.) Houseparty’s gonna houseparty.

When I found GQ Breakout Pablo Torre outside, he was showing off the incredible business card that house owner Jimmy Goldstein had given him just moments before. It was huge, about the size of an index card you used to study for algebra tests. Rare memorabilia.

Torre—who made the NBA’s life difficult with reporting that blew open the Kawhi Leonard scandal—joked to me that Clippers fandom is so tepid in LA that he hardly felt like he had to watch his back while in town from New York. (The biggest concern for his visit: a rainy forecast for the weekend.)

As Breakout AZ Chike told GQ for his portfolio interview, people “crossed worlds that hadn’t been crossed before.” Chike parlayed fellow Breakout Cameli early in the night before taking the stage a few hours later to run through heaters like “Packed Up” and “Look Like My Mama”—the same tracks that earned him GQ Breakout status. He told me he’s enjoying being back home in LA after touring his new album across the country, playing in new-for-him cities. Turns out DC showed an unexpected amount of love to a West Coast kid.

GQ Breakout Owen Thiele celebrated the season 3 renewal of Adults—announced earlier in the day—by zipping around the party armed with a disposable film camera. Watching him connect with True Whitaker of I Love LA felt like witnessing the cinematic crossover that we lowkey need to see play out on-screen.

Mavi, the North Carolina rapper who popped up in GQ’s September best new music portfolio, told me he’s finishing the project that he teased back then. He says he has so many songs in the tuck that he might thank his fans by dropping more than we’d expect.

Speaking of fresh music from new talents, Leon Thomas said he isn’t tripping expectations for his follow-up to the critically acclaimed, Grammy-winning “Mutt,” and previewed a project that’ll source inspiration from “p-funk, soul, and hip-hop.” Thomas was in the midst of rehearsing for an appearance at Tyler, The Creator’s Flog Gnaw festival this weekend, and joked that he got so sweaty during practice that we can expect him to tear it down on Saturday.

For the moment though, the weather was perfect, the music was hitting, the vibes were strong, and there was a lot more night left for partying. See how it all went down below. ✦

#6614. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6613. My Go-To Marinade for Chicken Is 3 Ingredients

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them.

By all logic I should be sick of this chicken. I have cooked it, give or take, a hundred times. When I don’t know what to make for dinner—or, honestly, don’t want to make dinner at all—it is there for me, like a gentle friend.

The marinade is deceptively simple: equal parts miso and honey, plus a glug of soy sauce. Nothing more. There’s no gotcha moment, no pepper hiding in plain sight or olive oil I forgot to account for. The flavor excels because each ingredient punches above its weight. Both fermented, the miso and soy sauce add umami depth, while honey supplies sweetness and makes the chicken glossy, like ceramics pulled straight from the kiln.

I’m often deflated when I see the word marinade in a recipe. No, I don’t have time for “at least an hour” or, more likely, the dreaded “preferably overnight.” Don’t they know it’s a Tuesday? This marinade, mercifully, is immediate. Because it is more of a paste than a liquid, you can slather it directly onto the chicken before hurling the baking sheet into the oven. (Of course, if you’re the type of person who has the wherewithal to start meal prep the night before, that works too.)

A short stint under the fierce heat of the broiler transforms the miso coating into a burnished, sticky crust in 15-ish minutes while you work on the rest of the meal. Old-school drawer-style broilers can get a little overexcited, so start peeking in after 10 minutes. Now is not the time to check the mail or start a load of laundry.

This chicken shines with rice tucked underneath, which catches every saucy streak. But you could build it out with roasted vegetables. Sometimes I’ll add oiled-up broccoli or asparagus to the baking sheet. Other times it’s just the chicken, with a shower of scallions if I’m feeling fancy. Then I make it all again next week.

#6612. The Best Advent Calendars for Crafters, Makers and Artists

Advent calendars for crafters come in a huge variety of options spanning crochet, coloring, clay and any other creative hobby you can think of!

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

For folks who love to spend a snowy day exploring their creativity, a craft Advent calendar is the perfect gift. Unlike classic Advent calendars, which contain chocolate or tea, these clever countdowns feature 12 to 24 days of fun activities to toil through when the brisk weather keeps you bundled up inside. And whether you’re shopping for men, women or kids, there’s an option out there for every hobby.

So grab your favorite faux fur blanket, pull up a seat, and turn on that imagination! Below are the best craft Advent calendars for artists, innovators and casual makers, tested by our editors.

I’m already a huge fan of the pottery kits at Pottd, so when I saw they offered a crafting Advent calendar, I just had to snag one. And let me tell you—testing the Pottd Advent calendar has been the highlight of my holiday season so far. From the outside in, the Pottd Advent Calendar is a truly magical 24-day experience. This year’s theme is Gingerbread Bakery. Inside the adorable gingerbread house calendar are 24 bakery-themed boxes, each containing a small craft.

While I won’t spoil all the surprises, inside is an assortment of fun hands-on projects, including air-dry clay creations, polymer clay miniatures, foam dough decorations and stands for displaying your creations. It also comes with all the tools, paints and accessories you need for each project. And if you need a little creative inspiration, each project also includes a QR code linking to a guided instructional video.

At $100, it’s definitely a bit of a splurge. But considering the craftsmanship and thought put into each project, I’d say the price is well worth it. This is one stunning Advent calendar—and the projects inside are bound to spark the spirit of the season!

Looking for a fiber-focused option? Snag the legendary The Woobles Advent calendar. This Advent calendar for crafters has everything you need to keep calm and stitch on. And no worries for newbies—The Woobles offer easy-to-follow video instructions for each kit, so you can learn a new skill as they craft some cute friends!

One of my favorite aspects of the yearly Woobles Advent calendar is its reusability. The calendar boxes themselves are historically cute and sturdy—I still keep craft items in my two boxes from previous years—but this year is even better! The holiday Victorian home design is absolutely swoon-worthy. Pulling out the day’s box reveals a cozy backdrop printed on the inside of the box, so you get a bonus surprise at the end of the countdown!

While the calendar has offered 24 days in previous years, this 12-day Advent calendar is still chock full of surprises. It’s also a lot more manageable to tackle eight projects instead of a full fleet of 20. Your recipient can open the first day on December 1 and take their time working through the projects instead of rushing through them, which I really appreciate.

Additionally, the boxes are printed with furniture for the home, so they double as play items. And as always, one of the days offers a collectible 2026 snow globe to add to their collection!

The Coco Wyo coloring book Advent calendar is your ticket to a cozy afternoon! With 24 mini coloring books stuffed with over 500 pages of adorable illustrations, your recipient is bound to enjoy hours of creative coloring magic.

Behind each door of this 24-day calendar is a themed coloring book, each filled with classic and newly drawn designs from Coco Wyo. Images feature calming activities, winter traditions and—of course—cute animals. The paper is nice and thick and the prints are clear, giving each book a high-quality feel.

The best part? Because they’re tiny, the coloring books are perfect for holiday travels. Just pick up a pack of markers or crayons and you have a cozy activity to tap into all season long!

This seasonally-appropriate Winter Sports Advent calendar from KiwiCo includes 12 DIY wooden craft ornament kits, offering a new activity every couple of days. Each one is a different Christmas character participating in a winter sport. Editor Mary Henn enjoyed putting together the ornaments with her daughter as a cute holiday bonding activity.

“Okay, this Advent calendar is such a unique and fun idea,” raves Mary. “My kiddo loved helping assemble a few of the ornaments during testing. Although the suggested age range is 5+ (likely due to the small parts), the instructions were simple to follow, and the assembly was easy enough for her to help with some of the projects!”

The bright, bold colors also make it fun and appealing for kids. Each kit is also individually wrapped, so there’s no loose pieces or missing materials. The packaging is thoughtfully designed with hidden doors, colorful pictures, and descriptions on the back. While it’s a little pricey at $50, the ornaments are well-made and should last for years.

“Each little wooden craft ornament is adorable,” raves Mary. “I especially love that some have movable parts, like spinning tops and sliding limbs, which make them even more fun and interactive.”

For folks who still appreciate the art of sending letters and documenting memos on paper, the Papier stationery Advent calendar is well worth the splurge. This luxury countdown is loaded with 24 desk delights that make crafting snail mail a dream. It truly checks all the boxes: luxurious, cohesive, joyful and, a personal favorite, practical.

“I loved last year’s letter-shaped calendar, but the design of the 2026 countdown is even better,” says Deputy Editor Katie Bandurski. “It’s a little more streamlined yet still oh-so impressive.”

When you lift the lid, you’re greeted with three drawers of perfectly packaged mini presents to open each day until Christmas. Each gift is exquisitely wrapped in thick paper in an array of cohesive yet distinct patterns.

“If you want an Advent calendar that feels like you’re truly opening a gift, rather than just pulling open a drawer, this is the best option I’ve seen in my years of testing,” says Katie.

This luxury calendar sells out almost every year, so we recommend ordering it as soon as you can. And if you miss out on the full-sized version (or want to spend a little less), Papier offers a 12-day version new for 2026!

LEGO Advent calendars are some of the best Advent calendars, hands down—and that’s not just my nostalgia talking. Unpacking this year’s LEGO City Advent calendar offered me the same magical experience I remember as a kid.

Behind each door is a variety of buildable toys, figures and accessories. Each and every day was fun to open, especially the days with builds inside them. The instructions are printed on the inside of the doors, so they’re rather simplistic. However, I found them overall thorough enough to figure things out.

Both my notoriously hard-to-please nephew and my millennial husband worked on the projects together. Their verdict? This was the best Advent calendar either had ever received! Believe me—there’s no better endorsement than that.

Here’s a gift for crafters, young and mature. This DIY ornament Advent calendar includes all the bells and whistles for designing their own felt Christmas tree ornaments. While it’s not set up like a traditional calendar—you won’t be opening any doors—the numbered craft kids prove to be exciting enough on their own.

Tester Katie Bandurski tried this Advent calendar and confirms that it’s fun for almost any age, but tots especially will benefit from the easy instructions. Plus—and this is a big one for parents—there’s no mess!

Kids craft 25 ornaments using felt and stickers—no sewing or glue required at all. And while each ornament has its own set of picture instructions, crafters can follow their heart and create something truly unique. The only thing to consider? They might need their own mini Christmas tree to show off their creations!

At Taste of Home, we’ve tried more than 100 calendars over the years, so we already have experience with many of the Advent calendars on the market. To find the best crafting Advent calendars, we drew from this existing pool of tested options. We then scoured the internet to see if there were any others worth ordering and testing.

From there, we did exactly what you’re supposed to do with Advent calendars—we opened them! After noting our unboxing experience, we took a closer look, examining technical details like shipping, packaging and value. We then assembled our crafts and noted any observations, including instruction clarity,

Craft Advent calendars are for everyone who enjoys making things. While some are geared towards kids or adults, many of the options we’ve tested work for almost everyone!

What’s inside a craft Advent calendar depends on the calendar you choose! There are tons of options available, from picks for painters to finds for fiber art fans. A crafting Advent calendar typically offers a new bite-sized craft or new crafting tool each day leading up to Christmas.

#6609. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6608. Anchovy-Garlic Pasta

Even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from said anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

Cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. Add 6 garlic cloves, finely grated, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Remove pan from heat.

Cook 12 oz. long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Gradually pour 1 cup pasta cooking liquid into anchovy mixture in pan, whisking constantly to incorporate. Place pan over high heat and bring sauce to a simmer. Add pasta and cook, tossing vigorously with tongs, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Remove pasta from heat and add 3 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Toss until butter is melted and pasta is coated and glossy, about 45 seconds. Add 1 cup coarsely chopped parsley, 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice and toss to combine, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep pasta saucy. Divide among shallow bowls to serve.

Babies may be small, but their wish lists are anything but simple. They speed through milestones overnight and grow by the minute, making baby gifting particularly challenging.

When my daughter was born, we were showered with gifts—from onesies to chic outfits, rainbow colored toys, and an endless amount of books. Whether it’s your first time gifting a new parent or you’re a seasoned pro, consider this your cheat sheet to gifting for the little ones. From newborn necessities to milestone-worthy finds, we’ve broken down the best gifts for each age and stage.

#6606. There's an Advent Calendar for (Almost) Everything

Souped-up Advent calendars are here to stay this holiday season, with just about every big player in food and beverage getting in on the trend.

Experts say there’s a mix of factors at play as for their rise in popularity: little treats and micro indulgences in an expensive world, the idea of “saving big” on high-value bundles, and the sensory satisfaction of unboxing 25(ish) little boxes leading up to Christmas.

“There’s something so special about having a small treat to look forward to each day,” Sockerbit Scandinavian candy founders Florence Baras and Stefan Ernberg said in a statement. Sockerbit is one of several newbies to the food Advent calendar space this year (and one of our new faves).

Advent Center, a hub for data and reviews for thousands of Advent calendars globally, says there are around 250 food and drink calendars on the market this year. The category makes up about a third of the 2026 calendars it lists.

Max Zeshut, Advent Center’s founder, said food and drink calendars work well because they’re a cheaper, noncommittal entry point into the ritual, compared to, for instance, a beauty box. And for all the new and zany iterations out there, chocolate calendars remain an anchor.

Broadly, the global Advent calendar market is anticipated to grow from $1.32 billion in 2024 to $2.47 billion by 2033, according to research compiled by Accio, a B2B platform. Food and drink calendars hold a huge share of that, with the help of mainstays like Bonne Maman, whose annual calendars have inspired “Jamvent” fan groups for a decade, alongside newcomers that announced inaugural calendars this season.

“As a small team, we try to be very conscious of the operational demands of every product launch,” Fishwife CEO and co-founder Becca Millstein told Bon Appétit. “Still, the demand [for calendars] grew too loud to ignore, so we decided to go for it.”

Millstein cited Fishwife’s success in the online gifting space as motivation to launch a calendar this year. Fishwife’s includes 12 doors of tinned fish and extras, retailing for $150. The company said the calendar’s “elements of surprise and delight” drives chatter and user-generated content on social media.

“In the end, we simply had to do it,” Millstein said.

When the Sichuan condiment company Fly By Jing’s Advent calendar launched in 2024, it sold out in about a month. That’s when founder Jing Gao knew the brand was onto something.

Gao said that 65% of its Advent calendars were purchased by new customers this year and that historically, 20% of customers who purchase a calendar go on to make another Fly By Jing purchase by the end of the year.

“To me, that really speaks to the power of discovery and giving people a chance to explore our flavors in a fun, unexpected way,” Gao said. “We never want that sense of discovery to go away, even for people who have been with us from the beginning. It's become such a fun creative outlet for our team. I think that joy really comes through in the experience.”

The stewards at Onyx Coffee Lab in Arkansas describe a similar phenomenon. “There's so much storytelling, education, and human connection surrounding coffee, and Advent gives us a unique opportunity to explore those things in ways that might not make sense within our everyday offerings,” Onyx’s co-founder Andrea Allen said. Their box features 24 different coffees, each a 56-gram package of whole beans that are roasted on a schedule for peak brewing by their respective reveal day.

At Bonne Maman, Advent calendar planning starts two years in advance. The development team pays close attention to seasonal ingredients and market trends to produce 24 limited-edition jams and spreads made just for the calendar. The result sells out every year, with production growing by 400% since 2017, according to a spokesperson. This year will mark 10 years of the Bonne Maman Advent calendar.

“We’re grateful to the fans who have made it part of their holidays,” a company spokesperson said. “On social media, we see everything from matcha pairings and coffee creations to new takes on toast, along with plenty of flavor-by-flavor reviews. Many fans also write to us to tell us which flavor they loved most. It helps us decide which flavors should return or come in larger sizes.”

Have we stretched Advent calendar hype to its absolute limits? Advent Center’s Zeshut says no.

“The clearest sign of demand is that people search for calendars that don't exist,” he said. “There's no official Monster Energy calendar this year, and 'monster Advent calendar' is still one of the most searched terms that brings people to our site,” he said. “I don't think we've reached peak calendar, but we may have reached peak chocolate.”

#6605. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6604. Why I’m Still Turning to Oils for Thinning Hair

Much like the internal debate over whether to get curtain bangs or dramatically chop off all your hair into a bob, there comes a point in everyone’s life when they start considering using an oil for thinning hair. Personally, I started my own hair-oil journey after noticing sparse patches along my hairline. Many have praised these natural oils for their ability to not only treat breakage and damage but also to help hair grow back. So I figured, why not try these so-called hair miracle products?

While I personally noticed an improvement in my hair density, experts say to temper your expectations. “It is important to recognize that not all oils have been clinically proven to stimulate new hair growth,” says Marisa Garshick, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at MDCS Dermatology. “Rosemary oil and pumpkin seed oil have some preliminary research supporting their potential benefits, while others—such as castor, argan, and jojoba oils—are more beneficial for moisturizing the scalp, strengthening the hair shaft, and reducing breakage.”

Corinne Erickson, MD, a board-certified dermatologist and founder of Georgia Skin Specialists, considers them “adjuncts to medical management for hair loss, not stand-alone solutions. While topical minoxidil remains the gold standard for thinning hair, there are several oils with early data showing help for hair thinning that are generally safe when used as directed.”

Generally speaking, many hair oils are safe when used as directed, though some can cause irritation or allergic reactions. You may want to use them alongside other nourishing hair products for the best results. With all that in mind, these are the best oils to consider for thinning hair.

Of all the hair oils, rosemary is the most promising for thinning hair. Dr. Garshick explains that rosemary oil’s anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties may support scalp health, and she cites studies suggesting it may help with pattern hair loss. Although evidence remains limited, she points to one small study in which rosemary oil produced similar improvements in hair count to 2% minoxidil after six months.

She and Dr. Erickson recommend Mielle’s Rosemary Mint Scalp & Hair Strengthening Oil, which mixes rosemary oil with castor oil, jojoba oil, and other botanical ingredients to treat breakage and nourish the scalp. “[It] is an easy, affordable option,” says Dr. Erickson. If you’re looking for something lighter, you can also try Dr. Groot’s Scalp Hair Thickening Serum, a serum made with rosemary, biotin, and caffeine designed to support scalp health and fuller-looking hair.

Dr. Garshick says that pumpkin seed oil contains phytosterols and fatty acids, which preliminary research suggests may inhibit DHT, a hormone implicated in pattern hair loss. “This may help explain [pumpkin seed oil’s] potential benefits for hair growth,” she says. However, much of the clinical evidence involves oral pumpkin seed oil supplements rather than topical applications, so it remains unclear whether applying the oil directly to the scalp provides the same benefits.

Dr. Erickson likes the Leven Rose Organic Pumpkin Seed Oil, which is pure and cold-pressed, with no fragrance or additives. “Promising, though not yet proven,” she says. You can also consider something like SVA Organic Pumpkin Seed Oil, another cold-pressed option you can easily massage into your hair as a pre-shampoo treatment.

Castor oil is another popular oil used in hair-growth treatments. Dr. Garshick says that although there isn’t strong scientific evidence that castor oil affects hair growth, it can help nourish your hair and scalp. She says that it is rich in a fatty acid called ricinoleic acid, which is known to add moisture and condition to the skin and your strands. “It may help reduce dryness and breakage, which can make the hair appear thicker and healthier over time,” she says.

Try something like the Fable & Mane HoliRoots Hair Oil, a pre-shampoo treatment that mixes castor oil with ashwagandha, an antioxidant-rich berry called amla, and a plant-root blend designed to strengthen strands and soothe the scalp. You can also try the Carol’s Daughter Goddess Strength 7 Oil Blend Hair & Scalp Oil, which blends castor oil with black cumin seed and six other nourishing oils to hydrate the scalp and treat breakage.

Avocado oil contains fatty acids and vitamin E, which can help moisturize and condition the hair. While there aren’t studies showing avocado oil directly stimulates hair growth, it may help create a healthy environment for hair to thrive. “By helping support a healthy scalp environment and strengthen the hair shaft, it may help hair appear fuller and healthier while minimizing breakage that can contribute to the appearance of thinning,” Dr. Garshick agrees.

She likes Kiehl’s Magic Elixir, a pre-shampoo treatment that combines avocado oil with rosemary leaf and safflower oil to moisturize the scalp and alleviate dryness. “It is especially useful for those looking to incorporate scalp care into their routine,” she adds, “while improving hair manageability, smoothness, and shine without adding another leave-in product.” You can also try the Grow Good Everything Serum, which has a nourishing mix of oils (avocado, coconut, sunflower seed, and more) to seal the cuticle and prevent split ends and breakage.

Argan oil is extremely nourishing for hair; it contains vitamin E, fatty acids, and antioxidants that protect hair from environmental aggressors that cause damage, keeping hair feeling smooth and hydrated. Dr. Garshick says that although it hasn’t been proven to stimulate hair growth, it can improve hair softness, reduce frizz, and minimize breakage, which helps hair retain length and appear fuller.

She recommends something like the Augustinus Bader The Hair Oil, which combines argan oil with vitamin E, baobab and pomegranate oils, and a special complex that smooths out frizz and treats breakage so hair looks—and feels—healthier and fuller. You can also try SheaMoisture’s 100% Argan Oil, which, as the name suggests, is made of pure argan oil to nourish and restore dry and damaged hair.

Are There Any Downsides to Using Oils for Thinning Hair?

Dr. Garshick says that while hair oils can help with dryness, breakage, or scalp issues, they might not be the best solution for hair thinning. She explains that some oils can cause irritation or an allergic reaction, while heavier oils can cause buildup or worsen scalp conditions.

“It is also important to remember that hair loss can have many causes,” she adds. Genetics, hormonal changes, nutritional deficiencies, and medical conditions could all be reasons your hair is thinning, so you may need a more effective treatment. For those noticing persistent shedding, a widening part, or thinning that is progressively getting worse, she recommends seeing a board-certified dermatologist to identify the cause and get the right treatment.

How Do You Use Hair Oils for Thinning Hair?

Dr. Erickson says you must always dilute essential oils in a carrier oil (like jojoba) to reduce the risk of scalp irritation. If you’re prone to flaking or scalp conditions like seborrheic dermatitis, she recommends skipping oils altogether.

You’ll generally just massage in your oil of choice to stimulate circulation on your scalp. Start slowly to see how your hair and scalp tolerate it, then increase frequency up to a few times a week. Dr. Garshick says dermarolling may help by creating micro-injuries that activate wound-healing pathways and growth factors, promoting healthy hair growth. But you’ll want to be careful, as there’s a risk of irritation, allergic reactions, and inflammation. So when in doubt, ask your doctor.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional insight into the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

For oils for thinning hair, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: oil type, featured ingredients, texture, ease of application, finish, and the hair-care concerns they address.
